name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Secretary of state candidate Ryan Peterman calls for election changes
description: Democratic secretary of state candidate Ryan Peterman said Saturday he believes recent changes to Iowa election law dealing with early voting and voter identification do not make Iowa elections more secure — but do make elections less accessible. Peterman, who is challenging incumbent Republican Secretary of State Paul Pate in the 2026 election, gave a […]
text:
Ryan Peterman, the Democrat running for Iowa Secretary of State in the midterm election, spoke at the Des Moines Register Political Soapbox Aug. 15, 2026 at the Iowa State Fair. (Photo by Robin Opsahl/Iowa Capital Dispatch)Democratic secretary of state candidate Ryan Peterman said Saturday he believes recent changes to Iowa election law dealing with early voting and voter identification do not make Iowa elections more secure — but do make elections less accessible.
Peterman, who is challenging incumbent Republican Secretary of State Paul Pate in the 2026 election, gave a speech at the Des Moines Register Political Soapbox at the Iowa State Fair, where he called for Iowans to elect a secretary of state who “knows who they work for.”
The Democratic candidate, a former naval officer, criticized his opponent for sharing voter registration data, including personally identifiable information like driver’s license and Social Security numbers, with the U.S. Department of Justice. Pate had announced in May that Iowa complied with the DOJ request after consulting with the secretary of state’s legal team and the Iowa Attorney General’s Office, which found that the U.S. attorney general had the power to demand this information.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
In a statement, Pate said, “we do not take the obligation to turn this information over lightly. The Department of Justice has assured us that the data will be protected appropriately under federal law, and we expect them to uphold that promise.”

Candidates speak at Register Soapbox
Saturday was the second day of candidate speeches at The Des Moines Register Political Soapbox at the state fair. Here’s the schedule.
Read about previous speakers:
Republican gubernatorial candidate: Zach Lahn
Democratic U.S. Senate candidate: Josh Turek
Libertarian U.S. Senate candidate: Thomas Laehn
Independent 1st Congressional District candidate: Michael Bridgford
Republican 2nd Congressional District candidate: Joe Mitchell
Independent 2nd District Congressional District candidate:  Dave Bushaw
Libertarian 2nd District Congressional candidate: Rick Stewart
Democratic 3rd Congressional District candidate: Sarah Trone Garriott
Democratic state treasurer candidate: John Norwood

Peterman told fairgoers that Pate was not required to take this action, because secretaries of state and attorneys general in other states had refused the DOJ demand for voter information. The DOJ has challenged in court the decision of 30 states to not share voter, and so far 20 of the cases have been dismissed, according to the Brennan Center for Justice. In July, the Democratic candidate filed four public records requests to obtain more information about what data Iowa provided to the DOJ.
He called for Iowans to choose a secretary of state in the 2026 general election who ensures “every eligible voter has an opportunity to cast a ballot, has an opportunity to make their voice heard, has a say in choosing the leaders who shape the future of our state and the future of our country.”
Peterman also criticized measures passed by the GOP-controlled Iowa Legislature in recent years to shorten the state’s early voting window to 20 days, saying he does not believe the shorter early voting window improved Iowa’s election system.
“The same amount of work has to be done, we have shorter amount of time to do it,” Peterman said. “Ballots need to be ready further in advance anyway, so we can apply the federal voting rules for overseas troops — so I don’t see who benefits. I don’t think it improves security, it just hinders accessibility. And I think we have to make sure that we’re focused on doing both.”
He said he was “not so naive as to believe that I can unilaterally change that on my own, but I will advocate to the Legislature to make (the early voting window) as long as we can” if elected to the office.
He also criticized a 2026 law removing the ability for a voter to confirm their identity through a fellow voter’s attestation, and would advocate for bringing back this way to confirm a person’s identity. He said there was “no evidence of fraud being committed because of attestation.”

title: Libertarian wants to repeal income tax, welfare programs, immigration policy
description: Rick Stewart, a Libertarian running for Iowa’s 2nd Congressional District, said Saturday that he wants to end income taxes, overhaul the nation’s immigration policy and replace government assistance programs with a universal basic income.  Stewart also called for a universal carbon tax and to “eliminate” all nuclear weapons.  Stewart is running against Repub[...]
text:
Rick Stewart, a Libertarian candidate running in Iowa's 2nd Congressional District spoke Aug. 15, 2026 at the Des Moines Register Political Soapbox. (Photo by Cami Koons/Iowa Capital Dispatch)Rick Stewart, a Libertarian running for Iowa’s 2nd Congressional District, said Saturday that he wants to end income taxes, overhaul the nation’s immigration policy and replace government assistance programs with a universal basic income. 
Stewart also called for a universal carbon tax and to “eliminate” all nuclear weapons. 
Stewart is running against Republican Joe Mitchell, Democrat Lindsay James and independent candidate Dave Bushaw, who spoke earlier in the day. It is an open race as current U.S. Rep. Ashley Hinson pursues a bid for the U.S. Senate. 
Stewart, who lives in Cedar Rapids, has run for office several times, as a Libertarian candidate for governor in 2022, for U.S. Senate in 2020 and in 2018 for Iowa secretary of agriculture.
“The one thing you should not do is you should not vote for a Republican or a Democrat,” Stewart said. 
When asked what sets him apart from Bushaw, who is also running against the major party candidates, Stewart said “45 years of experience.” 
Five policies that ‘won’t cost a nickel’ 
Stewart explained five policy priorities, which he said would not cost more than existing programs already cost. 
First, he called for an elimination of nuclear weapons, because he said they are an “existential threat” to the nation and “nobody needs them.” 
Next, he said he would do away with all income tax, which he said has complex regulations that end up being “just a place where politicians can pass laws.” 
Instead of income tax, Stewart suggested a land tax, which would be levied on top of property tax, based on the value of the land. 
“So income taxes are the worst conceivable idea,” Stewart said. “A land tax is the most fair tax of all.” 
The land tax, he argued, would be easier to understand, and pay, compared to the current income tax program. 
Stewart’s third policy point was an overhaul the current immigration policy that he said “costs a lot of money and makes a lot of people angry.” 
Instead, Stewart suggested a system that allows vetted immigrants to bid for lifetime green cards in an auction system to enter the country. He said refugee and humanitarian cases for immigration should be decided by U.S. citizens, rather than the government. 


Candidates speak at Register Soapbox
Saturday was the second day of candidate speeches at The Des Moines Register Political Soapbox at the state fair. Here’s the schedule.
Read about previous speakers:
Republican gubernatorial candidate: Zach Lahn
Democratic U.S. Senate candidate: Josh Turek
Libertarian U.S. Senate candidate: Thomas Laehn
Independent 1st Congressional District candidate: Michael Bridgford
Republican 2nd Congressional District candidate: Joe Mitchell
Independent 2nd Congressional District candidate:  Dave Bushaw
Democratic 3rd Congressional District candidate: Sarah Trone Garriott
Democratic state treasurer candidate: John Norwood


Stewart, who said he spends part of his year in Guatemala, said his immigration reform would also allow “anyone who’s not an actual criminal” to purchase a visa to visit the U.S. 
“That’s what we need to do here in America, is an immigration system that’s fair, honest, and makes money,” Stewart said. 
He also said a universal tax on carbon would help to reduce carbon emissions, which contribute to global warming. The money collected by the carbon tax, Stewart said, would then be passed along to everyone living in a participating country. The carbon tax rebates, as he called them, would be spread on a per capita basis. The citizen demand to receive the rebates, he argued, would push countries to participate in the carbon tax program. 
“This will work because it gives people the incentive to do the right thing,” Stewart said.
Stewart said that current programs, especially Social Security and Medicare, represent “income transfers” between people who are “relatively poor and working to people who are relatively wealthy and not working.” 
By redirecting payroll taxes from Social Security and Medicare and funding from other government assistance programs, Stewart argued the nation could supply a “universal basic income” to all citizens. 
“So this system is, practically, 100% funded already, and it will guarantee that the only thing that happens is relatively wealthy people will give money to relatively poor people,” Stewart said. 
He explained the universal basic income would be distributed monthly to every citizen 18 years and older, regardless of total income or work status. 
With the universal basic income, he said the nation needs to “eliminate every single welfare program in the entire country” including school lunch vouchers, or farm subsidies for example.  
“I happen to be very passionate about government,” Stewart said in closing. “The one we have is not the one we want. Vote for me because if you vote for a Democrat or a Republican, all you’re doing is you’re voting to perpetuate the current system.”

text:
Michael Bridgford, an independent candidate running in Iowa's 1st Congressional District spoke Aug. 15, 2026 at the Des Moines Register Political Soapbox. (Photo by Cami Koons/Iowa Capital Dispatch) Michael Bridgford said Saturday at the Des Moines Register Political Soapbox that a couple of independent candidates, like him, in the U.S. House would be able to “push” for votes on issues like term limits, campaign finance reform, and chamber leadership. 
Bridgford is running as an independent candidate in Iowa’s 1st Congressional District against Republican incumbent Mariannette Miller-Meeks and Democratic candidate Christina Bohannan. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Bridgford said he is a candidate for 1st District voters who are “frustrated” with Congress. 
“People feel as though they’re not being represented, they’re not being heard, and we’re going to change that this year,” Bridgford said. 
According to a Gallup poll from January, 45% of U.S. voters identified as independent in 2025. Bridgford said there is a “national movement” currently to support independent candidates. 
Michael Bridgford, an independent candidate running in Iowa’s 1st Congressional District, spoke Aug. 15, 2026 at the Des Moines Register Political Soapbox. (Photo by Cami Koons/Iowa Capital Dispatch)
Iowa’s 1st Congressional District is one of the less than 20 “toss-up” districts for the House. 
The major-party candidates, Miller-Meeks and Bohannan, faced off in 2024, when Bohannan lost to the incumbent by about 800 votes.
“When Iowa 1 sends an independent to Congress, it’ll be the most important district in this country,” Bridgford said. 
Affordability, agriculture and healthcare 
Bridgford, who is a small business owner from the Quad-Cities region, said affordability, agriculture and healthcare policies are some of his top priorities. 
He said the affordability crisis is driven largely by increases to the country’s money supply and a lack of consistency in trade policies. 

Candidates speak at Register Soapbox
Saturday was the second day of candidate speeches at The Des Moines Register Political Soapbox at the state fair. Here’s the schedule.
Read about previous speakers:
Republican gubernatorial candidate: Zach Lahn
Democratic U.S. Senate candidate: Josh Turek
Libertarian U.S. Senate candidate: Thomas Laehn
Republican 2nd Congressional District candidate: Joe Mitchell
Independent 2nd Congressional District candidate:  Dave Bushaw
Democratic 3rd Congressional District candidate: Sarah Trone Garriott
Democratic state treasurer candidate: John Norwood

Bridgford also said he would push for proposals like price transparency and pharmacy benefit managers reform to help address the high healthcare costs. 
When asked if he would have voted for Republican’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which made significant reforms to various programs, including Medicaid, Bridgford said he would have tried to “leverage” his position to “make it better for the average person versus just people at the very top.”
Bridgford said he grew up during the farm crisis of the 1980s, when his family lost their hog farm. 
“Unfortunately, our farmers now are approaching a similar type of crisis to the 1980s, and the politicians are playing political football with ag policy,” Bridgford said and referenced the stalled progress on a new farm bill. 
Bridgford said farmers need a new farm bill with year-round, nationwide E15 and more support for family farmers. 
Speaking with reporters after the Soapbox, Bridgford said he was not supportive of certain Republican policies, like the Save Our Bacon Act, which would block states from stipulating how livestock are raised. 
Bridgford said he is his campaign’s biggest donor and that he is in the race for the “right reason.” 
“The parties, they just want to fight,” Bridgford said. “They’re not interested in actually solving the problem.”

title: Dave Bushaw calls for building political independent ‘movement’ in Iowa
description: Independent congressional candidate Dave Bushaw asked for Iowans’ support Saturday at the Iowa State Fair as he works to build an “independent movement” past the 2026 election season throughout the state. Bushaw is running as an independent candidate in Iowa’s 2nd Congressional District, but has a history in Democratic politics, having worked as an organizer[...]
text:
Dave Bushaw, an Independent candidate running in Iowa's 2nd Congressional District, spoke at the Des Moines Register Political Soapbox Aug. 15, 2026 at the Iowa State Fair. (Photo by Robin Opsahl/Iowa Capital Dispatch)Independent congressional candidate Dave Bushaw asked for Iowans’ support Saturday at the Iowa State Fair as he works to build an “independent movement” past the 2026 election season throughout the state.
Bushaw is running as an independent candidate in Iowa’s 2nd Congressional District, but has a history in Democratic politics, having worked as an organizer for U.S. Sen. Bernie Sanders’ presidential campaign during the 2020 Democratic presidential nominating cycle. But during his speech at the Des Moines Register Political Soapbox, he criticized both the Democratic and Republican parties as “two wings of the same bird that feed corporate greed,” which he said do not represent working class Americans.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“The hard truth, folks, is that this freedom isn’t going to be won within the corrupt two-party establishment,” Bushaw said. “I became the first no-party candidate to secure ballot access in northeast Iowa in modern history because working-class voters wanted it to be that way.”
Bushaw will appear on the ballot with Democratic state Rep. Lindsay James and Republican Joe Mitchell, a former state lawmaker. The 2nd District is an open race, as current U.S. Rep. Ashley Hinson is on the ballot as the GOP nominee for Iowa’s U.S. Senate seat.
While the seat is expected to be less competitive than the congressional races for Iowa’s 1st and 3rd Districts, according to political forecasters, Democrats still hope the seat could be a potential pick-up in the midterms.

Candidates speak at Register Soapbox
Saturday was the second day of candidate speeches at The Des Moines Register Political Soapbox at the state fair. Here’s the schedule.
Read about previous speakers:
Republican gubernatorial candidate: Zach Lahn
Democratic U.S. Senate candidate: Josh Turek
Libertarian U.S. Senate candidate: Thomas Laehn
Republican 2nd Congressional District candidate: Joe Mitchell
Democratic 3rd Congressional District candidate: Sarah Trone Garriott
Democratic state treasurer candidate: John Norwood

Bushaw said his campaign did not have party infrastructure in the 2nd District, which covers much of northeast Iowa, or the financial support his major-party opponents have, but said his campaign came to the race with a small amount of money and “folks that were ready to fight.” Bushaw reported raising $12,555 in the most recent Federal Election Commission reporting period, falling below James, who raised $755,587 and Mitchell, who raised $377,769.
“While the media often fixates on enormous amounts of money raised and spent by these candidates in the Democratic and Republican Party — which I find more disgusting than impressive — we’re showing that working-class poor folks can build infrastructure and run a strong campaign without money backing them,” he said. “That’s called fiscal responsibility, and it’s a foreign concept to most politicians.”
While he called for voters in the 2nd District to support his campaign for Congress, he also said he plans to build a greater independent “movement” in future election cycles.
“This doesn’t stop in 2026,” Bushaw said. “I’ve been organizing for 15 years. … I intend on starting here in the 2nd District, but we are going to build an independent movement here in Iowa in all districts and across this country — 2028, 2030, and 2032. That’s a promise.”
If elected in 2026, the first measure he would introduce would be to allow for national ballot initiatives that would allow U.S. voters to directly weigh in on certain measures at the federal level, like the legalization of cannabis and campaign finance reform.
“There’s 435 members in Congress right now, and almost all of them are completely bought out by the corrupt two-party duo. I believe that representative democracy, in some facets, has outlived its usefulness. These aren’t the days of horse and buggy, when you had to send a ballot box on a you know, all the way across from Oregon to Washington (D.C.) — we all have cell phones, we all have computers. We’re hyper connected. I believe and I trust the American people to make decisions ourselves. … I trust the American people to make the right decisions on these things, so I want to give more direct democracy power to the American working people.”

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Libertarian Thomas Laehn says end federal tax credits for pipelines
description: Thomas Laehn, the Libertarian running for Iowa’s U.S. Senate seat, said Saturday at the Iowa State Fair he would eliminate federal tax incentives for carbon dioxide sequestration and production of low-carbon fuels if elected. Carbon sequestration pipeline projects have been a major point of contention in Iowa for years. They’ve also been a source of […]
text:
Libertarian Thomas Laehn, running for Iowa's U.S. Senate seat in 2026, gave a speech at the Des Moines Register Political Soapbox Aug. 15, 2026 at the Iowa State Fair. (Photo by Robin Opsahl/Iowa Capital Dispatch)Thomas Laehn, the Libertarian running for Iowa’s U.S. Senate seat, said Saturday at the Iowa State Fair he would eliminate federal tax incentives for carbon dioxide sequestration and production of low-carbon fuels if elected.
Carbon sequestration pipeline projects have been a major point of contention in Iowa for years. They’ve also been a source of internal conflicts within the Iowa Republican Party, with conservatives voicing differing opinions at the Iowa Capitol about the use of eminent domain in building pipelines.
Laehn currently serves as the Greene County attorney. He said during his speech at the Des Moines Register Political Soapbox he was approached by Iowa House lawmakers to draft legislation to stop the use of eminent domain, particularly in response to the carbon sequestration pipeline project led by Summit Carbon Solutions.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
That measure, which Laehn said he helped write, made it through the Iowa House and Senate in 2025 with “a lot more provisions than my original language.” Gov. Kim Reynolds vetoed the bill. Laehn said the governor vetoed the legislation — despite polls showing a majority of Iowans oppose the use of eminent domain for the construction of hazardous liquid pipelines. Laehn pointed out Reynolds had received campaign contributions from Bruce Rastetter, the founder of Summit Agricultural Group and co-founder of Summit Carbon Solutions.
“Now, this is all happened at the state level,” Laehn said. “I’m running for the United States Senate, so why am I talking about state politics?”
He said special-interest influence is “occurring in Washington, D.C., at an even larger scale.”

Candidates speak at Register SoapboxSaturday was the second day of candidate speeches at The Des Moines Register Political Soapbox at the state fair. Here’s the schedule.Read about previous speakers:Republican gubernatorial candidate: Zach LahnDemocratic U.S. Senate candidate: Josh TurekRepublican 2nd Congressional District candidate: Joe MitchellDemocratic 3rd Congressional District candidate: Sarah Trone GarriottDemocratic state treasurer candidate: John Norwood

Laehn brought up an article by the left-leaning outlet Iowa Starting Line stating Rastetter was “bankrolling Hinson” in the 2026 election. He linked this campaign finance information to Hinson’s support for 45Q tax credits, a tax credit incentivizing carbon sequestration which gives a credit of $85 per metric ton of CO2 to qualifying projects — a credit he said would mean billions “will be deposited into the accounts of Bruce Rastetter and his investors (of) our taxpayer money.”
“She’s also a proponent of sections 45Q and 45Z of the IRS tax code. When I’m elected to the United States Senate, one of the first pieces of legislation I will introduce will be to eliminate sections 45Q and 45Z of the IRS tax code, and then the funding for this boondoggle of a project evaporates, and the project collapses.”
Th Hinson campaign did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Rastetter has been a longtime supporter and financial backer of many Iowa Republican candidates. He has interests in several agriculture and energy industries in addition to the carbon pipeline.
Laehn also criticized 45Z tax credits for domestically produced fuels with lifecycle greenhouse gas emissions below a certain level that could also go toward some ultra-low carbon ethanol plants that would be connected to pipeline projects. Politico reported Hinson, alongside fellow Iowa Republican U.S. Rep. Mariannette Miller-Meeks, wrote a letter supporting preservation of these tax credits in 2025.
Iowa’s U.S. Senate seat is an open race this year, as U.S. Sen. Joni Ernst, who currently holds the position, is not seeking reelection. Laehn faces Hinson, the Republican candidate, and Democratic Iowa Rep. Josh Turek in the general election. Political forecasters rate the race as “leans Republican,” which election watchers say means the race is more competitive than Iowa U.S. Senate races in previous recent election cycles.
The Libertarian candidate said he was also critical of Turek because a super PAC, VoteVets, spent money to advertise on his behalf, and because the Senate Majority PAC, a Democratic organization, plans to spend $17 million in Iowa on ads focused on the U.S. Senate race.
“If Ashley is elected, she will owe her office and her allegiance to the Republican Party and the interest groups and economic elites who are funding her campaign,” Laehn said. “If Josh Turek is elected, he will owe his office and his allegiance to the Democratic Party and the economic elites who are funding his campaign. When I’m elected to the United States Senate, I will owe my office and my allegiance to all of you, to the people of the state of Iowa.”
Turek counters criticism that he is closely aligned with party insiders, arguing that he would work across party lines for Iowans’ interests. In his Soapbox speech Friday, he criticized U.S. Senate Democrats for withholding their vote on a farm bill.
Laehn was the first Libertarian to hold an elected partisan office in Iowa, according to his campaign website, winning his election to become Greene County attorney in 2018 and winning reelection in 2022. Unlike other Iowa Libertarian candidates, Laehn did not face challenges to his qualifications for ballot access in 2026.
Laehn said when he learned other Libertarian candidates faced challenges to their place on the general election ballot, his wife told him, “it shouldn’t take a law degree and a Ph.D. to figure out how to get on the ballot” — qualifications Laehn has. He also criticized the Iowa Legislature for making changes to state law that he said make it more difficult for candidates unaffiliated with major political parties to make it onto the ballot.
“What this really shows is how the two parties have entrenched themselves in Des Moines and in Washington D.C. and have erected all of these barriers and obstacles to third-party and independent candidates,” Laehn said.

name: Maryland Matters
title: Moore and Cox differ on data centers at Maryland conference
description: GOP gubernatorial nominee Dan Cox has latched on to data centers for his campaign, saying at a forum Saturday it's a "big difference between Wes Moore and me." Cox wants a statewide moratorium, but Moore wants tighter regulation and more local control.
text:
Dan Cox, the Republican nominee for Maryland governor, speaks during a candidate forum at the Maryland Association of Counties conference on August 15, 2026. (Photo by Christine Condon/ Maryland Matters)As two-time Republican nominee for Maryland governor Dan Cox (R) puts it, hyperscale data centers are a “big difference between Wes Moore and me.”
One among many.
Cox has called for a statewide moratorium banning hyperscalers, and has targeted Moore on one project in particular: a project proposed in Charles County by TeraWulf, which recently received federal approval to purchase a retired coal plant that it plans to use for the project.
During his remarks Saturday at a statewide candidates’ forum at the Maryland Association of Counties summer conference in Ocean City, Cox highlighted a pair of $6,000 donations that Moore received in 2025 from TeraWulf’s founder and his wife, according to state campaign finance records.
“The governor has a scandal, folks. He accepted a $12,000 donation to his campaign from the owner of TeraWulf, and then gave a power plant, the Morgantown power plant in Charles County, to that data center hyperscale developer,” Cox said.
Maryland Gov. Wes Moore (D) delivers remarks at the Maryland Association of Counties summer conference Saturday. Moore is running for reelection in November. (Photo by Christine Condon/Maryland Matters)
TeraWulf reached a deal with plant owner GenOn Holdings, and that deal was approved by the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission. But Moore’s administration has signaled its support for the project, including in a letter from the Maryland Department of the Environment, which pledged to assist the data center developer with running natural gas pipelines to the power plant site, first reported by the Baltimore Banner.
“Folks, we need a [data center] moratorium. I will institute it immediately so that we can study this,” Cox said. “It’s also outdated technology. We all know that Elon Musk is building these in stars. We also know that China is putting them at the bottom of the ocean.”
Moore was the first to the podium during Saturday’s event, which featured a round-robin of candidates for governor, comptroller and attorney general. Because candidates appeared separately, Moore did not have an opportunity to respond to Cox’s remarks at the podium.
The governor’s staff did not immediately respond to a request for comment Saturday afternoon. But the governor spoke about the importance of careful data center regulation in Maryland.
“Virginia has the largest concentration of data centers — not in the United States, in the world — and the way they did it there cannot and will not happen in the state of Maryland,” Moore said.
A recent poll found the governor with a comfortable 27-point lead over Cox, slightly smaller than his 32-point margin of victory over Cox, who was also the GOP nominee four years ago.
Moore also repeated what is becoming a common refrain of his: That any data centers in Maryland ought to bring their own energy, pay for their own infrastructure improvements, hire local union labor and meet environmental regulations. But Moore maintained that local officials should have the power to say no. Many major jurisdictions, both red and blue, have instituted temporary moratoriums of late.
Maryland Gov. Wes Moore (D) delivers remarks Saturday at the Maryland Association of Counties summer conference. (Photo by Christine Condon/Maryland Matters)
“If there is a local jurisdiction that does not want it, guess what? It will not go there, because local jurisdictions need to have a final say,” Moore said amid applause from the audience at the conference, which is geared toward county government officials in the state.
The forum also featured other candidates for statewide office. Comptroller Brooke Lierman (D) faced off against her opponent Sonya Dunn (R), a businesswoman and political newcomer who faces an uphill battle in deep blue Maryland. So, too, does attorney James B. Rutledge III (R), Attorney General Anthony Brown’s opponent in November. Brown, however, did not appear at Saturday’s forum.
Unsurprisingly, Cox came out swinging  at Saturday’s panel, which was moderated by Maryland Matters reporter Bryan P. Sears and Mileah Kromer, the director of the University of Maryland Baltimore County Institute of Politics. Cox opened his remarks by criticizing the sitting governor over residents who are choosing to leave the state for other states, arguing that two of his eldest children have also left the state due to affordability issues.
An October report from the comptroller’s office found that the state is losing an average of 40,000 people each year to states with lower housing costs.
“These are Marylanders. They’re citizens, and they said that they’re not going to be serfs of Wes Moore’s Annapolis,” Cox said Saturday.
When data centers come knocking, counties should have a ‘wish list,’ officials say

Moore, for his part, argued that the federal government under President Donald Trump (R) has played a major role in undermining the state economy, by firing government employees who live in Maryland, restricting or rescinding federal aid dollars and more.
“The budget gap exists for for two reasons,” Moore said. “It exists because for too long we have relied too much on the federal government, and it exists because we were spending more than we were growing.”
Moore touted that his administration has presented a balanced budget, as required, during each of his four years in office, and he pledged to diversify the state’s economy and control spending if reelected. Moore also touted improvements in Maryland since he took office, including a dramatic decline in homicides in Baltimore and reductions in vacant housing units in Maryland’s largest city.
“I came here four years ago — that was actually the first time that for many of you I got a chance to meet you. I did not come from the world of politics. I was coming to say that we were going to change that relationship between our state and our locals. That we’re going to strengthen it. We were  going to move in partnership,” Moore said. “Four years later, I can say that we’ve kept our word.”

name: Daily Montanan
title: Lawmakers sue AG, SOS over term limit decision
description: Two Republican lawmakers filed a lawsuit Friday over a term limit decision made by Attorney General Austin Knudsen this week that would remove them from the ballot in November. The legal action comes as the state Republican Party is preparing to replace the candidates on the ballot, barring a judge’s intervention.  Montana lawmakers are limited to […]
text:
The dome of the Montana Capitol, with the statue of Mike and Maureen Mansfield in the lower center (By Darrell Ehrlick of the Daily Montanan). Two Republican lawmakers filed a lawsuit Friday over a term limit decision made by Attorney General Austin Knudsen this week that would remove them from the ballot in November.
The legal action comes as the state Republican Party is preparing to replace the candidates on the ballot, barring a judge’s intervention. 
Montana lawmakers are limited to serving eight years in each the House and Senate within a 16-year period. Some lawmakers have stayed in office longer than 16 years by switching between chambers. 
But Knudsen’s decision overturned a 2012 decision by then-Attorney General and Democrat Steve Bullock, which interpreted the term limits statute as allowing candidates to run for election if they had eight years of the last 16 out of their previous chamber by the start of the next term.
Montana Attorney General Austin Knudsen testifies before the Montana Senate Judiciary Committee on Wednesday, Feb. 13, 2025. (Nathaniel Bailey for the Daily Montanan)
Knudsen instead says that serving for eight of the last 16 years disqualifies a candidate from election back into a chamber — even if the next term they serve would be outside the term limit window. 
The lawsuit, filed in Lewis and Clark County District Court by House Majority Leader Rep. Steve Fitzpatrick, Rep. Llew Jones and Ted Kronebusch, chairman of the Pondera County Republican Central Committee, says Bullock’s opinion was constitutional and Knudsen’s “ignores the statutory construct and seeks to turn nearly 15 years of practice and precedent on its head.”
The suit is asking the court to prevent the opinion from applying to the 2026 general election and a judgement permitting a candidate to seek office after an eight-year break in service, essentially consistent with Bullock’s 2012 opinion.
Senate President Matt Regier, a Flathead Republican, requested Knudsen look at Jones’s eligibility on July 9, just six weeks before the ballot certification deadline, which is August 20.
The lawsuit argues Regier lacked standing to ask the attorney general for an opinion on the matter in the first place. It also says Knudsen “lacked the authority” to issue the decision as well.
“The issue decided by AG Knudsen relates to the issue of eligibility for office and ballot certification, neither of which have anything to do with the office of the Senate president,” the suit reads. “The job of the Senate president is to administer and operate the Senate, not decide eligibility questions for candidates for that body.”
Montana law also prohibits the attorney general from issuing an opinion “depriving” a candidate for office from appearing on the ballot “absent a court order,” the lawsuit goes on to read.
Rep. Llew Jones, R-Conrad. (Provided by the Montana Legislature)
“Montana law specifically states Plaintiffs Jones and Fitzpatrick, when filing the declaration, met the constitutional requirements to hold elected office,” the suit says. “Indeed, the Secretary of State accepted each declaration as valid when both were certified for the primary election. The only way that determination can be overruled is by a court order.”
The suit also points out numerous candidates have been allowed in the past to move from chamber to chamber every eight years, and then return to the original chamber they started in after 16 years.
Additionally, the suit claims the opinion was “crafted in secret” and that Jones only knew about the suit when contacted by a member of the press.
“The Attorney General violated the right to participate found in the Montana Constitution, which is particularly egregious here given how the opinion affects the voters and the two candidates who desire to serve their communities and prevailed in the June primary election,” the suit reads.
Jones, chairman of the powerful House Appropriations Committee and an architect of the state budget, beat Rep. Zach Wirth in the Republican primary earlier this year. Jones was part of a moderate group of lawmakers sometimes referred to as the “solutions caucus” and was often at odds with Regier’s agenda last session.
Jones wrote a statement about the issue, which, in part, said:
“Steve Fitzpatrick and I both lead groups of legislators who put the folks back home ahead of the party bosses and the out-of-state donors who write the party big checks. Our independence angers people who would rather buy a delegation than persuade one,” Jones wrote. “The party-before-people crowd lost at the ballot box, so they now look to win by way of a like-minded Attorney General’s legal opinion. I take it as a badge of honor to be targeted for prioritizing those I represent, as every legislator should.”
Meanwhile, on Friday, the Montana Republican Party Central Committee passed a resolution “supporting Montana’s constitutional term limits” and establishing an “expedited process” to replace Fitzpatrick and Jones.
The resolution instructs the GOP Central Committees in Lewis and Clark, Pondera, Teton and Toole Counties to each appoint three members to a committee to designate a replacement candidate for Jones’s district. It also instructed the Central Committee in Cascade County to find a replacement for Fitzpatrick.
“Montana voters made their position clear when they adopted constitutional term limits, and the Montana Republican Party respects their decision,” MTGOP Chairman Art Wittich said in a statement. “At the same time, even at this late date, Republican voters in Senate District 9 and House District 24 should be able to vote for a Republican candidates in November. The MTGOP will act quickly to ensure their voices are represented on the ballot.”

title: DNC approves 2028 presidential nominating cycle starting in South Carolina, Nevada
text:
The Democratic National Committee on Saturday approved by voice vote its lineup of six early primaries for the 2028 election cycle, kicking off with South Carolina and Nevada.DNC Chair Ken Martin said during Saturday’s meeting that the early lineup reflects the diversity of the party’s electorate. “Our 2028 nominee, whoever they are, will have to earn the support across the full breadth of America — every region, every demographic, every generation, every economic station in life,” he said. “No shortcuts. No coronation. You want to lead this party? You go earn it.”Saturday’s vote ratified the DNC’s rules and bylaws committee vote in late July to recommend the lineup for approval by the full party. Throughout the meeting, speakers and party officials from each of the six states to hold an early contest praised the impact the calendar will have for regions that haven’t always been top of mind for national candidates. Jaime Harrison, the former DNC chair who challenged the late South Carolina Sen. Lindsey Graham in 2020, said the calendar will tell a “whole new generation” of voters that the party is fighting for them.Other speakers included Nevada Secretary of State Cisco Aguilar, New Hampshire Democratic Committeewoman Donna Soucy and Michigan Democratic Party Chair Curtis Hertel Jr.Martin said that the lineup is a “stronger, more representative path to selecting our nominee.”“This is much bigger than a lineup of dates on a calendar,” Martin said. “This is about our approach to winning back the presidency. It's about the kind of Democratic Party and the kind of country we aspire to be.” South Carolina, Nevada come out on topFor the second straight presidential cycle, South Carolina will kick off the party’s nominating process. The full lineup of primaries is as follows: South Carolina on Jan. 22, 2028Nevada on Feb. 1, 2028New Hampshire on Feb. 8, 2028New Mexico on Feb. 15, 2028Michigan on Feb. 22, 2028Virginia on Feb. 29, 2028The lineup includes at least one state from each of the DNC’s four regions. The party’s rules and bylaws committee also voted in July to expand the number of early primaries to six, selecting New Mexico and Virginia to hold the additional contests.Several speakers Saturday said the calendar will better serve Latino and Black voters. U.S. Rep. Teresa Leger Fernández, D-New Mexico, said the calendar will show Latino voters they aren’t ignored. “With over 4.2 million Latinos in the early voting states, Latinos will not (just) be talked about,” she said. “Our stories will shape the policies of the next president of the United States, who will be a Democrat.”Terry McAuliffe, the former governor of Virginia and DNC chair from 2001 to 2005, said the calendar will put the party’s 2028 nominee “through the crucible” and force them to reach rural, suburban, urban and military voters alike. Iowa left outNotably, the early lineup excludes Iowa, despite a push from its state party officials to keep it among the initial contests. The Hawkeye State had long held a first-in-the-nation spot in the Democratic presidential nominating cycle, including in 2020 and 2016. But after delays in reporting results of the 2020 caucus, leading to no declared winner on the night of the caucus, many national Democrats looked elsewhere to kick off the nominating cycle. In a speech opposing the 2028 calendar Saturday, Iowa Democratic Party Chair Rita Hart said that it “fundamentally misses the mark.”

 






Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear, a potential candidate for the 2028 Democratic presidential nomination, speaks at a campaign event at the River Place in Des Moines on June 7, 2026 in support of Iowa Democratic gubernatorial candidate Rob Sand. Iowa, with its first-in-the-nation caucuses, was a focal point of Democrats aspiring to the presidency for decades, but is no longer on the party's early nominating contest calendar. Photo by Robin Opsahl/Iowa Capital Dispatch)

“It's a product of broken promises, and it excludes huge swaths of the country and the voters that Democrats need to win the kind of majorities it takes to restore democratic principles and reject this misguided and corrupt Trump administration,” she said. “The 2028 calendar has no representation of states with a majority of central or mountain time zones, and no Midwest state is among the first four.”Hart noted that Republicans have kept the Iowa Caucus as its first contest of the 2028 presidential nominating process, and the resulting surge in spending in the state during its contest could harm Democratic candidates for elected office in the state if that spending is not met by Democrats. New Hampshire, which has also long held an early position in the nominating process, kept its position, however. Democrats look South The primary calendar reflects Democrats' effort to court voters in the South, as well as a partial shift away from the Midwest. Martin began the meeting Friday — held in Austin, Texas — by emphasizing Democrats’ chance at flipping a Texas Senate seat, long held by Republicans. An Emerson College and Nexstar Media poll conducted from Aug. 9-10 showed state Rep. James Talarico, a Democrat, within one point of Republican nominee and Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton. On Friday, the DNC also announced a new initiative to help local Democratic parties in Southern states build up their infrastructure in order to win elections. The DNC said in a statement Friday that the Southern States Resource Hub will seek to address “years of underinvestment” in those Southern parties, and allocate resources for organizing, voter registration, data collection, fundraising efforts and communications systems so they can better compete in a region with a rapidly changing electorate.

title: Democratic state treasurer candidate proposes IPERS changes
description: John Norwood, a Democrat running for state treasurer, said Saturday at the Iowa State Fair  that he would focus on structural issues within the state retirement fund and on investing Iowa’s tax dollars back into the state.  Norwood spoke at the Des Moines Register Political Soapbox. Norwood who has spent his career in the business […]
text:
John Norwood, right, a Democrat for state treasurer, spoke with folks at the Iowa State Fair Aug. 15, 2026 at the Des Moines Register Political Soapbox. (Photo by Cami Koons/Iowa Capital Dispatch) John Norwood, a Democrat running for state treasurer, said Saturday at the Iowa State Fair  that he would focus on structural issues within the state retirement fund and on investing Iowa’s tax dollars back into the state. 
Norwood spoke at the Des Moines Register Political Soapbox.
Norwood who has spent his career in the business and finance sectors, founding TBL Ventures and more recently, advising small businesses across Iowa, said he views the treasurer’s role as the state chief financial officer. 
He said to him money isn’t red or blue, “it’s green.” 
“It’s your money,” Norwood said. “You worked for it, you earned it, and when the government collects it, you deserve to know where it goes and how it’s being invested, and whether it’s creating long-term value for Iowa. The treasurer’s job isn’t to spend money, it’s to make money work.” 
Norwood said he would prioritize to putting the “brakes” on private school vouchers in the state, working to support new crop markets that could bolster Iowa’s agriculture industry and to prioritize state projects built with union laborers. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
IPERS management
Norwood said there are “management concerns” within the Iowa Public Employees’ Retirement System, or IPERS. Namely, he said the system’s CEO should be selected by the board, rather than the governor.


Candidates speak at Register Soapbox
Saturday was the second day of candidate speeches at The Des Moines Register Political Soapbox at the state fair.  Here’s the schedule.
Read about other speakers:
Democratic gubernatorial candidate Rob Sand
Republican gubernatorial candidate: Zach Lahn
Democratic U.S. Senate candidate: Josh Turek
Republican 2nd Congressional District candidate:  Joe Mitchell
Democratic 3rd Congressional District candidate: Sarah Trone Garriott

In early August, Gov. Kim Reynolds appointed a new IPERS CEO following the resignation of the former CEO, who had been placed on administrative leave, and the firing of the chief benefits officer. 
Norwood, speaking to reporters after his Soapbox speech, which included taking questions from the crowd, said he would have preferred to see an independent investigation into the situation and an interim CEO put in the position to allow the next governor to appoint someone to the role. 
Ultimately, Norwood said, the treasurer needs to “pay attention” to what’s happening with the retirement trust fund that pays out more than $2.7 billion in annual benefits.  
Investing in Iowa 
Norwood is running against incumbent  Republican Roby Smith, who won the seat in 2022 after beating the Democrat who had held the position for 40 years. 
Norwood said Michael Fitzgerald – the Democrat who held the position for decades – “did a wonderful job” and mentioned programs like the Great Iowa Treasure Hunt initiated under Fitzgerald.
He said the office needs to be treated like a “full-time job” and said he felt that was only possible if the treasurer lived in the Des Moines area, allowing them to regularly interact with the Legislature and state officials. 
Democrat for Iowa Treasurer John Norwood, Aug. 15, 2026 at the Des Moines Register Political Soapbox. (Photo by Cami Koons/Iowa Capital Dispatch)
Smith, who lives in Davenport, did not immediately respond to a request for comment. 
Norwood said rather than sending short-term taxpayer dollars out of the state to try and get a return, he would push those investments to be made at local banks and credit unions. 
“When we put the deposits in our local banks; they can make loans against those deposits, and that’s how we can grow the economy,” Norwood said. “That’s how we can work with agriculture.” 
In the last election cycle, Norwood ran as the Democratic candidate for secretary of agriculture, and lost to incumbent Mike Naig. 
Norwood said in order to grow Iowa’s rural and agricultural economies, the state would need to support more farmer-led initiatives and diverse markets rather than “rely on commodity markets of corn and soy.”
Norwood used Green Acres Milling, a farmer-owned oat milling facility based in southern Minnesota, which his company helped launch, as an example.
“I believe Iowa should encourage more regional farmer-led processing facilities, creating markets for, in this case, oats and other third crops,” Norwood said. 
A more diversified farm profile, Norwood said, would also help to improve Iowa’s water quality. But for banks, farmers and crop insurance to make the leap to add a third crop into the system, they would need support from the state. 
“We’ve gotta begin to align the financial drivers and understand the financial constraints,” Norwood said. “The treasury really should be working with the legislature and with the secretary of agriculture and the governor – you know, we’re all a team – in figuring out what we need to do specifically to add these third crops.”

title: Democrat Rob Sand calls for civility in contentious Iowa governor race
description: Iowa Auditor Rob Sand called for his opponents and his own supporters to be “respectful” Saturday as the race for Iowa governor heats up. When Sand, the Democratic nominee for Iowa governor in 2026, visited the state fair on Thursday, he was followed and booed by activists with the conservative organization Turning Point USA. Speaking […]
text:
Iowa Auditor Rob Sand, running for Iowa governor in 2026, gave a speech at the Des Moines Register Political Soapbox Aug. 15, 2026 at the Iowa State Fair. (Photo by Robin Opsahl/Iowa Capital Dispatch)Iowa Auditor Rob Sand called for his opponents and his own supporters to be “respectful” Saturday as the race for Iowa governor heats up.
When Sand, the Democratic nominee for Iowa governor in 2026, visited the state fair on Thursday, he was followed and booed by activists with the conservative organization Turning Point USA. Speaking to reporters after his speech at the Des Moines Register Political Soapbox Saturday, he responded to the incident by saying, “they’re kids.”
“I mean, I don’t know why they’re doing what they’re doing, or how they think that’s effective,” Sand said. “I felt bad for all the people around us who were trying to enjoy the fair and having their experience disrupted. So that’s all I had to say about that.”
At the same time, he said his message to his own supporters was, “Don’t behave like the kids from Turning Point USA.”
On Friday, when Sand’s opponent, Republican gubernatorial candidate Zach Lahn spoke at the soapbox, he was not heckled, but some people on the edge of the crowd held up signs calling the GOP candidate a “part-time Iowan.” The signs referred to reports that he frequently flew his personal airplane between Iowa and Kansas, because some of his children are based out of Wichita, Kansas, and because he was a previous resident and registered voter in Kansas until 2024.

Candidates speak at Register Soapbox
Saturday was the second day of candidate speeches at The Des Moines Register Political Soapbox at the state fair.  Here’s the schedule.
Read about previous speakers:
Republican gubernatorial candidate: Zach Lahn
Democratic U.S. Senate candidate: Josh Turek
Republican 2nd Congressional District candidate:  Joe Mitchell
Democratic 3rd Congressional District candidate: Sarah Trone Garriott
Democratic state treasurer candidate:  John Norwood

Lahn commented on the signs during his speech, saying it was “ironic” that what Sand “actually says is that a sixth-generation Iowan is less Iowan than an illegal immigrant.” The Republican also claimed his opponent had made the 2026 gubernatorial campaign “about personal attacks on me and my family.”
But Sand said this view of his campaign is not true. His speech at the Soapbox followed the format of many of his campaign stops, beginning by leading the group in singing “America the Beautiful,” and telling the crowd that Iowa needs an end to one-party control and regain a “balanced government.”
Sand has brought up Lahn’s residency at previous campaign events. At a June event, he referenced a Lahn campaign ad where the GOP candidate said “Iowa jobs are for Iowans.” Sand added: “And that includes governor.”
The Democratic candidate said he did not bring up Lahn during his speech at the fair because “I got plenty of stuff to talk about that doesn’t involve talking about my opponent.”
“At this point, typically when I’m bringing him up in my town halls, I tell people, ‘The most important thing that you need to remember about my opponent is he’s a human being,'” Sand said. “And he’s got people that he loves, and there are people in the world that love him too. And we can have a conversation about who’s better, and we can have sharp disagreements without getting worked up.”
In addition to criticizing Sand for making “personal attacks,” Lahn and Iowa GOP Chair Jeff Kaufmann held a news conference Friday where they said Sand was falsely portraying himself as a moderate candidate. But Sand said his track record as auditor shows he is not beholden to the Democratic Party. During his speech, he referenced his decision to promote an independent and Republican to senior positions at the state auditor’s office.
“I think that when different people who think differently from each other work together, we actually get to better answers,” he said.
The Democrat regularly brings up that he would be working with a Republican-controlled state Legislature if elected, which he argues would mean measures signed into law must be a compromise between Democrats and Republicans. When asked about concerns about potential gridlock, Sand said he would “work with anyone that I disagree with joyfully” — but said he does not have control over others’ actions.
“I can’t control what other people are going to do,” Sand said. “I can only tell you that if I’m governor, I’m going to be working with everybody to do the stuff that the vast majority of people in this state want to do. The smartest thing for the Legislature to do is to do all the stuff that I just campaigned on. If I win this race, get it done, and then try to have an argument four years from now that’s focused on other stuff where maybe they think they could win. That’d be the smartest thing for them to do, and I hope they’ll do it. If they want to just fight instead, well, I’ll sign stuff that’s good, and those folks can understand that I’ll veto stuff that’s bad.”
But he emphasized there was a current need for change, and that Republicans’ trifecta of control in Iowa has resulted in proposals he said hurt the state from being signed into law. He brought up the state’s Education Savings Account (ESA) program providing public funding for private school tuition and associated costs and a law restricting the state auditor from accessing certain information and going to court for subpoena enforcement as examples of problems that happen “when too few people have too much power for too long.”
“Somebody needs to play goalkeeper up there and be the adult in the room that recognizes a bad idea — like gutting the state auditor’s office, like having no income limits on the school vouchers program that has a total lack of accountability, like defunding water quality monitoring, and on and on,” Sand said.

title: Lawyer who filed records lawsuit against Laramie County sheriff financially backs opponent’s campaign
description:
Former Wyoming GOP Chairman Drake Hill and his wife contributed to the campaign of Cheyenne Police Sgt. Eric Norris, who is running for Sheriff Brian Kozak’s job. Kozak has accused the lawsuit of being politically motivated.
The post Lawyer who filed records lawsuit against Laramie County sheriff financially backs opponent’s campaign appeared first on WyoF[...]
text:
Former Wyoming GOP chairman Drake Hill, who is representing a Colorado law firm in a records lawsuit against Laramie County Sheriff Brian Kozak, donated $1,000 to the sheriff’s opponent in the Republican primary, newly released campaign finance records show. 
Hill made the contribution on June 22. Hill’s spouse, Cindy Hill, a former Wyoming state superintendent of public instruction, also financially backed the challenger, Cheyenne Police Sgt. Eric Norris, with a $1,500 contribution on June 19. The report shows another $158 in-kind contribution — a non-monetary donation — from Drake Hill for food at a fundraiser. 
Combined, the Hills’ support makes up more than 12% of the money Norris has raised for his campaign. 

Eric Norris, a sergeant with the Cheyenne Police Department, is running for Laramie County sheriff against incumbent Brian Kozak. (Norris for Sheriff campaign)

“The Hills reached out to me and said they wanted to support me because they found that my thoughts on how the sheriff’s department should be run were more along the lines of what they were looking to support,” Norris told WyoFile. “It was after we announced that we were going to run and started kind of talking about what our goals were, as far as focusing on crime rather than the next headline.”
In response to WyoFile’s message to both Cindy and Drake Hill inquiring about the donations, Cindy Hill shared a written statement specifying that her comments were offered “personally” and not on behalf of Hill Law Firm. She wrote that her and her husband’s support for Norris “has transpired from concern over recent events that I find shocking.” 
On June 30, Drake Hill filed a lawsuit against Kozak alleging the sheriff and his office “engaged in the obstruction of justice by blocking access to critical evidence” in the ongoing Colorado immigration proceedings of a Mexican national detained in Laramie County. 
The plaintiffs include a Denver, Colorado-based immigration law office, Lichter Immigration, and an investigator working for the firm, Laramie County resident Kevin Lewis, who are acting on behalf of the detained man, Mario Fabian Valenzuela Robles, in immigration proceedings that began with an April 23 traffic stop.
Cindy Hill described in her written statement that she and Drake Hill learned of Valenzuela Robles’ seizure on April 23 as they were walking out of the Anne Frank house in Amsterdam. “That was a moment that became frozen in time,” she stated. Lewis previously told WyoFile that Valenzuela Robles had worked on renovation projects at the Hill household. 
“We began to learn of the seizures throughout Laramie County and the hundreds of Laramie County residents who had been seized,” Cindy Hill recounted. “We also delved into the 287(g) agreement and saw that, in our view, the terms of the agreement with I.C.E. are not being followed.”
After a July hearing, Kozak’s office handed over some records that the law firm had requested. At the request of the plaintiffs, the judge, Robin Cooley, told the sheriff’s office to perform a certified computer search for other records. She also ordered an “in camera” review of additional records the plaintiffs wanted. This review is a legal process in which a judge privately inspects records to decide if they can legally be released. Cooley later dropped the in camera review after the parties consulted and agreed that the concerned records “are, in fact, public records in that they are financial records and bear no confidential information.” 
Cooley ordered that the defendants produce all writing, documents, communications, statements and digital records relating to Valenzuela Robles and file a verified report “detailing all steps” they took to comply with the order by Aug. 5. 
But on Aug. 6, Drake Hill asked Cooley to hold Kozak in contempt of court, accusing him of failing to comply with the court’s order to provide records by deadline. “In the absence of a compelling explanation for their failure to comply with the clear terms of the Court’s Order, the Defendants appear to be in contempt, necessitating Plaintiffs’ action to force compliance,” Hill wrote.
Laramie County Sheriff Brian Kozak sits for a photo in his office on Monday, May 4, 2026, in Cheyenne. (Mike Vanata for WyoFile)
The next day, Cooley set a hearing on the matter for Oct. 16. Laramie County Attorney Mark Voss, who is representing Kozak and his department in the case, soon after filed the verified report. “Any delay in the matter,” Voss wrote, was the result of the need for agencies to “conduct their normal activities” and the difficulty of sorting through a county email system that isn’t divided by agency. 
An initial search produced 7,700 emails, according to Voss. “Given the minimal contact with Mr. Robles, it was abundantly clear that the majority, if not all of this, was entirely irrelevant to Mr. Robles’s detention and contact with the Sheriff’s Department,” Voss wrote. Subsequent searches “using different configuration of the search terms” reduced that number to 1,107. Those were whittled down to 200 emails, which Voss had to review to “determine whether or not any of them were relevant or responsive to the records request and the Order compelling and/or whether they contained privileged material.” Voss stated in the court filing that the search produced a small number of relevant records that would be provided to the plaintiffs. 
In response to the contempt order, Kozak told a reporter at Cowboy State Daily that he believed the lawsuit was in part tied to the sheriff’s office’s investigation into the “Checkgate” controversy, a February incident that involved Teton County activist Rebecca Bextel handing out campaign checks to Wyoming Freedom Caucus members on the House floor two days before a vote on a bill she supported. Bextel is now running for governor as a Constitution Party candidate. 
Kozak, who didn’t return WyoFile’s calls by publishing time, reportedly stated that there “appears to be a connection between Lewis and Hill through their involvement with Honor Wyoming and the Freedom Caucus, some members of which are reportedly subjects of the Checkgate investigation.”
Drake Hill has served as an attorney for Honor Wyoming, a conservative political group. Lewis, who was a staffer in Cindy Hill’s office when she was state superintendent, was once registered as a lobbyist for the organization. Bextel has also described herself as an “active volunteer” for the group. 
“Neither Drake or I have been involved in what you are calling ‘check-gate’
controversy and know only what we have read in passing news,” Cindy Hill wrote in her statement to WyoFile. “Other than reading various articles, we have no more understanding or affiliation than the average reader.” 
Kozak told a reporter at Cowboy State Daily that he hoped Cooley would “take appropriate action” if the lawsuit was “misleading or unethical.” If not, he said he would consider filing a complaint with the Wyoming State Bar himself.
Cindy Hill described Kozak’s comments as “intimidation efforts” that “are intended to shut up those who would disagree and to shut down any awareness of harm he continues to cause.” She said Drake Hill “will continue to do his work in the same honorable way he always does” and “will not be intimidated.”
Last year, Kozak signed three 287(g) immigration enforcement agreements with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement. These contracts allow local, county and state law enforcement to act as an extension of ICE and conduct some immigration enforcement under the federal agency’s watch. 
Cindy Hill said in her statement that she and her husband had “looked to see who was running against the current sheriff” and found that Norris was a candidate. Hill elaborated that she was “impressed” with his military service and law enforcement experience. 
Norris previously told a reporter with the Wyoming Tribune Eagle that while he supports immigration enforcement efforts under 287(g) agreements, he’s concerned that other issues need more attention. “I’m not so focused on immigration and a headline,” Norris said after announcing his campaign.
“As far as the lawsuit, I haven’t had any real conversation with the Hills about anything there,” Norris told WyoFile. “The immigration stuff is completely separate from me. It doesn’t have anything to do with my campaign.” 
Kozak reported raising and spending no money on his campaign. 
Early voting is underway in Wyoming. The primary election is Tuesday.
