title: With PNW electricity demand surging, planners map out major grid upgrades
description: The Pacific Northwest will need a massive buildout of new energy infrastructure over the next six years to meet rising electricity demand, according to a draft regional power plan released Thursday.  Implementing the plan will cost the Pacific Northwest approximately $2.3 billion. And the rate of building will need to quicken to make it happen […]
text:
(Photo by Clinton Carpenter/Bonneville Power Administration)The Pacific Northwest will need a massive buildout of new energy infrastructure over the next six years to meet rising electricity demand, according to a draft regional power plan released Thursday. 
Implementing the plan will cost the Pacific Northwest approximately $2.3 billion. And the rate of building will need to quicken to make it happen by 2032. 
Last year, the Northwest Power and Conservation Council forecast regional electricity demand to increase anywhere from 50% to 100% over the next 20 years. That’s largely due to data centers, the electrification of vehicles and buildings, and population growth.
On Thursday, the council released a draft of its Ninth Power Plan. Deemed by one councilmember as the “roughest of drafts,” it will serve as a guide on the region’s path to meeting future electricity demand. Public comment for the draft is open until Oct. 16. 
The plan calls on Washington, Oregon, Idaho and western Montana to add 11,000 megawatts to the region’s grid. That’s about a third of the electricity the Northwest uses at peak demand, such as during a heat wave.
Getting there won’t be easy, and the plan doesn’t rely solely on renewable energy. 
“No single resource on its own will be able to meet our growing need for energy in the future,” said Jennifer Light, director of power planning. “Rather, a regional portfolio of cost-effective resources will achieve the right balance of economics, efficiency, reliability, and adequacy.”
Across the four-state region, the plan includes 9,000 megawatts of renewables and 2,100 megawatts of natural gas. 
In Washington, the plan calls for adding between 500 MW and 1,250 MW of natural gas to the grid by 2032. That is in accordance with the state’s clean energy policies, said Peter Jensen, a spokesperson for the council. 
While the plan directs the largest power wholesaler in the region, the Bonneville Power Administration, on which resources it should acquire, it also influences the decisions of other electricity providers in the region. The BPA operates under the U.S. Department of Energy and owns approximately 75% of the Pacific Northwest’s grid.
Throughout the two-year planning process, the BPA has “consistently expressed concerns” over the costs and complexity of the council’s energy conservation recommendations. 
This part of the plan focuses on how technology like efficient appliances, as well as building code changes, can reduce electricity demand. The region has spent billions on these types of upgrades over the last decade, according to the plan.
The BPA also questions whether the council’s proposed strategy would be less favorable for utility customers in Idaho and Montana, compared to Oregon and Washington, when it comes to providing access to energy efficiency assistance programs. 
The plan was created amid a great deal of uncertainty. Council staff pointed out that it was a challenge to predict how much electricity will be needed to supply data centers. Also unknown is how fast the region can upgrade and expand transmission line capacity and how extreme weather events could strain the grid. 
The council has published regional power plans about every five years since 1983, to lay out how the region will maintain an affordable and adequate power supply. The latest plan is expected to be finalized either by the end of this year or the beginning of 2027. 
The Northwest Power and Conservation Council was formed in 1981 following the passage of the federal Northwest Power Act. That act directed the four states to work together on regional energy planning and to stop the decline of native Columbia Basin fish species, which is primarily due to the development of hydroelectric dams in the region.

name: Missouri Independent
title: Missouri’s redistricting mess is a stress test for the rule of law
description: While the nation faces various stress tests for the rule of law upon which our country was built, Missouri courts are facing their own stress test in the hot mess of our current congressional redistricting. Our Legislature redrew our congressional maps in 2025 at the insistence of President Donald Trump. The chief aim was to […]
text:
Supporters of a referendum on Missouri's gerrymandered redistricting map rally at the state Capitol Building Tuesday, May 12 after the Missouri Supreme Court heard arguments on two cases involving the redistricting map (Rudi Keller/Missouri Independent).While the nation faces various stress tests for the rule of law upon which our country was built, Missouri courts are facing their own stress test in the hot mess of our current congressional redistricting.
Our Legislature redrew our congressional maps in 2025 at the insistence of President Donald Trump. The chief aim was to make the 5th District in the Kansas City area less favorable to incumbent U.S. Rep. Emmanuel Cleaver, a Black Democratic congressman who represents a majority white district.
The 5th District’s boundaries were stretched from the Kansas border to mid-Missouri, which includes a lot of rural voters who, it is presumed, would be less likely to vote for Cleaver than his current constituents. Nevermind that there might have been a racial motive; the U.S. Supreme Court in its dismantling of the federal Voting Rights Act has taught us to look away.
The hot mess is a series of court cases, 12 in all but only a few that ultimately matter, and I include names of decisions if the reader is looking for more.   Individually the cases are simple but overall seem complicated. Let me explain as simply as I can.
The road to where we are now started with the Missouri Legislature’s redistricting act passed in a special session in September 2025. Cleaver’s allies challenged the new boundaries for not being “compact” and “contiguous” as the Missouri Constitution requires. While one can see that the boundaries are contiguous, they certainly don’t look compact.
Notwithstanding the “compact” requirement, the Missouri Supreme Court — perhaps reflecting the U.S. Supreme Court’s inability to see anything wrong with partisan gerrymandering — upheld the Legislature’s work which reportedly was handed to them by someone in the District of Columbia. In any event, it was close enough for government work (Wise v. Missouri and Healey v. Missouri et al).
In another case challenging the Legislature’s work, there was a strong argument that the Missouri Constitution does not authorize redistricting except when the state receives its once-a-decade population count and its allocation of congressional seats as computed by federal law based on the U.S Census. Only three of the Missouri Supreme Court judges accepted the arguments, however, while the four-judge majority held that unless explicitly prohibited, the Legislature can do redistricting any time it wishes (Luther v. Hoskins).
That set the stage for the big upcoming court case: What to do with the petition of 300,000+ voters who petitioned to put the 2025 redistricting law on the November ballot?
Months ago, the petitioning organization, People Not Politicians, sued to force Secretary of State Denny Hoskins to acknowledge that there are enough signatures to meet the constitution’s requirement, which currently is about 110,000 valid signatures. No, the Supreme Court said, the secretary’s review was “ongoing”, and the constitutional deadline was Aug. 4, coincidentally the date of the primary election (Maggard v. State).
Though Hoskins had received verified signed petitions from local election authorities months ago, he refused to act until the deadline.
Fair enough, one might say. But the Supreme Court unanimously said if there are enough signatures, the redistricting law goes on hold retroactive to Dec. 9 when the petition was filed — the prior law stays in effect and the new law “shall take effect when approved by a majority of the votes cast thereon, and not otherwise.”
An hour before the deadline to certify voters’ signatures on Aug. 4, Hoskins announced that he refuses to put the measure for the ballot no matter how many signatures there were. That’s because the secretary came late to claim he has the power to disapprove the petition no matter what the Missouri Constitution or the Supreme Court says.
The People Not Politicians lawsuit asks the court to resolve a basic question: Does the Missouri Constitution, which guarantees citizens the right to challenge any “act of the General Assembly” include the act of redistricting?
Hoskins and Attorney General Catherine Hanaway say no, that is not what those words could have meant, even though citizens have done a referendum on congressional redistricting before in 1922.
There are exceptions to the constitutional provision requiring a vote of the people, but redistricting laws are not in the exceptions. The secretary’s reading of the Missouri Constitution evades or ignores its plain language. Hoskins and Hanaway’s theory apparently is also based on a federal constitutional challenge that a federal court already has turned aside.
Court-ordered changes to the ballot must be done by September 8.
The Supreme Court’s prior decision says if the petition has enough signatures and is constitutional, the new map is not in effect until the voters approve it. So, what if the court also finds that using the referendum to challenge a mid-cycle congressional redistricting is also protected by the Constitution’s voter-approval provision?
That would mean that the maps would change back to the earlier maps for the November election. This year’s candidates nominated in most congressional districts would be campaigning in districts that differ from the districts they campaigned in for the primary election.
But if anyone feels aggrieved by the change in maps, their complaint is with Hoskins — it was his decision to wait until the legal deadline, which was months after he received the verified signatures from the local election authorities. He could have raised his legal concerns back in December of last year, but he chose to go ahead and use the new maps that the voters’ signatures should have put on hold.
            The old map or the new map?  Despite the differences, it would seem useless to re-do the primary election. Close enough for government work. There are primary election victors ready to campaign and stand for election in all eight districts regardless of where the lines are drawn.
If Missouri courts have the fortitude to follow their own Supreme Court precedent as well as the Constitution’s guarantee that the people will have a veto, the rule of law will have survived for another day.
And what if the voters approve the new 2025 map on Nov. 3? The new law will go into effect after the people have voted. If the voters approve, the redistricting law will be in effect for the 2028 election. Unless, of course, the Legislature changes it in the 2027 or 2028 session, as the Supreme Court said it could.
But for the coming term of Congress, Missouri will have representatives elected from lawful districts. And, despite the gamesmanship dictated from the District of Columbia, the winner will be the rule of law.

title: Virginia-based PAC spends $549,000 largely backing Wyoming Freedom Caucus candidates
description:
Make Liberty Win has spent half a million dollars in Wyoming since May, outspending several campaigns of the candidates the group is backing. 
The post Virginia-based PAC spends $549,000 largely backing Wyoming Freedom Caucus candidates appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
CASPER—For college student Sofia Downing, a summer gig knocking on doors in Wyoming was the chance to make some money, see a different part of the country and get candidates with what she considers conservative values elected to office. 
“If you don’t like walking around, or you’re more of an introvert, probably not the job for you,” Downing said in late July, standing in the afternoon shade of a tree in the city’s Valley Hills neighborhood. 
Canvassing, however, is a great job for a young person passionate about politics, Downing said, “if you’re like me, very extroverted and just willing to try out new things and are very curious about the world.”
“This is why Young Americans for Liberty hires people of my generation to do this,” she said. 
Before arriving in Wyoming in June, Downing said the organization trained her on canvassing. She then spent several weeks knocking on doors in Oklahoma, where she goes to school, ahead of its primary election. Downing’s assignment in Casper was set to last until August’s primary election, she said, when “the results come in.”
When Downing encountered a WyoFile reporter in July, she had the tanned shoulders to prove she’d spent many days outside on the campaign trail. Downing carried a stack of door hangers portraying a bear wearing a “Liberty” branded felt hat with the end of a shotgun pointed at the hat’s brim. 

Sen. Bob Ide, R-Casper, on the Senate floor during the 2025 session of the Wyoming Legislature. (Mike Vanata for WyoFile)

“On August 18th, only YOU can preserve freedom in the state legislature,” the door hanger read, urging voters to reelect Sen. Bob Ide to Senate District 29 and to back Republican hopeful Ross Schriftman for House District 37, an open seat with Rep. Steve Harshman running for superintendent of public instruction. Both districts include parts of west Casper and surrounding areas.
Asked how the group selects which candidates to back, Downing said she did “not know the exact process” but was confident the candidates aligned with “the same conservative values.”
Since launching “Operation Win at the Door” in 2018, Young Americans for Liberty says its student activists have knocked on 7 million doors, cementing its efforts as “the most effective political operation to make liberty win,” according to its website. 
“Oftentimes, you’ll have candidates that say they will do one thing, but they will be pressured to go back against their campaign promises,” she said. “We are very stringent on that as well.”
While Young Americans for Liberty focuses on ground support during elections, its Virginia-based affiliated political action committee, Make Liberty Win, contacts voters through phone calls, text messages, mailers, and digital advertisements. In Wyoming, that’s no small change. 
Since May, Make Liberty Win has spent $549,000 in Wyoming races, according to its campaign finance report filed this week with the secretary of state’s office. In 14 legislative races, the PAC outspent the candidates’ own campaign committees — three of which saw the PAC spend twice as much as the candidates. 
As it did in 2024, the PAC is mostly spending money to boost candidates who are either members of, or ideologically aligned with, the Wyoming Freedom Caucus. 
Make Liberty Win’s spending also dwarfs other conservative PACs and organizations dropping cash in Wyoming’s 2026 legislative elections. The newly formed Defeating Communism PAC has spent around $173,000, for example, while Americans for Prosperity, has spent about $286,000.
While the campaign finance report filed this week details the PAC’s spending in Wyoming, it gives minimal details of the source of that funding. It lists just four contributions totalling $562,605, all from “Make Liberty Win.” 
Otherwise, the PAC’s filings with the Federal Elections Commission report raising $6.7 million nationally between Jan. 1, 2025 and June 20, 2026, with about $4.8 million of that coming from Young Americans for Liberty. None of the PAC’s donations were listed as being from Wyoming. 
How we got here
Make Liberty Win first spent money in Wyoming during the state’s 2024 primary election, reporting about $371,000 in its campaign finance report two years ago. The PAC made a messy entrance with its mailers that gave voters the wrong date of the election and misidentified political newcomers as incumbent lawmakers. 
In one mailer sent to Albany County voters, the PAC used the photograph of a Virginia man to promote a Wyoming man with the same name running for office. The PAC was sent a cease and desist letter from the Virginia man for its decision to use his photograph. 
A mailer sent out to Albany County voters is pictured. (Courtesy) 
When the Wyoming Freedom Caucus ousted several incumbents that year and set itself up to win control of the House in the general election, Barrett Young, Make Liberty Win’s executive director, chalked the win up to his organization. 
“Make Liberty Win’s robust voter contact program worked because we exposed the lies of the Wyoming Establishment, humiliating Governor Gordon in his attempt to slander our organization and conservatives across the Cowboy State,” Young wrote in an email on Aug. 22, 2024. 
“Unlike the RINOS, we can actually deploy people to knock on doors because our activists believe in something. Principled conservatives will walk away with a governing majority in the House, but we look forward to even greater victories [in] 2026 and beyond,” Young wrote. “Make Liberty Win will be back, bent on flipping the Senate and the Wyoming Governor’s Mansion for Liberty.” 
More recently, Young told Liberty Action, a partner of Make Liberty Win, that “places like West Virginia, Wyoming, Montana, these are the types of places where we can make the biggest impact.” 
In June, several Wyoming lawmakers attended an event at the Four Seasons Resort in Teton Village hosted by the PAC’s affiliated organization. 
“It was a privilege to gather with liberty-minded patriots from across the country, hosted by Young Americans for Liberty,” Cody Republican Rep. Rachel Rodriguez-Williams said in a June 3 post on X. “Wyoming is proud to host that energy, and I am proud to be part of it.”
The post included a photograph of Williams, who chairs the Wyoming Freedom Caucus, alongside Republican Reps. Scott Heiner of Green River, Nina Webber of Cody, John Bear of Gillette and Steve Johnson of Cheyenne. Williams is running for secretary of state. 
2026 report
The vast majority of Make Liberty Win’s spending in Wyoming this election cycle has covered the cost of “field distribution of literature,” or the kinds of door hangers student activists like Downing hand out while canvassing. Of the PAC’s half million or so in expenditures, about $424,000 went toward those materials. 
In Rep. Abby Angelos’ race in Campbell County’s Senate District 23, the PAC reported spending $24,678 on “field distribution of literature supporting Angelos.” For comparison, Angelos’ campaign reported spending a total of $19,600. Like Angelos, Sheridan Rep. Ken Pendergraft is seeking a Senate seat this election. Make Liberty Win reported spending about $15,500 supporting him, compared to the approximately $12,000 his campaign spent. 
However, the largest gap between the PAC’s spending and the candidates it supports were seen in three other races. 

Rep. Tomi Strock, R-Douglas, attends a 2025 session of the Wyoming House of Representatives in Cheyenne. Make Liberty Win spent more than $14,000 supporting Strock’s campaign. (Mike Vanata for WyoFile)

Rep. Bob Wharff, who is running for reelection to Evanston’s House District 49, reported spending about $4,600, while Make Liberty Win nearly tripled that with $13,800 of its own expenditures. In Converse County, Make Liberty Win spent more than $14,000 supporting Rep. Tomi Strock, whose campaign doled out about $7,600. Jim Corkery, who is running for Senate District 27 in Casper, spent about $6,200 vying for the seat now held by Sen. Bill Landen, who is retiring. Make Liberty Win, meanwhile, reported spending more than $12,000 supporting Corkery. 
Most of the PAC’s spending in Wyoming has been in support of candidates, but it’s also dropped more than $50,000 directly opposing candidates. That has included current and former lawmakers who have been a thorn in the side of the Freedom Caucus, like Sen. Cale Case and Rep. Lloyd Larsen, both of Lander, and former Speaker of the House Albert Sommers. 
Early voting is underway in Wyoming. The primary election is Aug. 18.

title: AG charges five non-citizens who allegedly voted in Michigan’s 2024 general election
description: Five non-citizens allegedly voted in the 2024 general election, and one U.S. citizen allegedly attempted to register her non-citizen husband to vote, Michigan Attorney General Dana Nessel announced Thursday. Of the six newest charges announced, two of the non-citizens charged are facing only misdemeanors. Voter registrations associated with every identified[...]
text:
The office of Attorney General Dana Nessel in the G. Mennen Williams Building in Lansing, Mich., on May 15, 2025. (Photo by Andrew Roth/Michigan Advance)Five non-citizens allegedly voted in the 2024 general election, and one U.S. citizen allegedly attempted to register her non-citizen husband to vote, Michigan Attorney General Dana Nessel announced Thursday.
Of the six newest charges announced, two of the non-citizens charged are facing only misdemeanors.
Voter registrations associated with every identified non-citizen voter, whether or not their investigation resulted in charges, have been cancelled, the press release continued.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Between 2025 and 2026, Nessel’s office has investigated 38 cases of suspected non-citizen voting spanning from 2009 to 2025. Of those, six cases have resulted in criminal charges, 10 have been closed without charges, and 22 remain under review, according to her office. 
“In my office, we’ve always taken election crimes seriously, and prosecute attacks on our voting systems to the fullest extent of the law,” Nessel said in a press release from her office. “We’re upholding election integrity by investigating all claims of non-citizen voters, as rare as they are, and holding bad actors accountable when they refuse to abide by the laws that keep our elections safe and secure.”
Nessel said the charges reflect “the severity of the allegations, the sanctity of our democracy, and the tremendous consequences of voting illegally— whether that’s done to try and ‘test’ security measures or to make an unlawful vote count.”
Michigan Attorney General Dana Nessel speaks during the Michigan Democratic Party Legacy Dinner in Detroit, Mich., on April 18, 2026. (Photo by Andrew Roth/Michigan Advance)
Michael Akioya, 39, of Oak Park, is a lawful permanent resident who allegedly registered to vote in 2016 and allegedly submitted an absentee ballot. Akioya was charged in March of 2026 with one count each of False Statement on an Absent Voter Ballot Application and False Statement on an Absentee Vote Ballot Return Envelope. 
Alondra Harker, 26, of Three Rivers, allegedly voted in person in her hometown in 2024, and is charged with Election Law – Fraudulent Registration.
The other three non-citizens — Harumi Michael, 60, of Wolverine Lake, Basanth Sadasivian, 29, residing in the United Kingdom, and Robert Piva, 67, of Roseville — all face at least one felony charge. 
Michael, a lawful permanent resident allegedly registered to vote and voted in person in the 2024 election in Commerce Township. Michael is charged with two counts of Election Law Forgery, one count of Unqualified Elector Attempting to Vote, and one count of Voter Registration – False Statement. 
Sadasivian, who does not live in the U.S., allegedly registered to vote in 2024 by email via the Federal Post Card Application system, a federal program for citizens living overseas, using a Bloomfield Hills address, and voted under that same federal system in the 2024 general election. Sadasivian is charged with one count of Election Law – Unqualified Elector Attempting to Vote.



Quotation







We welcome these charges because they show the system works.


–  Secretary of State Jocelyn Benson


Piva, a lawful permanent resident, allegedly registered to vote online in September 2024 and voted in-person at an early voting location in Roseville in October of that year. He has claimed his vote was an experiment concerning voter fraud, and faces one count each of Election Law Perjury, Unqualified Elector Attempting to Vote, and Election Law – Fraudulent Registration.
Meanwhile, the single U.S. citizen who was announced on Thursday to be facing charges, Kimberley DiDonato, 60, of Rose Township, is facing two felony charges — Election Forgery and Using a Computer to Commit a Crime.
She allegedly posed as her non-citizen husband and falsely claimed he was an American citizen in order to register him to vote online in April of 2024. She then allegedly contacted her local clerk in May to cancel that registration once she had received the voter registration card in her husband’s name, all of which she claims was intended to test the registration system for vulnerabilities to unqualified voter registrants.
Both Democratic and Republican elected officials responded to the charges quickly. 
“We welcome these charges because they show the system works,” Secretary of State Jocelyn Benson told reporters on Thursday. “They were a result of our investigation as well in partnership with the Attorney General’s office, and really emphasize and underscore at a time where noncitizen voting is thrown around to make people afraid or create and sow false seeds of doubt about our elections, that this is an example that the process works.”
Rep. Rachelle Smit (R-Martin) speaks at an election security event in Lansing, Michigan on June 5, 2024 (Photo: Anna Liz Nichols)
Meanwhile, House Election Integrity Committee Chair Rep. Rachelle Smit (R-Martin) used the charges to express support for the federal SAVE Act, legislation that seeks to impose strict voter identification restrictions. Smit called Michigan “the epicenter of the problem” of non-citizen voting.
“The charges filed today are just the tip of the iceberg, and further underscore exactly why the U.S. Senate must approve the SAVE Act to safeguard our elections and ensure only U.S. citizens are voting in our elections,” Smit said. “We must remember that these are just the cases where the individual voting was caught. How many others are doing the exact same thing and just escaping the law?”
Smit added that the charges raised more questions about “a system we all know to have serious flaws.”
“Passing the SAVE act in Congress will help, just like some of the voter security measures we’ve passed in Michigan that had subsequently been held up in the state Senate,” Smit said.

title: What do the numbers tell us about the Wyoming governor’s race?
description:
Newly filed campaign finance reports show where each candidate is finding support across Wyoming and the U.S.
The post What do the numbers tell us about the Wyoming governor’s race? appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
Come Wednesday, once primary election results have been tallied, Wyomingites will know who will likely be their next governor. 
Word-of-mouth enthusiasm, mailers, yard signs, candidate-sponsored polling and high-profile endorsements have all played their part in a tug-of-war to establish a Republican frontrunner. Now, recently released candidate filings show which way supporters have been leaning with their wallets. 
WyoFile compiled a series of data points from campaign filings available to the public through the Wyoming Secretary of State’s Office. Artificial intelligence prompts were used to transpose hundreds of pages of contribution and expenditure records from PDF files to a searchable spreadsheet format, which was then checked and verified for accuracy by staff and used to create the following graphs.
The first graph, which shows average candidate contributions and expenditures between the 2010 and 2026 elections, includes data from each cycle’s entire campaign season, with the latest beginning on Jan. 1, 2025. All other graphs show only contributions and expenditures from 2026. 
Here are some answers to some common questions about who is contributing what in Wyoming’s gubernatorial race.
Is the governor’s race getting more expensive?
We’ll see, but it’s looking that way. Average contributions to the six gubernatorial candidates as of Wednesday already surpassed 2018 contributions through the full election season, and average expenditures are about $100,000 behind. This year’s contributions are massively ahead of the 2010, 2014 and 2022 contests. (2010, like this year, lacked an incumbent.) (Note to readers: This graphic draws from a different data set than the others below.)



Who has raised the most so far this year?
Megan Degenfelder has collected the most money in 2026, narrowly beating out Eric Barlow. Brent Bien trails them both by a sizeable margin. About 75% of total dollars contributed to Barlow’s campaign came from individuals, compared to 65% for Bien and 29% for Degenfelder.



Which Republican candidate has collected the most contributions from individuals?
The number of contributions to Eric Barlow from individuals represents 96% of his campaign’s total contributions and amount to more than four times the number of individual contributions made to Brent Bien’s and Megan Degenfelder’s campaigns..



Which candidate gets the biggest checks?
Megan Degenfelder’s in- and out-of-state contributors give more on average than contributors to Eric Barlow’s and Brent Bien’s campaigns. Degenfelder’s average out-of-state contributions are more than triple her closest rival.



Who’s getting the most help from family?
Eric Barlow received $20,000 in contributions from his mother and his late father’s trust. Brent Bien received $750 from his brother, Bill Bien, of Harrisburg, Pennsylvania. Megan Degenfelder’s campaign received no direct family contributions, but received $522,000 in loans — $497,000 from her father, Steve, and a loan from herself for $25,000 — amounting to roughly 40% of her total campaign contributions.



What about anonymous and in-kind contributions?
Brent Bien has benefitted the most from anonymous and in-kind contributions, together representing nearly a third of his campaign’s total contributions.



Which candidate has received the most PAC money?
Megan Degenfelder’s campaign has received a total of $392,500 in PAC contributions, with all but $7,000 coming from Wyoming PACs. Barlow trails by about $150,000. Brent Bien has accounted for a total of $6,500 in funding from two Wyoming PACs.



Where’s the money from outside Wyoming coming from?
While the vast majority of contributions have come from Wyoming residents, people from 35 other states have contributed to the three Republican candidates’ campaigns. Bubble size corresponds to individual contributions to any of the three candidates, but doesn’t necessarily mean individual contributors. One Virginia man, for example, has contributed small sums between $6 and $11 to Eric Barlow’s campaign more than 30 times.



So what stands out about each candidate’s fundraising?
Eric Barlow’s campaign balance sheet shows the strongest support from individuals, with another significant chunk from Wyoming PACs. Brent Bien also sees sizable support from individuals, including anonymous and in-kind contributions. Megan Degenfelder’s largest source of campaign funding is loans from her father, followed by roughly equal support from Wyoming PACs and individuals.



For more information about candidates in Wyoming’s federal, state and legislative races, check out WyoFile’s 2026 Election Guide.

title: The future is ‘bright.’ Wyoming gubernatorial candidates attend youth town hall.
description:
Three candidates talked mental health, career opportunities and civic engagement with students during a Boys and Girls Clubs forum Thursday in Riverton.
The post The future is ‘bright.’ Wyoming gubernatorial candidates attend youth town hall. appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
RIVERTON—The vocabulary word of the day for the students gathered Thursday at the Boys and Girls Club was “constituent.”
It was apt for the students aged 11 through 17, who have been preparing for weeks to ask questions of Wyoming’s gubernatorial candidates. It was also appropriate for the three GOP candidates — Megan Degenfelder, Eric Barlow and Brent Bien — who glimpsed into the minds of the state’s future voters. Some of the club members will be old enough to vote in November. 
The students asked about a variety of issues, including: mental health, workforce needs, stress management and the use of public funds for youth-enrichment programs like theirs. 
The students — members of Boys and Girls Clubs in towns like Casper, Riverton and Glenrock — may only represent a small percentage of the state’s current population, noted moderator Preston Blakeley, area director of Boys and Girls Clubs of Central Wyoming. 
“But they are 100% of the future,” he said. “They deserve that opportunity to sit at this table and invest their voices in what’s going to happen in the future.”
Based on the sample of young people in attendance and the opportunities that exist in Wyoming, Bien observed, “I think the future is incredibly bright.”
New POV 
Wyoming Boys and Girls Clubs invited members this spring to participate in the forum, said Ashley Bright, CEO of Boys and Girls Clubs of Central Wyoming. Club members responded to a call for interest with video pitches, and 13 gathered in Riverton for the event.  
Members had worked with staff to develop and winnow questions. They took turns asking candidates how Wyoming loses its young people, about the pressures of public life and the state’s most significant challenges. 
The forum brought the candidates face to face with a different demographic than the crowds they’ve been courting during months of campaigning. 
Gubernatorial candidate and state Sen. Eric Barlow chats with sisters Brook and Brynn McCarthy, 14 and 17, on Aug. 13, 2026, in Riverton during a town hall hosted by Wyoming Boys and Girls Clubs Alliance. (Katie Klingsporn/WyoFile)
Barlow grew up on a Campbell County ranch, served in the Marine Corps and worked as a veterinarian. He was elected to Wyoming’s House of Representatives in 2013 and served as speaker of the House before switching chambers. Degenfelder grew up in Casper as a ranch kid, avid sports player and member of her local Boys and Girls Club, she told the forum. The University of Wyoming graduate was elected superintendent of public instruction in 2022. Bien is a retired U.S. Marine Corps captain who also grew up in Wyoming. He unsuccessfully challenged Gov. Mark Gordon in 2022. 
A fourth Republican candidate, Curt Blake, did not attend the forum.  
The candidate who prevails in Tuesday’s primary election will face Democrat Kenneth Casner and the Constitution Party’s Rebecca Bextel in the general election. 
Flip phones and prayer
Candidates distinguished themselves Thursday with different priorities and styles. 
Bien wore a bolo tie, Barlow donned cowboy boots and a tie and Degenfelder appeared in what has become her signature look: firetruck-red blazer, lipstick and nails. 
Superintendent of Public Instruction and candidate for governor Megan Degenfelder chats with Landon Bowman, 14, on Aug. 13, 2026, in Riverton during a town hall hosted by Wyoming Boys and Girls Clubs Alliance. (Katie Klingsporn/WyoFile)
Though Degenfelder has campaigned on the endorsement of President Donald Trump, she did not mention him. She talked about the rise of skilled vocational trades in Wyoming, promising economic opportunities for young people and the comfort she finds in her four dogs. When asked about how she handles criticism that comes with public office, she noted that the top of the hill is always the windiest. She also brought up Wyoming’s state animal, the bison. 
“They are one of the only animals that in a snowstorm turn and face into the storm because they instinctively know that that’s the quickest way through,” she said. 
When asked about young people leaving the state, Barlow said he himself left Wyoming for 16 years before coming back and finding meaningful opportunities. Rather than focusing solely on a job, he encouraged the members to think about what kind of life they want to live and build a career around that. When asked about how he deals with stress, he told them he prays each morning, goes on long walks and abstains from social media. To illustrate the latter, he held up his flip-phone. 
“There are places that are just not healthy to go,” he said of social media. Later, he stressed the importance of civil dialogue and said he’ll work with everyone, regardless of views, to forge solutions. 
Gubernatorial candidate Brent Bien talks to Jorja Lyon, 16, on Aug. 13, 2026, in Riverton during a town hall hosted by Wyoming Boys and Girls Clubs Alliance. (Katie Klingsporn/WyoFile)
Bien said one major thing he’ll do to make a better future for young people is limit government. He talked about how important his nuclear family was as a child, stressed community involvement and lauded the club members for getting a jump on that involvement. Losing young people to other states, Bien said, is not unique to Wyoming.
“It’s not a nuance to Wyoming by any means, but the objective here is to bring you back, and I think a lot of that comes down to the cost of living, those kind of things,” he said.

title: ‘When things are bad, scrub floors’
description:
To ease election anxiety, columnist Jessica Brauer suggests looking at the day as more than just an opportunity to vote.
The post ‘When things are bad, scrub floors’ appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
On the door of my office is a Post-It note that says, “When things are bad, scrub floors.”
The line belongs to Emma Goldman, a Russian-born anarchist and labor organizer who immigrated to the United States at 16. Her opposition to World War I and her anti-draft activism spurred J. Edgar Hoover, then director of intelligence for the U.S. Justice Department, to push for her deportation in 1919. After over thirty years of organizing, she said in her deportation trial that her love for this country was like that of a man enchanted by beauty with his eyes open to a woman’s flaws. 

Opinion

I look at Goldman’s words as often as I cross through the threshold of my workplace. It’s become a touchstone after tough days.
My tough days are no different from most. They’re made by way of overfilled calendars, tense conversations and a fight to keep my worn-out body in the community-building game. Sometimes tough means another grant funding denial or broken toilet, and other times it’s a jarring medical bill or more breaking news of a worrisome policy passed. 
As primary election day creeps closer, the anxious buzz of “What’s next?” is palpable. The mailbox stacks higher with near-daily mailers that read as if they’re the handiwork of schoolyard bullies. A sticky tension fills the dry, wildfire-hazed air. I look to my peers and wonder: What happens when these offices are filled? Has the strain and tension only just begun? No one really knows.
However, I do know how to scrub the proverbial floors. And I believe, to do so, is as nourishing for me as for the house. 
When I was young, I remember waking up in the night and finding my mom deep cleaning the hallway closet. She’d move all the coats and bins out and tidy the space spotless before going to sleep with the rest of the house. Then, I thought she’d lost her mind. Now, I know what it’s like to feel the relief of easy sleep after a restless rumble with a task. 
When my colleagues find me tidying file archives or Xerox toner tubes, they know, as much as I do, I’m doing it for my weary heart. When it feels like you can’t win, you can always organize your pens.
This week we’ll learn what’s ahead for us on November’s Election Day — in our city council chambers, on the state House floors, within the offices of our federal representatives in Washington. 
If we’re lucky, we’ll all be greeted with a victory worth celebrating. A trusted candidate will move forward, and a yard sign may proudly stay rooted in the lawn. And also, we’ll likely learn the news that something didn’t go the way we’d wanted. We’ll console a losing opponent, or realize we must now begin our due diligence to pick the next-best representative for us.
When I discovered that this month’s publication fell on the weekend before primary election day, my first thought was one of sheer panic. What do you say to the state you love so dearly as this season unfolds? How do you mourn your community’s integrity while staying hopeful for change? 
Goldman herself didn’t have much faith in the ballot box. But this week, that’s precisely the tool we have.
My hope is that during this important week ahead, you do two things. 
First, you vote. 
Second, you look around you — across your downtown streets, school classrooms, community gathering spaces and beyond — and give something some love, whether you pull sidewalk weeds, pick trash from the alleyway or help a stranger carry their groceries to the car. 
To scrub the floors of your place is to tend to its future well-being. 
As we wait for what’s next, let’s tidy and clear the debris of what’s gathered, knowing, like in any home, it will return to be scrubbed once more.

title: I didn’t know what to believe so I became a Wyoming election judge.
description:
Forget the shadowy conspiracies about ballot harvesting and undocumented voters. Guest columnist and frequent election judge Susan Stubson explains how she knows your vote is safe.
The post I didn’t know what to believe so I became a Wyoming election judge. appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
On Tuesday, primary day, I’ll wake up at 4:30 a.m. I’ll be dressed and out the door by 5:30 a.m.  I’ll swing through the drive-thru, order coffee: black, straight up, three shots of espresso. I’m gonna need it. 
I am an election judge. This is my story. 

Opinion

Election Day is like Christmas. The magic, the civic energy, the anticipation; Will there be a strong voter turnout? Who’s going to win? The first time I voted I had just turned 18 and it was a presidential election year.  I was still an unformed human, yet they trusted me with a ballot. I couldn’t believe my good fortune. I had a voice. It was thrilling. 
Now, the election process, forever a trusted institution, is under attack. In 2016, according to the Pew Research Center, 90% of voters say they were at least somewhat confident their own vote was accurately counted.  A decade later, only 55% are confident this November’s midterm elections will be conducted fairly and accurately.  
There is no cogent reason to support voter skepticism. In Wyoming, there have been four voter fraud convictions in the past 25 years. Nearly all the lawsuits filed by President Donald Trump and others contesting election processes following the 2020 presidential election have been dismissed or dropped for lack of evidence. Yet, trust in elections continues to slide.
I struggle to connect this weedy, thorny field of suspicion with reality. Frankly, all this unsupported, frothed-up fear regarding elections was killing my joy. So, several years ago, I volunteered to work the polls as an election judge and see for myself. Should I be concerned?  
For those who wonder whether an election is safe, this one’s for you. 
On Election Day, I arrive at my assigned polling station before 6 a.m. Coffee in hand, I also pack a water bottle, lunch, a book and Ibuprofen. I dress for all seasons, from arctic to stifling air. I bring a seat cushion. Sitting on a metal folding chair for 13 hours is no picnic. The seats are insufferable, an enemy to the coccyx.
County clerk personnel have been at the polling places hours before the volunteers. Who knows when they got there. While the county sleeps, hundreds of staff members are busy lugging, assembling, adjusting, just doing, like nervous bridesmaids minutes before the ceremony. They care.
Once we enter the polling place, we cannot leave. That’s the law. They warn us of that in our training. By resigning ourselves to being trapped in an industrial, acoustically barren building with suspect ventilation, we submit to the jurisdiction of the paranoid and conspiratorial masses, loopy on visions of ballot harvesters ferrying ballots to dark, webby places. Whatever it takes to convince the public and honor voter concerns, baseless or not, we’ll do it.  
I find an empty seat before a darkened monitor and wait to be checked in by an IT staff member. Each judge has a password specific to that computer. We sign a chain of custody form, which allows auditors to trace a ballot’s journey from judge to voter to tabulation. If there’s any funny stuff, the ballot can be tracked. 
At 7 a.m., the doors unlock, and the manager announces, “The polls are open!” We whoop and holler. We’re trained and ready to serve.  
It’s go time. 
Bring your tired, your weary, your mailers’ fatigue, your yearnings to the polls. Mostly, bring your ID.  
An election judge is a cog in the machination of this Great American Experiment, a witness to the mundane, to the bland ordinariness of an election cycle. Election judges are volunteers. Each year, they take a day off from work, arrange childcare, navigate school pick-up, off-load their obligations to work the polls. They are your neighbors, your friends. We do it because we believe in the system.  
Before the election, we attend training. The county clerk walks us through a 100-slide presentation developed by the Wyoming Secretary of State’s Office. We learn to navigate the election software, we do mock registrations. We run through a million different scenarios: a voter at the wrong polling station, name change, party affiliation confusion, felons whose rights have been restored. What to do when we make a mistake, which is inevitable. You name it, there’s a process for that. 
We take an oath for election officials not once, but twice — first at our training and again on Election Day. We swear to perform our duties impartially, to root out fraud or abuse. 
Through the years, the training has gotten more formal, more intense. It’s been hard to keep up with the rush of new election laws. The secretary of state’s office shows eight new election integrity laws in 2025 alone.  
The last election cycle was the first time we discussed security and what-to-do-if scenarios. That rattled me a little. 
We verify citizenship. In the 10 years I’ve worked at the polls, I cannot remember an undocumented person attempting to vote. My friends in the faith community who are busy ferrying groceries and school supplies to a rattled, undocumented community too terrified to leave their homes, tell me it’s unlikely an illegal alien would show up at the polls. Think through that my friends. 
For those suckling on the teat of a vast conspiracy to steal your vote, take a beat and ask yourself, do you really think an illegal immigrant is stealing our vote? To what end and for whose benefit? Play out your theory for me please.  
Instead, focus on the county clerks who work tirelessly every day to make sure elections run smoothly. Have faith in them. They take their work seriously and are proud of the work they do.  
You’ve seen museum curators handle the Magna Carta, the Dead Sea Scrolls, the Mona Lisa, Michelangelo’s David. Pick your treasure. That’s how your ballot is tendered. 
County clerks are the guardians of our constitutional rights, they understand the right to vote is sacred, a gift given to us by the glorious fiat of our citizenship. 
That feeling of walking into the poll booth for the first time has never left me. A poll booth has always felt like a secret garden, those cardboard walls envelop you, a lushy hedge for your thoughts, just you, your opinions and an empty oval waiting for the press of your pen. What a gift. 
Your vote is cherished, honored, respected and handled with care. County clerks, their staff, all the poll workers, they don’t care how you vote. They care the system is safe. They care you vote. 
See you Tuesday.
Susan Stubson serves on WyoFile’s board of directors. Neither she, nor any other member of the board, has the authority to direct or determine coverage. —Ed.

title: Sun ‘Strutts’ its stuff through wildfire smoke
description:
On Yellowstone Lake, wildfire smoke tints the sunrise and sunset.
The post Sun ‘Strutts’ its stuff through wildfire smoke appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
Over Yellowstone Lake, wildfire smoke turns the rays of the rising and setting sun orange, a phenomena caused by Rayleigh scattering of light.
Rayleigh scattering is the result of particles — such as those in wildfire smoke — that are smaller than light’s wavelengths. They diffuse rays and create specific colors. Without extra particles, the sky appears blue. With smoke, orange or red.
The phenomena takes its name after the third Baron Rayleigh, one John William Strutt. Strutt lived in Essex, England, from 1842-1919. A scientist as well as a nobleman, he won the Nobel Prize in physics for codiscovering argon. He described the light-bending properties of airborne particles, “the first theoretical treatment of the elastic scattering of light,” according to a Wikipedia summary.
You could say that with wildfire smoke, the sun Strutts its stuff.
The photograph above shows the morning phenomena at Yellowstone Lake’s West Thumb. West Thumb is a “caldera within a caldera,” a lake lobe created by a volcanic explosion 174,000 years ago. The Thumb is about 5.5 miles long and 4 miles wide.
Boating in Yellowstone Lake is rewarding but fraught with peril. Aside from car wrecks and illnesses, drowning is the largest single cause of death in Yellowstone. Yellowstone Lake is the site where the most have occurred — about 40, according to former Yellowstone National Park historian Lee Whittlesey.
“All things considered, no body of water in Yellowstone Park and probably in all of the United States is more potentially dangerous,” he writes in Death in Yellowstone. The most recent drowning — of a kayaker from Denver — occurred in June.
At 7,733 feet, Yellowstone Lake is the largest lake in North America above 7,000 feet. It is 20 miles long, 14 miles wide and covers 132 square miles. Cold water and winds make safety challenging.
Yet the lake’s remote southern arms provide a window into wilderness where paddlers can hear elk bugle and wolves howl.

title: An 1876 Colorado ‘railroad war’ climaxed with the kidnapping of a federal judge
description: On the morning of Aug. 15, 1876, Judge Amherst Stone left Golden on a northbound Colorado Central Railroad train to Boulder, where he was expected to formalize a ruling that would put the financially troubled railroad into receivership. He never arrived. Just north of Ralston Creek, near the site that would eventually be known as […]
text:
A Colorado Central Railroad train in Clear Creek Canyon is pictured in this late 19th-century photograph by Joseph Collier. (Courtesy of Denver Public Library Special Collections, C-78)On the morning of Aug. 15, 1876, Judge Amherst Stone left Golden on a northbound Colorado Central Railroad train to Boulder, where he was expected to formalize a ruling that would put the financially troubled railroad into receivership.



← Aug. 6–12
Aug. 13–19 

This story is part of Colorado at 150.

He never arrived. Just north of Ralston Creek, near the site that would eventually be known as Rocky Flats, the train was stopped by a pile of railroad ties that had been placed on the track.
“Twenty-five armed men took Judge Stone from the train six miles this side of Ralston; took him to the mountains,” read a frantic telegram that arrived in Denver that afternoon, according to the following day’s Rocky Mountain News.
The “railroad wars” of the Wild West were largely fought in courtrooms and bank offices, but for a brief moment in the history of the newly proclaimed state of Colorado, they carried the threat of real violence.
The Colorado Central, which ran along the northern Front Range and up Clear Creek Canyon as far as Floyd Hill, was the pride of Jefferson and Boulder counties, controlled by a board of directors made up of local businessmen and elected officials. But the company had fallen behind on interest payments in the depression that followed the Panic of 1873.
The subsequent move by “Eastern capitalists,” including railroad tycoon Jay Gould, to “steal the road from the territory,” as the Boulder Banner put it, was bitterly resented by residents there. Years after the “Golden Gang” had lost out to the “Denver Ring” in the battle over which city would be Colorado’s capital and main railroad hub, the planned appointment of Denver’s David H. Moffat as the receiver of the insolvent Colorado Central confirmed the worst fears of its longtime investors.
“The idea of a receiver has all along been violently opposed by the county stockholders,” conceded the Golden Globe. “But had a receiver been appointed less identified than is Moffat with the Union Pacific, there would have been no such disgraceful scene as that which was witnessed the other day.”

Nearly 60 years later, longtime Golden resident Carlos Lake would confess to being one of the masked men who’d boarded the train and abducted Stone. The scheme had been hatched by several prominent locals, including two county judges, to prevent the judge “from getting to Boulder on the last day of the term of court, when the appointment was to be made.”
“When I got to where the judge was, I put my hand on his shoulder. He never had seen me until he turned around; I had a big gun and I stuck that under his nose,” Lake would write. “I reached around and grabbed him by the arm and pulled him out of the seat and away we went and got down to the platform.”
The sheriffs of both Boulder and Jefferson counties ordered deputies to pursue Stone’s kidnappers, while several irregular companies of state militia marched from Denver on Gov. John Routt’s orders. But Lake and his fellow abductors eluded capture, and held Stone overnight before letting him go the next day.
Colorado history rhymes

Denver newspapers, close allies of Moffat and the rest of the city’s business elite, howled with outrage over the incident: “MOB LAW — Colorado Central Banditti on the Rampage,” declared the Rocky Mountain News (which had, only weeks earlier, excused the extrajudicial executions of two murder suspects by a Cañon City lynch mob).
Stone’s kidnapping reignited old tensions between Denver, which was firmly in the hands of a Republican political machine, and its more Democratic-leaning neighbors. Boulder residents denounced the kidnapping but took exception to Routt’s arrival in town at the head of 60 militiamen, “who were stationed in our streets, as if the whole town were a lawless mob.”
In Golden, the weekly Globe, Colorado’s leading Democratic newspaper, at first estimated that “probably not one-tenth” of Jefferson County residents approved of the mob’s actions.
“This very act, had it occurred in one of the southern states, would have been denounced as a Ku Klux outrage,” wrote the Globe’s editors on Aug. 19. “It is true that the people have had every provocation for feeling outraged and trampled upon by a corporation, which seeks to obtain sanction to its robbing schemes in the courts, but this is no reason why they should resort to brute force and violence against one of the judiciary.”
In a terse addendum later in the same column, however, the Globe was forced to admit that public opinion was much more in favor of the vigilantism than it had hoped.
“Since putting the above in type, public sentiment has changed,” the editors added. “Nearly every man we meet considers the abduction a proper and expedient measure. Some say that the mob should have strung the judge to the first tree. The most intense excitement prevails.”
The fight over ownership of the Colorado Central went on for several more years. Local investors, led by William A.H. Loveland, briefly regained control of the railroad in 1877, but after further bankruptcy proceedings its tracks were acquired by the Union Pacific in 1879. The railroad reached Georgetown the same year, and part of its right-of-way survives today as the Georgetown Loop tourist attraction.
Though a grand jury was convened to investigate Stone’s kidnapping, no one was ever charged. Lake made his confession at a 1935 Elitch Gardens picnic hosted by the Society of Colorado Pioneers, while serving as the group’s vice president — and with Gov. Edwin “Big Ed” Johnson, Denver Mayor Ben Stapleton and other prominent state officials in attendance.
“From the way Gov. Johnson and the others received the confession of Lake, it is safe to predict that no action will be taken at this time,” reported the Golden Transcript.



Selected sources

The Rocky Mountain News, Aug. 16, 1876
The Golden Globe, Aug. 19, 1876
The Boulder Banner, Aug. 17, 1876

name: Maryland Matters
title: County leaders look for options as budgets get tighter
description: County leaders said they need more options to help weather mounting budget pressures driven by reductions in state aid coupled with costs shifted to local governments and mandated education spending.
text:
Local government leaders are looking to Annapolis for flexibility in revenue generation and crossing their fingers that a solution for a projected structural budget gap next year does not mean that the state will cut aid or require counties to pay more for services covered by in the state budget. (File photo courtesy of the Executive Office of the Governor.)County leaders said they need more options to help weather mounting budget pressures driven by reductions in state aid coupled with costs shifted to local governments and mandated education spending.
Those same leaders are understandably edgy as they wait for signs of how state government — the bigger dog on the porch — will resolve its own fiscal crisis. Past solutions have frequently come at the expense of county governments who rely on billions in state aid to balance their books and deliver key services.
“There’s a lot of things that hold down to counties, and unfortunately, counties don’t have anybody else,” said Harford County Treasurer Robert Sandless. “The feds kick things down to the states. States kick things down to the counties, and then we turn around and there’s nobody to kick it down to.”
Sandless, speaking to a packed room of local government leaders attending the Maryland Association of Counties summer convention in Ocean City, warned of an additional concern involving volatile income tax payments to the counties.
“What I’m telling you is that there’s going to be a reckoning next year, probably with your income tax,” he said. “We’ve already been told by the comptroller that we are over-distributing as a whole, and so we’re going to see more of that kind of that volatility.”
All of this comes at a time when the state has pushed down additional costs to the counties and mandated beefed up education spending.
SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE
“What we’re struggling with now is a state government that continually pushes down their liabilities and responsibilities to us, and that’s what’s going to break us,” said Talbot County Finance Director Martha Sparks. “Those things that we don’t have any control over: blueprint, additional costs for SDAT [the State Department of Assessments and Taxation], teachers’ pensions. That’s what the state needs to do to give us relief, not other options to raise revenue to pay their bills. ”
At the state level, there is a projected structural budget gap of about $3 billion for the coming fiscal year. Lawmakers and Maryland’s governor will face tough decisions including budget cuts that reduce spending in future years and the potential for tax increases.
One possibility is an increase in income tax, potentially for high income households. Changes to the sales tax might also be discussed.
Maryland has not raised its sales tax since 2008 when it went from 5% to 6%. An increase of a penny could generate an additional $1.2 billion in revenue. Sales taxes are seen as regressive as they hit lower-income families disproportionately harder than higher-income groups.
Another possibility would be to apply the sales tax to services. The legislature could also raise the rate and expand its application.
Local governments have fewer options, relying heavily on property taxes and local income taxes.
A legislative panel is looking at potential revenue sources for local governments including the potential for local taxes on restaurants and changes to land use taxes.
Some have also floated the idea of a local component to the sales tax that would go to jurisdictions.
It’s unclear what recommendations — if any — will come out of that group by the time the General Assembly reconvenes in January. And it may be difficult to get lawmakers to agree to more local taxing authority as it could likely restrict what the state can collect to cover its own budget needs.
Last year, Baltimore Mayor Brandon Scott (D) proposed a 2% increase in the sales tax that would go to the city. The proposal ultimately stalled.
Maryland is one of nine states that does not authorize local governments to levy a sales tax, according to Felix Facchine, chief of staff to Howard County Executive Calvin Ball (D).
“Part of the problem is that Maryland doesn’t actually collect sales tax by point of origin right now,” Facchine said.
The state is projected to collect $6.6 billion in sales taxes in the current fiscal year, according to a projection issued by the Board of Revenue Estimates in March. That panel will update its estimates next month.
The lack of data makes it difficult to determine sales taxes collected in each jurisdiction, Facchine said.
Sandless said he hopes for a menu of options from which each county can pick and choose.
“What I’m hoping for is that while not all of the solutions that we have are going to be ideal for every county, you know, vacant land, you know, makes a lot more sense in densely urban areas than it does in more rural counties,” Sandless said. “But I’m hoping that they provide us all with the same toolbox set, so that we, as local leaders, can figure out what works best.”

name: Tennessee Lookout
title: Local officials in the dark about contract naming Adams as ICE call center site
description: Local officials on Thursday were still seeking information about a multi-million-dollar government contract with an Alaska-based corporation designating Adams, Tennessee as the location of a national immigration enforcement call center.  A summary document posted on the federal government’s contract website shows it has entered into a contract of up to $63 m[...]
text:
Robertson and Montgomery County officials have no information about a Department of Homeland Security call center to be established in rural Robertson County, where this detention was photographed,  to aid local law enforcement agencies across the nation. (Photo: John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)Local officials on Thursday were still seeking information about a multi-million-dollar government contract with an Alaska-based corporation designating Adams, Tennessee as the location of a national immigration enforcement call center. 
A summary document posted on the federal government’s contract website shows it has entered into a contract of up to $63 million with a subsidiary of Alaska Native corporation Koniag to run a round-the-clock call center to provide real-time information to police and sheriffs across the nation who have entered into cooperative agreements with Immigration and Customs Enforcement.
Officials in Robertson and Montgomery counties — the rural town of about 600 people straddles both jurisdictions — said they had received no information about the plans to establish a federal call center in the rural community. 
“We have our folks looking into it,” Montgomery County Mayor Wes Golden wrote in a Thursday email. Golden said he had learned about the existence of the contract from a media report on Wednesday. 
Chris Traughber, assessor of property for Robertson County, said Thursday there had been “lots of inquiries here but no new information.” Traughber said he had checked with the county’s planning department, which routinely assesses infrastructure capacity and property uses. They hadn’t heard anything either, he said. 
Federal contract documents show ICE 24-hour call center planned for Adams, Tennessee

Representatives of Immigrant and Customs Enforcement and Koniag Services did not respond Thursday to requests for further information. 
In a statement to the Lookout on Monday, a Koniag spokesperson declined to respond to questions about the size, precise location or workforce involved.  
“Unfortunately, we are not at liberty to discuss this very recently awarded contract at this time,” Joanie Barr, senior vice president for business operations for Koniag Government Services, said via email Monday. 
While details about the operation remain opaque, Koniag in recent days began posting job descriptions for senior- level positions at a call center operating under contract with “government clients.” 
The company by Thursday had posted 29 positions. Job listings refer to the location of performance as either Nashville or “in the Nashville area.” The positions require varying levels of federal security clearances.
Among the listings: “facility manager of an IT call center operations in support of our government clients in the Nashville, Tennessee area.” The job description says the position “oversees the design, leasing, buildout, and day‑to‑day operations of a secure, mission-critical Level II facility supporting safety, and security functions.”

SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX. 
The government’s description of the contract responsibilities, in a document published in November soliciting bids, said its primary function would be to operate a call center capable of handling an estimated 6,000-7,000 daily inquiries from law enforcement agencies across the nation that have entered into cooperative agreements with Immigration and Customs Enforcement. 
It is not yet known whether any component of the government’s request for bids has been altered or amended. The Tennessee Lookout requested a copy of Koniag’s contract Thursday. 
The number of so-called 287(g) cooperative agreements between ICE and local law enforcement agencies have proliferated under the second Trump administration as it seeks to carry out its mass deportation aims. 
The agreements deputize local police officers, constables and sheriffs’ deputies to perform many of the functions of ICE agents, increasing the reach of the government’s immigration enforcement powers. There are currently more than 2,300 such agreements across the nation. 
The contract solicitation document describing the functions of the call center appears to more closely integrate the work of local police and federal immigration authorities. 
Another job listing on the company’s website is for an intelligence analyst ”to support critical missing persons investigative operations in Nashville, TN” and requires “knowledge of the National Center for Missing & Exploited Children (NCMEC) resources and reporting protocols” and “experience supporting task force operations or multi-agency investigative teams.”
The description posted in November describes an “integration and location cell” to locate unaccompanied migrant children as part of the contractual agreement. The document specifies that entails “provid(ing) 287(g) partners and field offices with (unaccompanied migrant children) targeting focus and material,” interpreted by immigration rights advocates as providing intelligence for immigrant children to potentially be deported.

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: NC’s State Board of Elections must stand up for student voters
description: Ahead of November’s midterm election, anti-voter majorities on county boards of elections across North Carolina have targeted student voters by proposing plans to remove or exclude on-campus early voting locations. If approved, these plans will make voting harder not only for students, but for hundreds of faculty, staff, and community members who work on or[...]
text:
NC A&T State University tried unsuccessfully on Jan. 13, 2026 to have the NC Board of Elections approve an early voting site for the 2026 primary elections on the Greensboro HBCU's campus.(Photo: Lynn Bonner/NC Newsline)Ahead of November’s midterm election, anti-voter majorities on county boards of elections across North Carolina have targeted student voters by proposing plans to remove or exclude on-campus early voting locations. If approved, these plans will make voting harder not only for students, but for hundreds of faculty, staff, and community members who work on or live around these campuses.
Having grown up in Boone, I’m extremely familiar with this tactic to restrict student access to early voting locations. In 2013, I watched the Watauga County BOE cut an on-campus polling place at Appalachian State University for the 2013 municipal elections and again for the 2014 midterms. Even after a court found that the board had removed this site in 2014 explicitly to suppress student voters and ordered it restored, the Watauga Board tried to remove it again for the 2016 primaries. Thankfully, the State Board of Elections stepped in to overrule that decision on a bipartisan basis.
 A coordinated attack on North Carolina’s student voters
Earlier in 2026, several counties took a page from the Watauga BOE playbook and began cutting on-campus early voting sites for this year’s primary election. Jackson, Guilford, and Pasquotank counties are poised to do the same for the November election.
For the 2026 primary, the Jackson County BOE and the State BOE voted to remove an early voting site at Western Carolina University, which had existed in every primary and general election since 2016. For the upcoming 2026 general election, the county board failed again to find the required unanimous consensus needed to reopen the WCU site,  leaving the decision in the hands of the State Board. The evidence shows that this is a deliberate, coordinated attack on young voters.  During a Jackson County BOE meeting on the issue, it was revealed that the state auditor’s office pressured Board members to vote against the WCU site—staff from the State Auditor’s office went so far as to send text messages to Jackson Board members urging them to cut the on-campus site, imploring the Board Members, “don’t let them have a vote.”
In Pasquotank County, a majority of the BOE passed a plan to move their only early voting location away from Elizabeth City State University’s campus—a site Pasquotank voters have used in general elections since 2020. Similarly, a majority of the Guilford County BOE rejected calls from community members to include early voting sites at UNC Greensboro and NC A&T. Together, these institutions serve nearly 34,000 students, in addition to faculty and staff.
 On-campus early voting sites are critical for students’ access — and safety
Students and other young voters face unique challenges getting to the polls. College-aged voters are among those least likely to own a car, and many do not have a driver’s license—in 2023, only 60% of 18-year-olds had a license, compared to nearly 90% of those over 35. Particularly in rural parts of North Carolina without robust public transportation, voting off campus without a car can become time-consuming, burdensome, and even dangerous.
For both the 2026 primary and general elections, for example, the proposed alternative location to the closed Western Carolina University on-campus site is nearly a mile-and-a-half walk from campus along a busy road with no sidewalks or crosswalks. Why would Jackson County not provide a more accessible polling location for an institution that serves 11,000 students—nearly a quarter of the County’s entire population—and employs hundreds of voter-eligible faculty and staff?
 Not just for students, but for the entire community
On-campus sites benefit more than just student voters. In addition to providing a centralized early voting location for faculty, staff, and surrounding residential communities, on-campus polling locations often provide critically needed infrastructure to better accommodate voters with disabilities—like ample parking and modern ADA-compliant facilities. This is particularly helpful during early voting when voters may choose any early voting location countywide to cast their ballot, allowing voters with disabilities to choose a site that suits their needs.
The decisions made in the coming weeks will determine whether thousands of North Carolina students can vote where they live, study, and contribute to their communities. The State Board of Elections has both the authority and the responsibility to prevent unnecessary barriers to participation.
Patrick Williamson is policy counsel with the nonprofit Fair Elections Center.

title: UMWA calls for ‘immediate’ enforcement of silica rule as black lung hits new high in WV, Appalachia
description: The United Mine Workers of America made an “urgent demand” of the federal government on Thursday for the “immediate, uncompromised” enforcement of previously approved policies and rules that would protect coal miners from incurable black lung disease. The call from the UMWA comes after new research this month shows that black lung rates have increased […]
text:
X-rays of a patient with black lung disease. (National Archives at College Park photo)The United Mine Workers of America made an “urgent demand” of the federal government on Thursday for the “immediate, uncompromised” enforcement of previously approved policies and rules that would protect coal miners from incurable black lung disease.
The call from the UMWA comes after new research this month shows that black lung rates have increased to an almost 50-year high after years of decline, with the highest rates of the disease found in miners from central Appalachia. 
“More needs to be done, and it needs to be done now,” said UMWA International President Brian Sanson in a news release. “Miners are wearing masks, they are following rules, and yet they are still breathing in killer dust. We will not stand by while federal regulations are ignored and sat on while our members and coalfield workers pay for it with their lives.”
According to the peer-reviewed research, which was published by workers with the National Institute of Occupational Safety and Health in the American Journal of Respiratory and Critical Care Medicine, a third of miners in central Appalachia who have spent 25 years or more underground now have black lung. That’s a fourfold increase compared to 1999, per the research.
Previous research reported that 1 in 5 miners in central Appalachia, about 20.6% of them, had been diagnosed with the disease.
The new research also shows that miners with as few as 15 years of experience underground are also suffering from a rise in disease rates that has not been seen in nearly 40 years.
And while the rates are increasing, the federal government has time and time again delayed interventions that experts say will slow the development of black lung in vulnerable miners. 
A federal rule that would have limited the allowable exposure limits for silica dust in coal mines for the first time ever was initially set to go into effect for coal operations in 2025 after being finalized by the U.S. Department of Labor and the Mine Health and Safety Administration in 2024. 
The rule, if implemented, would have been the first of its kind for silica dust in mines, despite evidence showing the dangers of exposure have existed for decades and other industries already enforce exposure limits. 
In addition to levying limits on exposure and implementing new action levels when a certain amount of silica dust is present in mines, it would have also required mine operators and companies to offer free medical monitoring for their workers with the hope of detecting black lung and other respiratory diseases earlier.
But, under the Trump administration, implementation of the rule was pushed from April 2025 back to August 2025. That month, it was pushed again to October. And in October, it was delayed yet again.
The lack of implementation stems from a lawsuit led by the National Sand, Stone and Gravel Association against the Labor Department requesting that the federal government block the implementation of the rule completely. None of the statutes affecting the NSSGA were slated to go into effect until 2027, per the rule.
In April, federal regulators indefinitely delayed the rule until court proceedings wrap up.
Now, the UMWA has three demands for the federal government and the court system that advocates believe could have immediate impact for affected miners:

Lift the legal stay that is stopping enforcement of the silica dust rule and begin enforcement of it immediately, without further administrative delays
Refuse requests from industry groups to rely on personal respirators or job rotations for required ventilation controls instead of implementing limits on silica dust exposure while underground
Increase federal oversight through random dust sampling on mines and enforce strict penalties against operators that are found to be not in compliance

Sanson said too much leeway has been given to industry groups and operators while miners have been left out to dry with little to no protections against black lung.
“Mining associations filed lawsuits arguing this rule hurts business, but what about the human lives destroyed every single day this rule sits on a shelf?” Sanson said. “Every day federal regulators drag their feet and sit on this rule, another working father, mother, husband, wife, sister or brother contracts an incurable, fatal disease. Someone’s life is forever changed. A company’s profit margin cannot take precedence over a miner’s right to draw a breath.”
