name: Louisiana Illuminator
title: Louisiana signs $192.6 million no-bid contract with Motorola for public safety, police technology
description: Louisiana lawmakers signed off Thursday on a 10-year, no-bid contract worth $192.6 million to provide public safety equipment and technology for law enforcement and the prison system.
text:
Louisiana lawmakers signed off Thursday on a 10-year, no-bid contract worth $192.6 million to provide public safety equipment and technology for law enforcement and the prison system. (Photo courtesy of Mark43)Louisiana lawmakers signed off Thursday on a 10-year, no-bid contract worth $192.6 million to provide public safety equipment and technology for law enforcement and the prison system. 

The deal gives Motorola $138.2 million to upgrade and maintain the Louisiana Wireless Information Network, a statewide radio system used during natural disasters The state will also pay the company $54.4 million to provide radios, license plate readers, body cameras, in-car video systems and related technology to police agencies, according to a draft of the contract. 

The arrangement goes into effect immediately and will expire Aug. 13, 2036. State agencies that will receive new cameras and radios through the deal include Louisiana State Police, Department of Wildlife and Fisheries, Department of Public Safety and Corrections, Division of Probation and Parole, Office of Juvenile Justice and State Fire Marshal. 
Motorola already had an exclusive, $49 million contract to maintain the statewide emergency radio network through 2030. The new arrangement is worth nearly four times that amount. It extends the company’s relationship with Louisiana for another five years and dramatically expands the services it will supply. 
Axon Enterprises Inc. has been providing Louisiana State Police its body cameras since troopers started wearing them in 2017, but the company was looking to charge nearly twice as much for its equipment over the next five years, Evelina Broussard, Gov. Jeff Landry’s chief information officer, said at a legislative hearing Thursday. 
Broussard said her office was able to secure greater savings for the state by agreeing to bundle Motorola services together over a longer period of time. As part of the deal, Motorola has also agreed to offer sheriffs and local law enforcement agencies the same discount on equipment it is giving the state. 
While the contract was not competitively bid, Louisiana State Police ran pilot programs using both Motorola and Axon equipment in 2025, according to documents shared with lawmakers. State officials said they chose to recommend Motorola because it was the more affordable option. 

“Motorola wins on the price,” state police chief administrative officer Robert Burns told lawmakers Thursday. 
Most state law enforcement agencies in the country use either Motorola or Axon for similar equipment, he said. 
Louisiana and local governments must spend at least $12.2 million per year combined with the company in order for the state to gain access to the deep discounts, according to a draft of the contract. 

In an interview, Landry’s Deputy Commissioner of Administration Bryan McClinton said the spending benchmark should be easily met since the state already plans to spend that amount of money annually on the radio network alone. 

Senate Democrats worried the contract was rushed through the approval process. Lawmakers first discussed it at a budget committee meeting on July 23. 

Senate Democratic Caucus Chairman Gerald Boudreaux of Lafayette said he was disappointed no additional hearing on the contract had been held before the lawmakers voted Thursday. 

Senate Pro Tempore Regina Barrow, D-Baton Rouge, said she was frustrated a draft of the contract hadn’t been provided to her until the day before Thursday’s meeting. 

“This is a lot to read and digest in 24 hours, and I think that is totally disrespectful,” Barrow told Landry administration officials. 

Broussard, Landry’s chief information officer, pushed back on criticism that the deal had not been subjected to enough public scrutiny. The governor’s budget staff could have entered into contracts for the public safety services without coming to the lawmakers for approval, she said. She chose to do so in order to be open with the legislators. 

“This is probably the most transparent deal that’s ever been done,” Broussard said. 

Though the contract lasts for 10 years, Senate President Cameron Henry, R-Metairie, said lawmakers have the authority to end it early. The agreement is contingent on the Louisiana Legislature providing money for the equipment and services in the annual state budget. 

“It’s a 10-year contract as long as we fund it for 10 years,” he said.

name: New Hampshire Bulletin
title: Beat the clock: The politics of daylight saving time in New Hampshire
description: The perennial debate over daylight saving time in the U.S. is coming around again, but for one New Hampshire state representative, it’s never gone away.  In fact, the matter has haunted Rep. Timothy Horrigan, a Durham Democrat, since the moment of his birth, on Oct. 3 — or was it Oct. 4? — 1956. At […]
text:
The sun sets behind Mount Cardigan on a late fall afternoon. The question of how to distribute the limited sunlight that falls on New Hampshire in the winter months is the subject of a long-running debate that has recently reemerged nationally. (Photo by Molly Rains/New Hampshire Bulletin)The perennial debate over daylight saving time in the U.S. is coming around again, but for one New Hampshire state representative, it’s never gone away. 
In fact, the matter has haunted Rep. Timothy Horrigan, a Durham Democrat, since the moment of his birth, on Oct. 3 — or was it Oct. 4? — 1956. At least, that’s how his mother always told it, Horrigan said in a phone interview last week.
When Horrigan was born in South Bend, Indiana, there was disagreement within the state about whether to observe standard time or daylight saving time, an hour ahead. Most people on the ground were observing daylight time, but official policy put the state on standard time, Horrigan said — so though, as his mother recalled, the clock on the delivery room wall showed 12:30 a.m., records put his first breath at approximately 11:30 p.m. on Oct. 3.
The uncertainty sown in that moment gave rise to Horrigan’s belief that eliminating the twice-yearly time change would be a straightforward way to simplify modern life. 
Horrigan has taken that belief to the State House, proposing multiple bills on the topic since 2011.
In his attempts to rally his fellow legislators around the idea of abolishing daylight time, Horrigan has emphasized a range of benefits he said New Hampshire would experience from such a change. Periodically shifting the schedule of our days by an hour, he says, is disruptive to people’s internal clocks and their overall health; ending the practice would alleviate that.
Indeed, medical professionals including the American Medical Association have called for the abolition of daylight saving time, citing health research on the negative effects of disruptions to the body’s natural daily rhythm. And other research suggests that the practice of changing the clocks can also disrupt roadways, with mixed impacts from sleep disruption and light changes causing some crashes to increase in the wake of the adjustment.
Horrigan also experiences seasonal affective disorder, sometimes called seasonal depression. Research, and Horrigan’s own experience, indicates that more sun exposure can help alleviate those symptoms; thus, the brighter mornings that year-round standard time would lead to, Horrigan believes, would help him and others make the most of the limited sunlight of the darkest months of the year. 
“Just going out, getting more sunlight helps,” he said. “… It would be more useful for me, like most people, to have the extra hour of daylight in the winter in the morning.”
Yet Horrigan’s proposals to end daylight saving time have thus far been quashed. This year, that pattern continued with House Bill 1149, which proposed New Hampshire adopt standard time year-round. The bill, co-sponsored by Rep. Joe Alexander, a Goffstown Republican, was voted down without leaving the House on a 13-2 recommendation from the House Committee on Executive Departments and Administration.
New Hampshire has also seen pushes in the other direction. Former Rep. Josh Yokela proposed a permanent shift to Atlantic Standard Time, which would in effect make daylight time permanent, in 2017, 2019, 2021, and 2024. Each measure was ultimately defeated or sent for interim study.
Nationally, standard time detractors include some in the field of agriculture. The American Farm Bureau Federation favors adopting daylight saving time permanently; the move would “provide consistency and reduce disruptions for farmers and ranchers,” the federation said in a statement. 
But in New Hampshire, feelings among farmers are nebulous — and the local branch of the federation does not have an official stance on the matter, said Robert Johnson, policy director for the New Hampshire Farm Bureau Federation.
In Johnson’s experience, New Hampshire farmers have a range of personal preferences and don’t rely only on the hands of the clock to time their work. 
“For the most part, I don’t believe there would be a great impact, as farms operate more by the sun and natural routines rather than artificial changes to the clock,” he said in an email. 
Those in some other fields have stronger feelings. New Hampshire broadcast media outlets would face “real problems” if the state fell out of step with nearby major markets, including Boston and New York, New Hampshire Association of Broadcasters representative Scott Spradling said during testimony on HB 1149 earlier this year. 
Horrigan said he believed he had addressed this by including a requirement in his bill that New Hampshire do away with daylight saving time only once Vermont, Massachusetts, Rhode Island, and Maine had all done so, or agreed to. But that’s not enough, Spradling said. He requested more coordination with other states if New Hampshire is serious about changing its time traditions.
“There’s a process by which this should be done, and it really … needs to involve the federal government because it needs to be the entire Eastern Seaboard making this decision and moving together and not disrupting commerce,” he said. 
Indeed, the debate is occurring at the national level, too, with two opposing measures proposing a national shift to standard time and to daylight saving time currently before Congress. President Donald Trump has favored the latter, deemed the “Sunlight Protection Act.”
“For many years, the vast Majority of Americans have asked to make Daylight Saving Time permanent,” he wrote Wednesday in a post on Truth Social. 
However, recent polling on the topic indicates that the public is, in fact, ambivalent. 
A Gallup poll released in March 2025 found that 54% of Americans wanted permanent standard time, compared to 40% in favor of permanent daylight time. Yet an AP-NORC poll released in October 2025 showed those numbers approximately flipped: 42% of Americans favored permanent standard time, and 56% wanted permanent daylight time, it said.
According to AP-NORC, while Americans are divided on which way to go from here, few like the practice we currently embrace of changing the clocks. 
That rings true for Horrigan, too, he said. He hopes the national debate yields some change, even if it’s a switch to permanent daylight time.
“I think if we just go one way or the other, that’s a lot simpler,” he said.
If Congress can’t decide, Horrigan, who is running for reelection, said he hopes to keep the long-running conversation going in New Hampshire himself.
“It’s an important issue, but it’s sort of a simple issue. … It’s nice having something that’s not quite as partisan, and everybody kind of knows the subject matter and has an opinion,” he said. “We’ll see what happens.”

name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: Young, Loeffler pitch expanded small business lending during Indiana visit
description: Federal small business loan limits should be dramatically increased to help farmers and manufacturers contend with rising equipment costs, U.S. Small Business Administration chief Kelly Loeffler said Thursday during an Indiana visit with U.S. Sen. Todd Young. Loeffler, a member of President Donald Trump’s cabinet, joined the Indiana Republican senator for a[...]
text:
U.S. Small Business Administration Administrator Kelly Loeffler and U.S. Sen. Todd Young discuss agriculture and small business issues on Thursday, Aug. 13, 2026, at the Indiana State Fair in Indianapolis. (Photo by Casey Smith/Indiana Capital Chronicle)Federal small business loan limits should be dramatically increased to help farmers and manufacturers contend with rising equipment costs, U.S. Small Business Administration chief Kelly Loeffler said Thursday during an Indiana visit with U.S. Sen. Todd Young.
Loeffler, a member of President Donald Trump’s cabinet, joined the Indiana Republican senator for a tour of an Indianapolis manufacturer before heading to the Indiana State Fair, where the pair met with farmers and participated in a discussion focused on agriculture and small businesses.
Young said businesses around Indiana are looking for greater certainty as they make decisions about investing and expanding, while farmers continue to face elevated input costs.
“The world is dynamic and uncertain right now, and that’s always the case, but especially so right now,” Young told reporters at the fair. “So, to the extent our policymakers can bring more certainty to public policy. That leads to capital investment in businesses, so that we can take our small businesses and grow them in the large enterprises that employ a lot of Hoosiers and other Americans.”
Young said he’s also hearing support from businesses for continuing federal tax policies and rolling back regulations.
Loeffler similarly argued that tax cuts, deregulation and the administration’s trade policies are helping boost manufacturing in rural communities. The two earlier toured Thomas & Skinner, a more than century-old Indianapolis-area small business.



Quotation







I think increasing the loan amounts would be rocket fuel for the economy.


– U.S. Todd Young


But during an agriculture-focused panel later Thursday, Young acknowledged challenges remain for farmers.
“I’ll say input costs go up and down. We’re in a cycle right now, and the input costs are elevated,” Young said. “Our farm community talks about that, but we’ll always need to be able to invest in more productivity so that you can manage those ups and downs more effectively.”
Loeffler said one way the federal government could help is by significantly increasing the amount small businesses can borrow through SBA-backed lending programs.
The maximum for SBA small business lending was last increased in 2010, Loeffler said, while the cost of farm and manufacturing equipment has risen considerably since then. She said the agency has started allowing borrowers to “stack” different loan types to reach $10 million, but wants to see an increase.
“Let’s double the loan size for people in production like agriculture and manufacturing to get up to that $20 million because that’s really what it takes in terms of scale today,” she said.
Young, a member of the Senate Small Business and Entrepreneurship Committee, indicated that he would support revisiting those limits.
“I think increasing the loan amounts would be rocket fuel for the economy,” Young said.
Young also said Thursday that he could soon take on a larger role shaping those policies. He said he is “probably going to become the next chairman of the Small Business Committee, depending on how the election goes in November.”
Trade, regulations and technology
Much of Thursday’s discussion focused on agriculture. Loeffler and Young praised the Trump administration’s efforts to reduce federal regulations and open foreign markets to U.S. products.
Loeffler highlighted efforts to change diesel exhaust fluid requirements and other regulations affecting farmers, truckers and other heavy industries. Young separately pointed to the administration’s support for farmers’ ability to repair their own equipment.
“A farmer ought to be able to fix their own combine without paying through the nose, and unfortunately, some of these manufacturers they design their systems these days so that you have to pay a lot of money for service,” Young said.
GOP cuts in federal food aid scramble passage of long-delayed farm bill

Trade was also up for discussion.
Loeffler argued the administration is pursuing “fair trade” by challenging tariff and non-tariff barriers facing American agricultural products. Young said efforts to address non-tariff barriers, particularly those affecting U.S. biotechnology products entering European markets, have received too little attention.
“When given a level playing field, I have to tell you our producers outcompete the entire world, and that’s all we want,” Young said.
The senator additionally pointed to Indiana’s investments in biotechnology, semiconductor manufacturing and drone technology as areas that could create new opportunities for farmers, manufacturers and rural communities.
Young said farmers are already more sophisticated in their use of artificial intelligence and drones than he had expected.
“Though there are a lot of uncertainties and risks in our ag economy right now, that’s inspiring, and it’s also encouraging as we get deeper into this disruptive age,” Young added.
Loeffler said access to workers remains one of the most common concerns she hears from small businesses nationally. Manufacturers the pair visited Thursday said they would hire more workers if they could find people with the necessary skills, she said.
Young weighs in on redistricting, farm bill
Young also fielded questions on issues beyond small business and agriculture during a media availability before the panel.
Asked whether Indiana has experienced — or could face — repercussions from the Trump administration after state lawmakers rejected a Republican push to redraw the state’s congressional districts, Young did not directly address whether he had seen evidence of retaliation.
“No, I stayed out of that,” Young said before pivoting to the November elections.

Have a news tip?


CONTACT US



He said Republicans he has spoken with around Indiana are “really unified as a state Republican Party” and predicted the party would benefit in the midterm elections.
Young said he also believes Congress is nearing agreement on a new farm bill.
Senate Agriculture Committee Chairman John Boozman of Arkansas has made “every effort” to advance the legislation and is engaged in tough negotiations, Young said.
“I’m told we’re pretty close, and you know, listen, we need to come together for the good of our rural communities and give them the risk management programs and the other basic programs that are required to feed the world,” Young said.

name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: Braun is playing fast and loose with gas tax suspension
description: I love saving money at the gas pump, but I fear the precedent Gov. Mike Braun is setting by ignoring state law in favor of unilateral executive power. And so should lawmakers. His gas tax holiday could turn into a loss of eight months in road funding — all without the involvement of the legislative […]
text:
Indiana Gov. Mike Braun speaks with leaders of St. Mary's Early Childhood Center in Indianapolis during a visit on Thursday, April 30, 2026. (Photo by Leslie Bonilla Muñiz/Indiana Capital Chronicle)I love saving money at the gas pump, but I fear the precedent Gov. Mike Braun is setting by ignoring state law in favor of unilateral executive power. And so should lawmakers.
His gas tax holiday could turn into a loss of eight months in road funding — all without the involvement of the legislative branch of state government. The first four months alone are expected to cost the state $533 million in losses reimbursed to the Indiana Department of Transportation and local units of government.
It’s a slippery slope to just start picking and choosing the laws our elected officials follow or not. And all people should be concerned about the rule of law, even if they agree with the ultimate result.
There are several reasons why the latest maneuver is on shaky ground.
The 1981 law allowing the governor to suspend transportation-related laws has two key elements. The first says a governor can declare an energy emergency for 60 days. The second says it can be renewed once. After that, the General Assembly must act for it to continue.
Braun used 30-day increments and renewed it three times under the first emergency. And last week he created an entirely new emergency, based not on the Iran war driving up gas prices but on Canadian wildfires and a four-year-old conflict in Ukraine.
It’s clearly a pretext to do what he wanted — extend the gas suspension — without calling in legislators for a special session.
GOP leadership in the House and Senate are on board. But that doesn’t make it right.
Braun announces new energy emergency, continues Indiana’s gas tax suspension

During the pandemic, when then-Gov. Eric Holcomb extended a public health emergency dozens of times, some fellow Republican lawmakers didn’t like it. But there was nothing in the law limiting the extensions.
That’s unlike this situation, where the law is pretty clear.
When legislators returned in 2021, one of the first things they did was restrict future health emergencies by a governor. And they made sure governors couldn’t pretext a new emergency.
“If a state of disaster emergency that applies to the entire state has ended, the governor may not call a new state of disaster emergency that applies to the entire state unless the new disaster is wholly unrelated to the earlier disaster,” the law now says.
Sound good? Too bad legislators didn’t think of that back in 1981 when writing the energy law.
What’s more is that I don’t think Indiana ever met the definition of an energy emergency in the first place. I’m not a lawyer, but I’ve read a lot of statutes over the years. Here is the exact definition:
“As used in this chapter, ‘energy emergency’ means an existing or projected shortfall of at least eight percent (8%) of motor fuel or of other energy sources that threatens to seriously disrupt or diminish energy supplies to the extent that life, health, or property may be jeopardized.”
The Braun administration has not provided proof of any shortfall at all, much less of 8%. And life, health or property is not being jeopardized. Let’s face it. This is just because the price is too high. Nothing more. There are no supply issues.
When reporters asked Braun what would happen if someone sued over his actions, he questioned what motives would be behind such a move.
The motives are simple to me. This is a question about the separation of powers between the executive and legislative branches. In this case, the legislative leaders agree, but imagine if they didn’t. Lawmakers don’t have the ability to call themselves into session, so one person could drain Indiana’s coffers by more than $1 billion with these repeated “emergencies.”
This is at worst breaking the law, and at best breaking the spirit of it.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Many immigrants with legal status could lose Medicare coverage
description: Hundreds of lawfully present immigrants in CT could lose Medicare health coverage in January, and officials must decide whether to help.
text:
Hundreds of immigrants lawfully present in Connecticut are slated to lose their Medicare coverage by January, the latest federal cutback that’s spurred some lawmakers and advocates here to call for state intervention.
But whether state officials will intervene early next year hinges not only on this fall’s gubernatorial campaign but also on which other distressed groups the General Assembly is looking to assist.
“This is year another inhumane, unconscionable action by an administration that targets people who have paid into Medicare, who have lawful status,” said Maggie Mitchell Salem, executive director of Integrated Refugee & Immigrant Services, or IRIS, a New Haven-based nonprofit.  “And it creates very real harm for individuals and families in the state of Connecticut and across the country.”
Salem is referencing a provision in the 2025 federal budget reconciliation measure, commonly referred to as the One Big Beautiful Bill Act or House Resolution 1, through which President Donald Trump and Congress changed rules that allow certain noncitizens to participate in Medicare and other benefits.
Lawfully present immigrants had been eligible for the federal medical insurance program if they met certain work history, disability or age requirements. The reconciliation measure limited eligibility to green card holders and certain immigrants from Cuba, Haiti, Micronesia, Palau and the Marshall Islands.
The Congressional Budget Office estimated that roughly 100,000 individuals nationally would lose Medicare coverage because of this provision. And though it didn’t provide state-by-state data, Connecticut contains 1% to 1.1% of the health insurance program’s caseload. That would translate, roughly, into 1,000 to 1,100 lawfully present immigrants here slated to lose coverage.
And though it is unclear exactly how many immigrants might lose coverage, Salem and the co-chairs of the General Assembly’s Public Health Committee — Sen. Saud Anwar, D-South Windsor, and Rep. Cristin McCarthy Vahey, D-Fairfield — said there could be a measurable impact on Connecticut’s hospitals and federally qualified health centers, which already are under financial strain.
Those that cannot afford healthcare not only seek free service through hospitals and health centers but also tend to wait until minor health conditions become severe, Anwar said.
“It is very clear in study after study that prevention is always better than cure, and our emergency rooms are overwhelmed,” he added.
“Hospitals are deeply concerned that new federal policies restricting access to Medicaid and Medicare, including changes affecting immigrant populations, as well as the loss of [Affordable Care Act] subsidies, will leave more people uninsured and increase uncompensated care,” the Connecticut Hospital Association wrote in a statement this week.
The CHA also called for “state and federal leaders to partner with hospitals to protect access to coverage and address growing financial pressures across the healthcare delivery system.”
Connecticut reached a new taxing arrangement with its hospitals this past spring that’s designed to bolster the industry by more than $1.6 billion over the next five years.
Shawn K. Frick, president and CEO of the Community Health Center Association of Connecticut, added that, “This loss of coverage due to HR 1 threatens the health of Connecticut residents and adds stress to an already-stretched healthcare system. Our health centers remain committed to serving all people, regardless of insurance status or ability to pay.”
The cost of treating the uninsured via hospital emergency rooms and health centers ultimately is borne by insured patients, taxpayers and healthcare providers, McCarthy Vahey noted, and said preserving access to care benefits many. 
“All of these [federal] changes to healthcare, in the end, are just going to make healthcare more expensive and make our population more unhealthy,” she said.
Both Public Health Committee chairs welcomed a discussion on using a special state reserve to assist immigrants losing Medicare.
Gov. Ned Lamont and the legislature have set aside $550 million from past state budget surpluses to mitigate cuts to federal healthcare, social and other programs. Lamont’s budget office reported last month that more than $263 million remained in the fund.
But when the 2027 legislation session convenes Jan. 6, some legislators are expected to recommend tapping the fund to help many groups, including low- and moderate-income families who’ve lost federal subsidies to buy health insurance; more than 30,000 adults and children who’ve lost Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program benefits; and about 110,000 poor adults expected to lose Medicaid coverage.
Sen. Cathy Osten, D-Sprague, co-chairwoman of the Appropriations Committee, said a legislative debate on Connecticut’s role in mitigating federal program cuts is almost a certainty next year. Some forms of temporary assistance may become ongoing. Others may end.
But Osten said state intervention in the healthcare arena likely will have many advocates. Residents “need to have some stability, and if they have to worry every year if they can afford health care, it’s going to be a problem.”
Lamont, a fiscal moderate hoping to win a third term this fall, has cautioned that Connecticut cannot backfill all federal cuts. But the governor also has compromised with his fellow Democrats in the legislature’s majority to approve several temporary assistance programs using the special state surplus fund.
Referring to all groups in need, the governor said this week, “We’re going take care of them as best we can.” But Connecticut also has existing job training, education and other programs to help at-risk residents reduce their need for public assistance — from any level of government — and Lamont added he hopes broader structural solutions can be found as an alternative to a temporary bailout whenever possible.
His Republican opponent, Sen. Ryan Fazio of Greenwich, said Connecticut cannot ask its taxpayers to solve all problems created by the federal government, adding the special surplus is “effectively a slush fund” that Lamont and the Democratic majority can use to support their constituencies.
“We need to prioritize vital services for Connecticut residents,” Fazio added, noting the special surplus fund was created outside of the formal budget and isn’t subject to normal fiscal caps.

name: New Hampshire Bulletin
title: New Hampshire is again at the center of the birthright citizenship fight
description: A federal courtroom in Concord has once again become the center of a national argument over who is an American citizen. On Aug. 11, the American Civil Liberties Union and other groups asked the U.S. District Court in New Hampshire to block President Donald Trump’s latest effort to restrict birthright citizenship. The filing came just […]
text:
The U.S. District Court, District of New Hampshire, Aug. 27, 2025. (Photo by Ethan DeWitt/New Hampshire Bulletin)A federal courtroom in Concord has once again become the center of a national argument over who is an American citizen.
On Aug. 11, the American Civil Liberties Union and other groups asked the U.S. District Court in New Hampshire to block President Donald Trump’s latest effort to restrict birthright citizenship. The filing came just days after the president signed two new executive orders targeting “birth tourism” and additional categories of children born in the United States.
New Hampshire’s role is not accidental. The original challenge to Trump’s 2025 birthright-citizenship order was filed here on behalf of several organizations, including New Hampshire Indonesian Community Support. After further litigation, advocates brought the nationwide class action known as Barbara v. Trump in the same federal court. The ACLU of New Hampshire’s case history traces how the dispute grew from Concord to the U.S. Supreme Court.
On June 30, the Supreme Court ruled in Trump v. Barbara that the president’s earlier order violated the 14th Amendment. The court held that children born in the United States to parents who are unlawfully or temporarily present are citizens at birth.
The administration has now returned with a narrower approach. The Aug. 6 orders focus on alleged birth tourism, certain foreign-government employees, immigration or citizenship fraud, and people classified as enemy aliens. The White House argues that these measures fit within exceptions recognized by the Constitution and the Supreme Court. The challengers contend that they are another attempt to accomplish by executive order what the court has already said the Constitution forbids.
That disagreement deserves attention even from people who strongly support tougher immigration enforcement.
Fraud is not protected by the Constitution. The federal government can investigate people who lie to obtain visas, prosecute immigration fraud, revoke immigration benefits where the law permits, and remove noncitizens who are legally removable.
But those powers do not necessarily answer the citizenship question.
A tourist may have concealed the purpose of a trip. A parent may have violated immigration law. Someone may even have committed serious immigration fraud. The harder constitutional question is whether misconduct by a parent gives the executive branch authority to change the citizenship of a child born in the United States.
The 14th Amendment says that “all persons born or naturalized in the United States, and subject to the jurisdiction thereof” are citizens. Historically, the exceptions to that rule have been narrow, most notably children of foreign diplomats who are not subject to ordinary U.S. jurisdiction in the same way as other people physically present here.
That distinction matters because citizenship at birth is not normally an immigration benefit that an agency awards after deciding whether a newborn’s parents behaved properly. It is a constitutional status that attaches at birth.
This is why the renewed litigation in New Hampshire is about more than immigration.
Presidents frequently respond to court decisions by changing policies. Sometimes a court identifies a defect and the executive branch legitimately repairs it. Sometimes a narrower rule truly does comply with the court’s reasoning.
But there is also a point at which repeated executive efforts to approach the same constitutional boundary raise a larger question: Who gets the final word about what the Constitution means?
Birth tourism is unpopular with many Americans, and commercial enterprises that coach foreign nationals to misrepresent their intentions or evade immigration rules deserve scrutiny. Congress and the executive branch have substantial tools to address those practices directly.
What is different is using parental misconduct to redefine a child’s constitutional citizenship.
That is what makes the latest filing in Concord worth watching.
New Hampshire has become an unlikely testing ground for a much larger principle: whether a president who disagrees with the Supreme Court’s interpretation of a constitutional guarantee can continue carving away at that guarantee through progressively narrower executive orders.
The administration may ultimately persuade the courts that some of its new categories fall within historically recognized exceptions. The challengers may persuade the New Hampshire court that the new orders merely repackage a constitutional theory the Supreme Court already rejected.
That question should be resolved through careful judicial analysis, not political slogans.
But one principle should remain clear regardless of the outcome: the federal government has broad power to enforce immigration laws, punish fraud, and protect national security. What it does not possess is unlimited power to redefine constitutional citizenship by executive order.
That is why a case now unfolding in a federal courtroom in Concord matters far beyond New Hampshire.
It is a test not simply of who becomes an American at birth, but of whether constitutional boundaries remain boundaries when a president wants to move them.

name: Maryland Matters
title: New collaboration unveiled on Conowingo Dam, as Maryland awaits federal OK on settlement
description: Rural county leaders, state officialsk and Constellation Energy representatives -- at odds a year ago over a proposed settlement of issues at the Conosingo Dam -- sat down Thrusday to discuss the settlement agreement in a new collaboration between the three.
text:
Cecil County administrator Dan Schneckenburger speaks to a group of county and state officials about the Conowingo Dam during the Maryland Association of Counties summer conference on August 13, 2026. (Photo by Christine Condon/ Maryland Matters)When it comes to the Conowingo Dam, tensions have cooled between leaders in rural Maryland counties and state officials, as well as dam owner Constellation Energy.
That fact was on display Thursday at the Maryland Association of Counties summer conference in Ocean City, when leaders from all three camps convened — this time to discuss a settlement agreement through which Constellation will pay $340 million for various environmental projects over the next several decades, in exchange for a crucial water quality certification from the state.
Initially, Republican officials in several rural Maryland jurisdictions, under the banner of the Clean Chesapeake Coalition, challenged that deal, as they were long aggrieved by sediment overflow events from the at-capacity dam, which is located in Cecil County. But state environmental officials persuaded them to drop their challenge.
Now, the Clean Chesapeake Coalition is no more, replaced by an advisory group with a far more collaborative tone, Cecil County Administrator Dan Schneckenburger said Thursday.
The Conowingo Dam on Oct. 2, 2025, the day that Maryland and Constellation announced a revised water quality certification for the hydroelectric dam, and a $340 million legal settlement. (Photo by Christine Condon/Maryland Matters)
“We pivoted to: Let’s try to work together,” Schneckenburger said. “We’ve always been on different sides of this issue — maybe not addressing it the way we wanted to see it addressed. So we ultimately said, ‘Let’s put together an advisory group, and we can work on implementation of the settlement.’”
But there’s still a possibility that a wrench could be thrown into Maryland’s plans.
The Federal Energy Regulatory Commission still must decide whether to sign off on Maryland’s certification, and whether to issue a new 50-year license for the dam to continue operating.
And in January, President Donald Trump’s (R) Environmental Protection Agency proposed a rule change, setting new limits on state water quality certifications, known as Clean Water Act Section 401 certifications.
State officials believe that their water quality certification —and the millions of dollars worth of accompanying environmental projects — is not in jeopardy, since they filed the license application with FERC last fall, well before the new draft rule was issued, said Adam Ortiz, deputy secretary at the Maryland Department of the Environment, which negotiated the settlement with Constellation and local riverkeepers. The state is expecting FERC approval next year, Ortiz told the audience.
“We’ve been checking in: ‘How’s it going over there? Are we ready to proceed?’ And there’s no indication that there’s going to be a problem,” Ortiz said during Thursday’s meeting. “That doesn’t mean that there’s not a possibility that is a problem.”
The new rule, if it moves forward, would limit states’ abilities to object to “non-point” pollution sources, focusing instead on “point sources” such as industrial sites that discharge wastewater directly into the environment, Ortiz said.
The dam is considered a non-point pollution source, since it does not generate pollution of its own but instead acts as a pass-through for contaminants flowing down the Susquehanna River, including farm fertilizers from upstream, and into the Chesapeake Bay.
Maryland Department of the Environment Deputy Secretary Adam Ortiz speaks to a group of county and state officials about the Conowingo Dam Thursday. (Photo by Christine Condon/Maryland Matters)
Federal officials believe that the new rule would protect “water quality while eliminating regulatory overreach that has imposed unnecessary burden on critical infrastructure projects,” according to documents released about the alteration.
For now, Maryland officials are moving forward with the settlement terms, and anticipating the results of a detailed U.S. Army Corps of Engineers study, which is likely to determine whether the overcrowded, 9,000-acre impoundment at the dam should be dredged.
Under the settlement deal, Constellation will pay $18.7 million into a fund that the state could use to dredge behind the dam if the Army Corps finds it a viable option. The state could also use the money for another environmental purpose if dredging it deemed inadvisable — or use it for further dredging study if necessary.
The Army Corps, in a recent presentation to the county leaders, described its effort, which will use a supercomputer to model the behavior of trapped sediments at various points in the river and under various conditions. It’s expected in June 2027.
“We’re very impressed with the scope of this study,” Schneckenburger said. “All of us on this county advisory group were like: ‘OK, we’re going to get a briefing, and it’s not going to be much.’ Well, it is a lot. We’re really doing a first-class evaluation.”
In the meantime, Constellation remains committed to continued clean-up of debris at the dam, including after storm events, said Maurice Simpson, director of government and regulatory affairs at Constellation.
“I know that this has been a long road. It has been contentious at times. But we’re very grateful for the partnership, the leadership of this coalition, holding us accountable, bringing us to the table,: Simpson said. “We are committed to continuing to be your partner in this.”

name: Wisconsin Examiner
title: Wisconsin prisons are struggling to improve mental health care
description: While consultants have recommended reforms to how Wisconsin addresses mental health in prison, the Wisconsin Department of Corrections reports obstacles in the way of many of the reforms, according to a document obtained by the Examiner. In Wisconsin’s adult prisons, nearly half of incarcerated people have a mental health diagnosis.  “We are seeing that more[...]
text:
The Waupun Correctional Institution, Wisconsin's oldest prison. The Department of Corrections has been facing obstacles in implementing a consultant's recommendations for improving mental health care in prison, where nearly half of those incarcerated have a mental illness diagnosis. (Wisconsin Examiner photo)The Wisconsin Examiner’s Criminal Justice Reporting Project shines a light on incarceration, law enforcement and criminal justice issues with support from the Public Welfare Foundation.
While consultants have recommended reforms to how Wisconsin addresses mental health in prison, the Wisconsin Department of Corrections reports obstacles in the way of many of the reforms, according to a document obtained by the Examiner. In Wisconsin’s adult prisons, nearly half of incarcerated people have a mental health diagnosis. 
“We are seeing that more and more individuals that come into our facilities are sicker than many of their peers in the community,” Jared Hoy, secretary of the Department of Corrections, said at a webinar in March. 
Hoy said he believes this is the result of a lack of affordable healthcare and mental health resources in the community. He said that people coming into the system may not have had consistent mental healthcare, meaning that clinicians are often trying to solve more advanced problems. 
“And we kind of become this safety net, to meet those needs that maybe have not been met in the community,” Hoy said. 
In November, the DOC released a report with recommendations for change to the prison system as part of its partnership with the consulting firm Falcon Correctional and Community Services, Inc. One recommendation involves keeping incarcerated people with a serious mental illness from ending up in restrictive housing — also known as solitary confinement — by instead sending them to alternative units if they commit a violation. 
The DOC reports that it is facing hurdles to implementing this proposal and some of the other recommendations for change to the prison system’s response to mental illness, according to a slideshow document received by the Examiner. 
Mental Health Director Kevin Kallas and Psychology Director Marlena Larson of the DOC presented the slideshow to a committee of the Wisconsin Mental Health Action Partnership, according to a member of MHAP who shared the document with the Examiner. The Department of Corrections did not respond to an inquiry about whether the agency produced the document. 
For some of the recommendations, the department indicated in the slideshow that it would need at least one of the following: additional staffing, material resources, new construction or remodeling, technology upgrades or significant changes to current policies or operations. Among the recommendations DOC said it needs more resources to address is sending people with a serious mental illness to a mental health unit instead of restrictive housing.
slideshow
Falcon’s 137-page report stated that the majority of its recommendations will require funding, and often budget approval. 
It’s unclear whether the DOC’s understanding of what’s needed to implement the report’s recommendations has changed since agency officials presented the slideshow in March. A department spokesperson said Kallas was not available for an interview and did not respond to further requests for comment. 
It’s also unclear how much progress the DOC has made so far on putting Falcon’s ideas into action. In November, DOC communications director Beth Hardtke told the Examiner that after receiving the recommendations in the report, the DOC immediately began implementing many of the changes.
The Examiner reported last month on the process of implementing reforms laid out in the contract between the DOC and Falcon, which the Examiner obtained in mid-May. 
Susan Franzen of the prison reform advocacy group Ladies of SCI questioned the DOC slideshow’s representation that it does not have the resources to implement a proposal about providing meaningful out-of-cell time and programming to people on clinical observation. Franzen argued the agency can make change with the resources it has. Incarcerated people can be placed on clinical observation for a deteriorating mental illness or a risk of physical harm to self or others. 
“Because that seems to be a go-to all the time — of, if we have to get them out of their cell, we need more staff, we need more ‘this,’” Franzen said. “No, you need to be more creative in your scheduling and think outside the box.”
The Wisconsin DOC and many other corrections departments use  suicide-resistant cells for at-risk patients without regard for the specific causes of the individual patient’s problems, the Falcon report says. The report says that these cells are designed to minimize self-harm, but they don’t guarantee safety or provide what’s needed to reduce the patient’s risk of self-harm and help them become more resilient. 
The report promotes providing these incarcerated people with meaningful time out of their cells, as well as personalized re-assessment, treatment and programming.
Focusing on the most severe needs
Nearly half of people incarcerated in adult prisons are identified as needing mental health services, as of May 2025 — a “much higher” rate than other state correctional departments, according to the Falcon report. 
In the slideshow, DOC indicated its intent to focus more on patients with “acute needs or recurrent problematic behavior.”
An “unsustainable” number of incarcerated people have to be seen by psychological services every six months, and this interferes with the more intensive care needed for patients with higher needs, according to discussions with prison staff about mental health that were cited in the Falcon report. The report advises that the agency remove people who no longer need the infrequent appointments from the caseload.
While the report’s discussion with staff about mental health doesn’t cover whether psychological services staffing problems are a factor, the DOC is facing a vacancy rate of 29% for psychological services staff. 
Tom Denk was released from prison in 2022 and is now co-president of 
ESTHER, an advocacy group in northeast Wisconsin that works on criminal justice issues. He said there are more people with mental and physical illnesses in prison than outside it, and that most people in prison need some sort of care. 
“And out here, there’s a shortage of providers, so we can imagine how much more of a shortage there is when basically almost everyone really needs that kind of thing,” Denk said. 
Suicide watch 
The Falcon report includes recommendations for protocols when an incarcerated person is under observation due to a deteriorating mental illness or a risk of physical harm to self or others. In the slideshow, the DOC indicated the agency could implement a proposal to replace small sleeping mats with suicide-resistant mattresses.
The agency labeled the following recommendations in red, indicating there are obstacles to implementing them:  

Moving clinical observation rooms out of restrictive housing and into more appropriate environments 
Providing meaningful out-of-cell time and programming
Reducing restraint use through increased use of one-on-one observation by staff
Analyzing why someone ends up in suicide observation and developing targeted interventions 

At one of Wisconsin’s oldest prisons, Green Bay Correctional Institution, almost three quarters of incarcerated people have a mental illness diagnosis, as of a fiscal year 2025 report. 
Former GBCI officer Jeff Hoffman told the Examiner that he was the assigned sergeant in the restrictive housing unit, and saw these issues “up close and personal.”
“Staff working on these units aren’t properly trained to understand and deal with these individuals,” said Hoffman, who left the prison in early 2023 after almost 23 years. “We were trained in the security aspect. Not mental health.” 
Hoffman added that staffing levels are a concern, with staff either being too few in number or too tired from extra hours of work, and that mental health is an issue for staff and healthcare workers as well as incarcerated people. 
DOC policy states that adult prisons must provide at least six hours of mental health training to security staff at the start of their employment, including for suicide prevention, symptoms of mental illness and proper response to incarcerated people with mental health problems. Adult prisons are required to provide training to new employees on preventing staff suicide.
Adult prison staff who have contact with incarcerated people take an annual update training in suicide prevention, and prisons are required to conduct quarterly drills simulating staff members’ response to a suicide attempt by an incarcerated person. 
Green Bay Correctional saw “a large number” of episodes of self-harming and/or disruptive behavior, according to GBCI’s annual report for fiscal year 2025. The report attributes this to the “unique features” of the incarcerated population there, which reportedly includes a high number of young men, many of whom have “poor coping skills with lengthy prison sentences.” 
Suicide attempts, self-harm behaviors and threats of self harm have historically led to a high number of placements of incarcerated people on observation at the prison, the GBCI report said. There was a “drastic upward trend” in these placements in fiscal year 2025, with 900 observation placements to date, the GBCI report said. 
Hoffman said that staff frequently have to move incarcerated people to suicide observation for making false claims that they are going to commit suicide. According to psychologist and jail suicide expert Lisa Boesky, incarcerated people might resort to this as an attempt to be moved out of a chaotic housing unit or away from a cellmate, for example. Meanwhile, the rise in suicide threats within the prison puts additional pressure on the system. 
Solitary confinement 
In the slideshow, a few proposals for reform of restrictive housing — also called solitary confinement — were labeled green, meaning that the department could significantly implement those ideas. 
The Examiner reported last year on how the Department of Corrections employs incarcerated peer specialists to mentor their fellow prisoners. The department said it could review how certified peer specialists are used in restrictive housing units and expand their role. The agency also indicated it could continue efforts to limit the amount of time incarcerated people spend in solitary.
Denk said he didn’t hear about peer support when he was in prison, but that it’s a great help to staff and incarcerated people.
“I wish there was even more of that, because when it comes to clinical staff, there’s only so many of them,” Denk said. 
The following solitary confinement proposals were labeled red, meaning there are obstacles to implementing them:

Providing each incarcerated person with at least two hours of time outside their cell each day. 
Tracking how much time incarcerated people spend outside their cells in real time, and tracking their participation in programming. 
Staff from different disciplines reviewing the “status, programming and needs” of people in solitary each week, instead of every 30 days. Under current policy, if a person has a solitary sentence of 60 days or more and a serious mental illness — such as schizophrenia or clinical depression — reviews must take place at least every other week.

Under another proposal marked red, the department would have a method to understand the root causes behind why an incarcerated person is repeatedly being placed in solitary confinement. Prison staff would develop individualized plans for these people to try to break the cycle. 
For example, if a person keeps ending up in solitary because they have received threats and fear the area of the prison where the general population of incarcerated people live, staff could work with the person to identify specific areas where they would feel safe, the Falcon report suggests.
Over two-thirds of people sent to restrictive housing for over 120 days were on the department’s lists of people identified to be receiving mental health services, the report found; 17% of people sent for over 120 days met the definition of having a “serious mental illness,” such as schizophrenia or clinical depression.
Incarcerated people can be placed in solitary due to safety concerns about them staying in the general population, but most placements are punishment for a violation.

name: Maryland Matters
title: Greens take on data centers, a literal hat trick by Kagan, Tablada retires, in political notes
description: The Green Party adds a prominent data center opponent as a campaign adviser, Sen. Cheryl Kagan literally pulls questions out of a hat for a quiz of election officials and longtime state and county environment official Horacio Tablada retires, in political notes.
text:
Taylor Frazier McCollum speaks out in Prince George's County against a proposed data center at the former Landover Mall on Sep. 10, 2025. (Photo courtesy Taylor Frazier McCollum)The Maryland Green Party is doubling down against data centers.
In a news release Monday, the party’s candidate for governor, Andy Ellis, announced he was bringing on a Prince George’s county anti-data center activist, Taylor Frazier McCollum, as a campaign organizer focused on the issue.
“I am thrilled she is joining our campaign to do this work,” Ellis said in the news release. “Data centers are the perfect issue for the Green Party right now because their rapid buildout shows the corruption of the two party system and how much we need a politics rooted in a Green Party vision: Peace, Justice, Democracy, and Ecological Wisdom.”
Ellis has called for a data center ban, along with the recision of any tax breaks already distributed to data centers.
Frazier McCollum grew up in the Landover area of Prince George’s County, where a data center was proposed at a former mall site. She started an online petition opposing the site, and became a leading voice against the projects in the county.
The Ellis campaign faces an uphill battle against incumbent Maryland Gov. Wes Moore (D) in heavily Democratic Maryland. Moore has not supported a moratorium. He has called on data centers to bring their own power, cover their costs, hire local workers and more.
Asked last week whether he would support a ban, Moore said: “I’ll work with the with the legislature to see exactly where we go with this. But I’ve been very clear about where my guidelines are.”
Moore faces a challenge on this issue from both sides. The Republican candidate for governor, Dan Cox (R) said in a July appearance on WBAL NewsRadio that he would also issue a moratorium if elected, citing concerns about rural lands being developed for power lines to serve data centers.
Hat full of tricks
Ahead of the 2026 general elections, and beyond, county officials face so many challenges to ensure that Maryland elections are safe and accurate, you could pull them out of a hat.
Sen. Cheryl Kagan used a hat to hold a list of elections-related topics to structure discussions with election officials during a Thursday panel. (Photo by Danielle J. Brown/Maryland Matters)
Sen. Cheryl Kagan (D-Montgomery) did just that for the elections-focused panel she moderated Thursday at MACo – literally pulling election-related topics from a cap and having State Administrator of Elections Jared DeMarinis and Baltimore County Elections Director Ruie LaVoie to give their thoughts on those issues during a Thursday panel at the summer conference of the Maryland Association of Counties. Each panelist only had 90-seconds to respond to the prompt.
When Kagan pulled a piece a paper out of a cap that simply said “voter rolls,” DeMarinis launched into a discussion on voter roll accuracy, and why some people who should not be able to vote might still be on the rolls.
“It’s a fundamental right which we are talking about,” DeMarinis said. “The ideas is that you don’t want to have a person take away your right based on improper evidence. So when you say, ‘This person has moved away or has died,’ we can’t just take your word on it.”
LaVoie there are checks and balances that “help us make sure that our voter rolls are up-to-date and accurate.”
“Part of the burden is the voter needs to make sure their address is updated, their name – if they get married – that that’s updated,” she said. “Because when we cancel a voter, that means a lot to me because that person no longer has the right to vote.”
The 90-second question-and-answer format skimmed the surface of staffing shortages, efforts in election transparency, accessibility at polling locations, and election misinformation.
In fact, DeMarinis decided to break the 90-second rule a few times to elaborate on important topics, such as the potential threat of federal immigration presence near voting locations, saying that state election officials are developing “contingency plans” if voters feel unsafe on Election Day.
“With all of the changing election environment, election officials have to be more adaptable than we’ve ever had to be,” LaVoie said.
Longtime environmental leader to retire
Horacio Tablada, a longtime environmental worker in state and county government in Maryland, announced his retirement Tuesday.
Horacio Tablada served briefly as acting secretary of the Department of the Environment. (Photo courtesy Maryland Department of the Environment)
Tablada worked for the Maryland Department of the Environment for 37 years, including a brief stint as Maryland Secretary of the Environment, replacing Gov. Larry Hogan’s (R) environmental secretary shortly before the end of the governor’s term. Before that, Tablada led the department’s Land Management Administration and then served as a deputy secretary.
Tablada retired from the state in 2023, and then led Baltimore County’s Department of Environmental Protection and Sustainability for the last three years.
In a statement issued by the county government, Tablada said he aimed to approach his roles with a focus on serving the public.
“Simply put, I treat every person with the same level of courtesy and respect whether they are a high-ranking official or an everyday person with an issue that’s important to them,” Tablada said in a statement.
Beginning Aug. 20, Tablada will be replaced by his deputy Brady Locher, a 14-year veteran of county government, who will serve on an acting basis.
In a statement, county officials applauded the longtime public servant, noting that, during his tenure with the county, he “expanded the County’s urban tree planting program to 2,500 trees annually, increased stormwater pond renovation projects, strengthened efforts to protect waterways and the Chesapeake Bay, and advanced planning for future dredging projects in County-owned navigation channels.”
Baltimore County Executive Kathy Klausmeier (D), recalled working with Tablada both during her time in the General Assembly and as county executive.
“During his career in service to Maryland, he has been committed to protecting our environment, and has worked with communities and businesses to find practical solutions,” Klausmeier said in a statement. “I appreciate his leadership, his dedication to public service, and everything he has done for Baltimore County and for the State.”

name: Kansas Reflector
title: How the air conditioning of Kansas homes is like an old-timey carnival trinket
description: I don’t remember many epiphanies that I had as a fourth grader. But I remember one. I was standing in the tiled hallway of my suburban elementary school while other kids squealed and raced past the open classroom doors. On this day, the entire campus — the gymnasium, the parking lot, the playground and the […]
text:
Memories of old-time carnival gave Friday columnist Eric Thomas a striking insight into the world's climate crisis. (Illustration by Eric Thomas for Kansas Reflector)I don’t remember many epiphanies that I had as a fourth grader. But I remember one.
I was standing in the tiled hallway of my suburban elementary school while other kids squealed and raced past the open classroom doors. On this day, the entire campus — the gymnasium, the parking lot, the playground and the classrooms — transformed into our annual carnival.
The parent-teacher association provided all of the classic games. There was a cake walk (always choose the red velvet). The music room had a contest in which lucky students went home with live goldfish (sorry, parents). And then there were dozens of games with penny trinkets as the prize.
My epiphany came from the finger trap.
Perhaps you remember these from your childhood, too. Or maybe your kids brought one home this summer from a friend’s birthday party. I won mine by flipping over the lucky rubber ducky floating in a kiddie pool that stretched out on the floor of the first grade classroom.
The finger trap was a green-and-pink woven tube, about 6 inches long. Slide a finger into each end — so innocent, simple and safe.
But try to escape by pulling your fingers away from one another and you will discover the trap. The harder you try to escape, the more stuck you become.
This truism came to me, a 10-year-old, as an epiphany. It was a physical logic puzzle with a counterintuitive solution. (In part, that is how the gimmick became known by another name that rests on stereotypes.)
The finger trap remains memorable because of its metaphorical lesson: Forcing things can make them worse.
That’s why I was thinking about finger traps last week — four decades later — on a summer vacation to Europe.
The continent has descended into a hot and stewy fever. The Swiss and Italians that we met spent equal time welcoming us and apologizing for the heat. The oppressive weather has triggered wildfires, likely killing more than 10,000 people and rewiring daily life.
As a Kansan, you’re nodding along. We have been baking too — just look at our run of 100-plus degree heat index readings.
What’s different for the Europeans is air conditioning — or rather, the lack of it.
In Kansas, more than 9 in 10 homes have air conditioning, according to 2000 data from the U.S. Energy Information Association. According to that data, 85% of Kansans have central air, while about 15% rely on individual window-style units. A more recent study from the U.S. Census Bureau estimates 98.6% of occupied homes in Kansas have air conditioning.
Almost every business provides AC, as well. When I visited the local Costco warehouse store today, enormous garage doors at the front of the store yawned wide open, sharing the football fields of cold air with the sizzling sidewalk outside.
The Shawnee Mission school district this week showed off its air-conditioned buses.
Also this week, I sat in the passenger seat with a fellow Kansan at the wheel. She explained how she loves setting the car’s air-conditioning to 58 degrees while opening the sun roof to let in the sun and fresh air.
“It’s the perfect mix,” she said.
I stared back blankly.
Then — being the ultimate buzz kill that I am — I described the suffering in Europe. During our days as tourists, our group discovered how draining the non-stop heat can be. Outdoor restaurants thirsted for more shade. Rolling AC units snaked through small boutiques. One winery became a de facto sauna. Climate change is transforming the quaint cobbled streets into skillets and clay houses into ovens.
As Kansas tourists, we realized how much we take for granted each day in America with our customary intermittent reprieves: when we step into a chilled shop or rest in an air-conditioned restaurant.
With high temps outside and no AC, there’s no relief in Europe.
As the New York Times reported during the heat wave, many Europeans resist air conditioning for both cultural and environmental reasons. Some balk at making air conditioning part of daily life. Others correctly worry that more air conditioning and its required energy use will further accelerate climate change.
Here in Kansas, we wrap our loving arms around AC. Our state uses almost 30% of our household energy consumption on air conditioning and the air handlers that are part of air conditioning units. This consumption ranks eighth in the nation out of the 50 states plus the District of Columbia, according to the Energy Information Association.
Besides air conditioning, other forms of household energy consumption in Kansas place us near the national average. For instance, we rank near the middle in energy use on TVs and related equipment and 40th in energy spent on clothes washers. But air conditioning is a Kansas household priority.
Kansas and Oklahoma expend essentially the same amount of energy on air conditioning as a part of their whole energy budget. Every other state bordering Kansas uses at least 12% less. Just to the north, Iowa uses more than 36% less on air conditioning. It’s clear that we Kansans could use less by dialing up the thermostat a few degrees.
To be fair, our summer temperatures on the plains likely fuel this consumption. Only southern states such as Texas, Nevada and Florida spend more of their household energy dollars on AC than Kansas. Arizona, for instance, spends a staggering 46.75% of household energy on air conditioning.
(Yes, I acknowledge my AC complicity in this. After all, while we were in Europe, our son was back in the Kansas suburbs in a five-bedroom house cooled just for him — and our dog.)
Why does the tug of war between climate change and air conditioning remind me of the carnival novelty finger trap?
As we Kansans struggle to escape the heat, we dial down the temps in our houses. But that air conditioning demands fossil fuel and accelerates the rise in global temperatures. Escaping this week’s heat makes it less likely that we will escape the larger, global heat wave of climate change.
Europe is heating more quickly than the rest of the world. The continent relies on the cooling effect of the Arctic ice sheet. The reflective white of the arctic is melting away day by day during the summer, replaced by the dark blue hue of the ocean, which absorbs heat.
As my friend and I hiked through a valley in Switzerland, we gawked at the color of the river surging past our gravel path. Even after years of hiking in the Colorado mountains, I had never seen a mountain stream so frothy and white. The river appeared almost chemically treated, like the slurry of detergent and water from a washing machine.
The milky appearance results from rapid glacial thaw, we learned. The glaciers in the surrounding mountain store rock “flour,” tiny bits of rock that eventually cloud the rivers.  This summer has been particularly damaging to glaciers, which have been melting at unprecedented rates and thereby making the rivers murky.
In short, Europe is disproportionately warmed by our Kansas air conditioning.
To make my tortured finger trap metaphor hold for worldwide climate change and air conditioning, we must add another wrinkle.
As I stood in the hallway, fourth-grade me realized that he only needed to relax to escape the finger trap. Expend less energy? A quick escape.
However, the collective action problem of climate change demands that everyone work together to escape together. We must have a coordinated effort that relaxes our habits, dials down our thermostats and burns less fossil fuel.
The alternative: that we end up stranded in a trap of our own making.
Eric Thomas teaches visual journalism and photojournalism at the William Allen White School of Journalism and Mass Communication at the University of Kansas in Lawrence. Through its opinion section, Kansas Reflector works to amplify the voices of people who are affected by public policies or excluded from public debate. name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: Federal grants to Indiana fell last year by more than $700M
description: When Medicaid is excluded from the results, the percentage drop in competitive federal grants grows to double digits.
text:
The U.S. Capitol building in Washington, D.C., amid fog on Tuesday, Dec. 10, 2024. (Photo by Jennifer Shutt/States Newsroom)The state of Indiana took in $733 million less from the federal government last year compared to the previous year, according to an analysis by award indexer Granted.
The grand total in the previous federal fiscal year — which ran from Oct. 1, 2024 through Sep. 30, 2025 — was $22.6 billion, down 3%.
That’s although Medicaid grants increased to $15.9 billion, up from $14.7 billion, according to the July analysis. Money for the low-income health insurance program made up 70% of federal receipts.
But when Medicaid is excluded from the results, the percentage drop grows to double digits. Competitive grants to Indiana fell to $6.7 billion, down 22% from the previous $8.6 billion subtotal.
‘Powerless’: Indiana families describe the toll of losing Medicaid access

The Biden-era Broadband Equity, Access and Deployment program represents the largest share of the $1.9 million drop, according to Granted founder Nathan Eagle, who tapped the federal government’s spending database for net financial assistance awards.
Indiana received $868 million in federal fiscal year 2024 to bring high-speed internet to every Hoosier. The line item for the one-time program then fell to zero in the 2025 fiscal year.
The Indiana Broadband Office, meanwhile, is busy putting the money to work. It has received approval to allocate about 40% to internet service providers in the first round of awards, according to a January newsletter, but there’s plenty left to do.
Funding for New Empowering Rural America also decreased to zero, from nearly $679 million. The program, another initiative of former President Joe Biden’s administration, offered loans and grants to rural electric cooperatives transition for renewable energy projects.
President Donald Trump’s administration has introduced a similar effort, Powering Affordable Reliable Technology, which will furnish partially forgivable loans for investment in biomass, geothermal or hydroelectricity, as well as energy storage systems. The program will begin accepting letter of interest next month, according to its website.
Indiana additionally netted $292 million less for the Epidemiology and Laboratory Capacity program, which is meant to strengthen the nation’s ability to detect, prevent and respond to infectious diseases.
That line item, Eagle cautioned, “is a net deobligation rather than a thin award year, so it reads as money coming back rather than money not arriving.”
The state chose not to participate in the Summer Electronic Benefit Transfer program to feed hungry schoolchildren, so that award dropped to zero, down from nearly $164 million. 	


Need to get in touch?
Have a news tip?


CONTACT US



Indiana has only participated once, in the first year of the initiative. The state passed $120 monthly onto 669,000 children in the summer of 2024, while schools and their cafeterias were closed. Officials opted out last summer, and have said they’ll do so again next summer, Fox59 reported.
Additionally, funding for the Drinking Water State Revolving Fund also decreased to about $77 million, down from $214 million.
There were some increases beyond Medicaid, however, including three transportation infrastructure program.
Nationally Significant Freight and Highway Projects grew to $143 million from zero, Federal Transit Capital Investment nearly cracked $142 million compared to just $8 million and Highway Planning and Construction landed at $1.4 billion, up from about $1.3 billion.
Grid Infrastructure Deployment and Resilience rounds out the top five, increasing to nearly $103 million from under $5 million.
