name: Florida Phoenix
title: Rich guys with racecars want to roar into Florida panther habitat
description: Do you like where you live? I sure do. I live in a house built 100 years ago. It’s got a porch swing out front. It’s in a quiet neighborhood with brick streets. You could say it’s my ideal habitat. And no, I don’t mean it’s in a subdivision called “The Habitat” — although, thanks […]
text:
The test track seen in this aerial photo was built outside Naples 40 years ago for the Ford Motor Co., but since then has been surrounded by preserved lands. Now a company called Hyper Club wants to turn the track and the 530 acres around it into a motorsports-themed development, smack dab in the middle of panther habitat. (Photo via Ralph Arwood)Do you like where you live? I sure do. I live in a house built 100 years ago. It’s got a porch swing out front. It’s in a quiet neighborhood with brick streets. You could say it’s my ideal habitat.
And no, I don’t mean it’s in a subdivision called “The Habitat” — although, thanks to the long Florida tradition of developers naming their project for what they’ve paved over, it could be.
No Florida creature has lost more of its habitat to such developers than our state animal, the Florida panther. Thousands of acres have been wiped out by new homes, stores, offices, mines, and even one college campus.
Now here comes one of the most egregious I’ve ever seen. A company called the Hyper Club LLC has proposed what Gulfshore Business describes as “a private motorsports club that would add driving circuits, resort-style amenities, and up to 100 residential units.”
“Racecar” is my favorite palindrome, even better than “radar.” But people with a lot of roaring racecars would be my least favorite neighbors.
That these folks would be doing regular recreations of “Days of Thunder” is not the big problem. The big problem is where it would happen: 530 acres smack in the middle of what’s left of panther habitat.
The proposed subdivision would center on an automotive test track built in the 1980s. Its neighbors include the Florida Panther National Wildlife Refuge, the Picayune Strand State Forest, the Fakahatchee Strand Preserve State Park, and Collier County’s own Dr. Robert H. Gore III Preserve.
Matthew Schwartz via subject.
“Think of all the work that went into assembling all those preserve properties,” said Matthew Schwartz, executive director of the South Florida Wildlands Association. “And they want to plop their project right in the middle of it.”
Schwartz has rounded up nearly 10,000 signatures on a petition to reject the project. But this is a worrisome time for environmental advocates like him because the Trump administration recently altered the definition of what constitutes “harm” under the Endangered Species Act.
Under the old definition, “harm” could include alteration or destruction of habitat for the species. Under the new one, the only way anyone can cause harm in the habitat is by killing or injuring the wildlife covered by the law — nothing more.
Imagine if someone drove a bulldozer through my porch swing and kept going through my living room, bathroom, and bedrooms, but didn’t touch me. To the administration, that would mean the bulldozer didn’t cause any harm.
“That’s even more ridiculous than the Hyper Club,” Schwartz said.
 Lord, Mr. Ford!
I’ve heard of Florida developments that were centered around golf, around flying planes, and even, believe it or not, around surfing. This is the first time I’ve heard of one focused on fast cars.
I’m picturing it as a place for people with such a need for speed they spend their nights watching “Ford vs. Ferrari” and “Grand Prix” and their days listening to driving songs like “Radar Love,” “Life Is A Highway,” and “Cadillac Ranch.” The air is filled with the smell of burning rubber and shouts of “Adrenaline is just fuel with feelings!” Vroom vroom!
Bruce Bond via screen grab.
“We saw this as probably the best potential site within Collier County, or in the Southwest Florida region, because it had so much history as an automotive test center,” one of the development partners, Bruce Bond, told the Naples Daily News.
About that history: The property belonged to the development company that bears the same name as the county, Collier. In 1985, it built the test track and sold it to the Ford Motor Co. as a winter alternative to Ford’s main test track in Michigan. Looking at the isolated spot they chose makes me echo Jerry Reed and say, “Lord, Mr. Ford!”
Sure enough, when I dug through old newspaper articles, I learned that the proposed test track unleashed a storm of controversy. It got built because the Florida chapter of the Audubon Society worked out a deal.
In exchange for Audubon dropping its objection to the track, the developer agreed to set aside 32,000 acres that would eventually be purchased by the federal government and become part of the Florida Panther National Wildlife Refuge.
In other words, the vast preserves around the track were to make up for the harm the track had done to panther habitat.
“Protection of this most sensitive piece of panther range is essential,” one Audubon official said at the time.
The track, built on just 53 of the 530 acres, includes a 1.2-mile handling course and a 2-mile straightaway. It hasn’t been in constant use since it was built. At one point, the track sat idle for two years.
The track was fenced off to keep wildlife out, but parts of the fence fell down, according to neighbors. You can see the result on a map the Conservancy of Southwest Florida compiled. It shows all the places around the track where radio-collared panthers have popped up.
A map of where panthers have popped up on and around the property. (Via Conservancy of Southwest Florida)
Amber Crooks via LinkedIn
“We do have a lot of concern about where [the development] is placed,” Amber Crooks of the Conservancy told me. “That’s 100% in the panther’s primary zone for adult breeding.”
Crooks pointed out that other species show up there too — bears, for instance, and the endangered bonneted bat. None of them would appreciate the noise, lights, and traffic produced by a residential development there, much less one full of racecars.
The hydrological alterations to the site and all the automotive pollution the Hyper Club generates could create problems too, she told me. Right next door, the state and federal government just spent more than $700 million turning 55,000 acres of the old Golden Gate Estates subdivision into the Picayune Strand flowway as part of the Everglades restoration project.
While all that restoration work has been going on, Crooks said, chunks of the nearby landscape are being developed into sprawling new communities with names like “Kingston” and “Bellmar.”
“You’ve heard of ‘death by a thousand cuts,’” Crooks said. “Now it feels like they’re lopping off whole limbs.”
 Airport sounds
Bond has repeatedly insisted that everyone’s concerns about panthers are overblown.
“There really is not a risk to the panther or even to other animals in the area,” he told WINK-TV. And he maintained a straight face, too!
When I have questions about panthers, the first person I usually call is Deborah Jansen. She was present at the first official panther capture in 1981, and she spent the following decades studying them as a biologist at the Big Cypress National Preserve.
Deborah Jansen with two panther kittens. (Photo via Ralph Arwood)
Although she’s retired now, Jansen was familiar with the controversy over the Hyper Club. Panthers, which tend to be nocturnal, will be disturbed by the increase in roaring engine noise and other residential activities, such as lights, she predicted.
“These are animals that tend to avoid humans,” she explained.
Jansen referred me to a friend of hers named Mac McCord. For the past seven years, McCord and his wife Lisa have lived on eight acres by the test track. The couple have put in a lot of work restoring their property, getting rid of exotic vegetation and planting natives galore, including 1,200 cypress trees.
Mac and Lisa McCord with their dog Xena, via Mac McCord.
They mounted motion-activated cameras all over their yard and snapped lots of pictures of panthers wandering through. One photo shows a female panther scratching at a tree trunk just 100 feet from the test track property line, McCord told me.
Before they bought their property, the McCords checked the zoning for the test track, which was classified as a “planned unit development.” Everything had been built there that was allowed under that zoning, so they weren’t worried about alterations.
When the test track was being used by auto manufacturers to check gas mileage, he said, “you really didn’t notice it.” Mostly the drivers would start a single car or truck off by going 70 mph and then let it coast to check its fuel usage.
But since Hyper Club took possession, he said, “now all you hear are high-powered vehicles. One weekend they had F1 race cars on the straightaway. It sounded like an airport.”
He and his wife have looked over the plans submitted by the Hyper Club, including its request for a change to the county zoning and a federal permit application to wipe out 142 acres of wetlands. The McCords are definitely opposed.
“This is just going to destroy everything we’ve worked for,” McCord said.
A female panther scratches a log on Mac McCord’s property 100 feet from the test track property, via McCord.
 Copacetic with nature
I spent some time on the phone this week with Bond’s partner in hyping the Hyper Club, car enthusiast John DeAngelis. To my surprise, he did NOT keep repeating Sonic the Hedgehog’s catchphrase, “Gotta go fast!”
“We’ve never had any panthers on that site,” he insisted, echoing Bond. He boasted that the test tracks’ nine-foot fence stops them. I didn’t tell him that panthers can jump 15 feet straight up in the air. It’s the way they surprise their prey, and the occasional unwary landowner.
Later in the conversation, though, he told me, “We’ve had a couple of bear encounters.” Then he told me they were working to make their plans “copacetic with nature.”
As you’ve probably guessed, DeAngelis is NOT a trained biologist. He’s co-founder of a Naples construction management firm.
Bond isn’t a biologist either. He’s a financier who, according to DeAngelis, is known as “the Father of the ETF,” which stands for “exchange-traded funds.” He’s apparently made big B-U-X with the E-T-Fs. Bloomberg says he’s a billionaire.
What they have in common is a love for racing, and I do not mean “running a weekend 10K.”
I asked DeAngelis what kind of vehicles he owns. He quickly rattled off a list with the names “Ferrari” and “Porsche” prominently featured. Then he added, with a chuckle, “I have a few cars that teenagers would think are cool.”
John DeAngelis via DeAngelis Diamond website.
Bond, who recently bought a home in Naples, belongs to a fast-car club in Chicago. He mentioned to DeAngelis his desire to start one in their neck of the woods, too. After all, it’s such a pain to rent out the Homestead-Miami Speedway for your birthday parties.
That led to their decision to buy the test track for $10 million and plan how to convert it, DeAngelis said. If they can get the zoning changed and the permits they need from state and federal agencies, he figures they could be up and running in 22 months. Pedal to the metal, man!
When I asked him to define what a finished Hyper Club would be like, he said, “It’s got like a golf course feel, but it’s for drivers.”
But it’s not for permanent residents, he said. The 100 homes they would build would serve as temporary quarters for visitors, well-heeled folks who own powerful cars and want to unleash all that horsepower.
He told me the development would feature shielded lights to prevent nighttime glare and that it would wipe out only 30% of the natural landscape, allowing 70 % to remain intact. But then he told me their vision for the future, and it’s more bad news for panthers.
DeAngelis told me so many people from Miami and Tampa would be attracted by the excitement of racing that the Florida Department of Transportation would have to build a new Interstate 75 exit ramp there.
He didn’t seem to comprehend that that would destroy even more panther habitat. That would not be copacetic with nature.
I don’t want to say that DeAngelis and Bond have more dollars than sense, but that thought did cross my mind. They’re quickly learning that they’ve riled up a big chunk of the public.
As we were talking, DeAngelis kept telling me how he and Bond are being sensitive to “the adjacencies.” Finally, I stopped him and asked what that word meant. Turns out that’s what he and Bond call the nature preserves next door to where they want to build.
Hey wait, that’s what they can call their development: The Adjacencies! It’s perfect.
But if they’re smart, they will instead withdraw their proposal and sell the property to some agency to preserve it for the panthers. That, to me, would make for a perfect finish.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: CT doesn’t have a childcare crisis. It has a childcare policy crisis
description: If Connecticut truly wants to solve its childcare crisis, it must stop treating family childcare as an afterthought.
text:
Every few months, we hear the same message: Connecticut has a childcare crisis because there aren’t enough providers.
As someone who has spent more than three decades in early childhood education, I see it differently.
The crisis isn’t simply a shortage of providers. The crisis is that Connecticut is making it nearly impossible for small family childcare homes and independent childcare centers to survive.
The people writing these policies often talk about expanding access to early childhood education. They celebrate Universal Pre-K and the Early Childhood Endowment as investments in children. Those goals are admirable. Every child deserves access to a quality early education.
But what isn’t being discussed is the cost these policies are imposing on the small programs that have been serving Connecticut families for generations.
Family childcare providers and small centers have always operated on a delicate balance.
Infant care is extraordinarily expensive to provide. State regulations require very low child-to-teacher ratios, and babies need constant, individualized care. The true cost of caring for infants is often greater than what families can reasonably afford to pay. For years, providers made that work because toddlers and preschoolers helped balance the books. Tuition from older children offset some of the financial loss of infant care, allowing programs to serve children from infancy until kindergarten.
That balance is disappearing.
As more preschool-aged children leave independent providers for publicly funded preschool classrooms, the revenue that once kept small programs financially healthy disappears. The mortgage doesn’t disappear. Insurance premiums don’t disappear. Food costs don’t disappear. Utility bills don’t disappear.
Licensing requirements certainly don’t disappear.
The infants are still there, but the financial model that made caring for them possible is collapsing. Providers are left with impossible choices: dramatically increase infant tuition, stop accepting infants, reduce services, or close their doors entirely.
That isn’t expanding childcare. It’s reshaping it in a way that threatens the very programs many working families rely on.
At the same time, Connecticut continues to place increasing regulatory burdens on small providers.
No one is arguing against health and safety standards. Children deserve safe, nurturing environments, and providers should absolutely be held accountable for protecting them. But family childcare is not a commercial childcare center. It is someone’s home.
Treating those two settings as though they are identical is like comparing apples to oranges. Large centers have administrative staff, office managers, maintenance personnel, and dedicated budgets for compliance. 
Most family childcare providers have one person doing everything. They are the director, the teacher, the cook, the janitor, the bookkeeper, the curriculum coordinator, the maintenance department, the finance office, the marketing department and the parent liaison.
And after working 10- or 12-hour days caring for children, they go home —not to another job, but to their own families.
Yet they are increasingly expected to comply with the same layers of documentation, administrative requirements, and regulatory oversight as organizations with multiple employees and entire administrative teams.
The expectations continue to grow, but the resources do not. 
Perhaps nowhere is this more apparent than during licensing inspections. In a family childcare program, inspectors may examine virtually every room in the home —even rooms children never enter.
Providers have described receiving violations involving their own children’s bedrooms, private closets, or other personal spaces that are completely inaccessible to enrolled children. Parents naturally ask: if children never enter those rooms, how does inspecting them improve children’s safety?
The same pattern appears in paperwork. A parent forgets to write a ZIP code. A signature is missing a date. A line is left blank.
These are administrative mistakes. They are frustrating, but they do not place children in immediate danger. Yet they can still become licensing violations attached to the provider’s record.
Over time, many providers begin to feel that inspections have shifted away from collaboration and toward finding technical mistakes.
Whether or not that is the state’s intent, many providers experience inspections less as opportunities to improve and more as exercises in searching for deficiencies. That creates a culture of anxiety rather than partnership.
Providers spend days preparing paperwork instead of preparing learning experiences. They worry that a harmless clerical error will outweigh years of exceptional care.
Many describe feeling that they are constantly waiting for the next violation instead of being recognized for the thousands of things they do right every single day.
The result is predictable. Experienced providers are retiring early. Others are choosing not to renew their licenses. Some are deciding the emotional and financial burden simply isn’t worth it anymore.
Every time one of those programs closes, Connecticut loses far more than a few childcare spaces. It loses trusted relationships. It loses flexible care for working families. It loses overnight care, evening care, mixed-age learning, and neighborhood programs that cannot easily be replaced.
Ironically, as policymakers celebrate expanding preschool opportunities, many communities are quietly losing infant and toddler care —the very care that working parents struggle most to find.
If Connecticut truly wants to solve its childcare crisis, it must stop treating family childcare as an afterthought. It must recognize that small providers are not miniature childcare centers. They are small businesses operating inside family homes.
Policies should reflect that reality. Regulations should focus on meaningful health and safety, not technical paperwork errors that have no impact on children’s well-being. Oversight should be rigorous, but it should also be collaborative, practical, and proportional.
Most importantly, Connecticut must recognize that every new mandate has a cost. For a large organization, it may mean another administrative task. For a family childcare provider, it may be the final reason they decide to close.
If we continue down this path, Connecticut won’t lose childcare because providers no longer care. We’ll lose childcare because the people who have dedicated their lives to caring for children have finally decided they can no longer afford —financially or emotionally— to keep doing the job.
Michelle Gagliardi writes on behalf of the Connecticut Family Child Care Coalition.

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Iowa Libertarians nominate new candidates for lt. governor, 3rd District
description: The Iowa Libertarian Party nominated new candidates Wednesday for lieutenant governor and 3rd District to appear on the 2026 ballot. The Libertarian Party of Iowa’s State Central Committee met to officially nominate two candidates to appear in two races where previous Libertarian candidates had been taken off the ballot by the State Objections Panel. Charles[...]
text:
Charles Aldrich was nominated Aug. 12, 2026, as the ,Libertarian Party of Iowa's candidate for lieutenant governor. He is shown here as a 2024 candidate for Iowa's 4th congressional district, speaking at the Des Moines Register's Political Soapbox at the Iowa State Fair Aug. 11, 2024. (Photo by Robin Opsahl/Iowa Capital Dispatch)The Iowa Libertarian Party nominated new candidates Wednesday for lieutenant governor and 3rd District to appear on the 2026 ballot.
The Libertarian Party of Iowa’s State Central Committee met to officially nominate two candidates to appear in two races where previous Libertarian candidates had been taken off the ballot by the State Objections Panel. Charles Aldrich, who ran in 2024 as a Libertarian candidate in the 4th Congressional District, will be the party’s lieutenant governor nominee, running with gubernatorial candidate Nicholas Gluba. Jacob Heard, an attorney who previously ran for Iowa House District 44, became the nominee for Iowa’s 3rd Congressional District.
The two candidates were nominated with unanimous support at the meeting to replace two candidates who ended their campaigns — and who faced court challenges to their ability to appear on the 2026 general election ballot.
In June, the State Objections Panel said the previous 3rd District Libertarian nominee, Marco Battaglia, did not qualify for the ballot because the name he used as a candidate was too different from his legal name, Mark T. Anderson. The panel also ruled Gluba’s ticket, which included Jules Cutler as the lieutenant governor nominee, did not qualify because Cutler had not submitted an affidavit of candidacy for lieutenant governor by the June 2 deadline.
The candidates disputed the objections — Cutler said she was told by a secretary of state’s office she did not need to submit the paperwork, and Battaglia had appeared on the ballot using his non-legal name in previous elections — and eventually challenged the panel’s decision in court. A Polk County District Court judge upheld the panel’s decision in a July ruling.
While both Gluba and Battaglia initially said they would challenge the decision, Battaglia ended his campaign due to a medical emergency, and Cutler later announced she would also withdraw as a lieutenant governor candidate.
The state Libertarian Party nominated Aldrich to replace Cutler on the gubernatorial ticket. Speaking to the committee Wednesday, Aldrich spoke about his experience running for office in previous elections, and said he was “ready to run as lieutenant governor.”
Iowa Libertarian Party Chair Stephanie Berlin said the party was moving forward with the new nomination to ensure the voters who supported Gluba’s campaign had their voices represented at the ballot box in 2026.
“I got to asked the question, why are we doing this?” Berlin said. “Eight thousand and change people signed petitions to put Gluba on the ballot. It’s a huge miscarriage of justice to disenfranchise that many Iowans. In order to run as a gubernatorial candidate, we must have lieutenant governor candidate. So, this will hopefully close that gap for us to move forward.”
Heard was also nominated to replace Battaglia at the meeting. Berlin said while Heard was not able to attend the meeting and did not deliver comments,  he had told her he was “ready and happy” to run for the seat.
The candidates nominated at the Wednesday meeting could still face challenges to their qualifications. Challenges to the two newly nominated candidates would also be reviewed by the State Objections Panel.

title: Democratic gov nominee David Crowley shows party unity, while Tiffany turns his attention to him
description: In a show of unity following a divisive and chaotic primary, Democratic gubernatorial nominee David Crowley met for breakfast with the losing candidates in the primary along with lieutenant governor nominee Sarah Godlewski and top Wisconsin Democrats. Democrats are competing to hold onto the governor’s office against Republicans U.S. Rep. Tom Tiffany and Dav[...]
text:
In a show of unity following a divisive and chaotic primary, Democratic gubernatorial nominee David Crowley met for breakfast with the losing candidates in the primary. (Photo by Baylor Spears/Wisconsin Examiner)In a show of unity following a divisive and chaotic primary, Democratic gubernatorial nominee David Crowley met for breakfast with the losing candidates in the primary along with lieutenant governor nominee Sarah Godlewski and top Wisconsin Democrats.
Democrats are competing to hold onto the governor’s office against Republicans U.S. Rep. Tom Tiffany and David Varnam and hope to flip control of the state Senate and Assembly in November.
U.S. Sen. Tammy Baldwin, U.S. Rep. Mark Pocan, Democratic Party of Wisconsin Chair Devin Remiker, Joel Brennan, state Sen. Kelda Roys and state Rep. Francesca Hong gathered with the nominees at a cafe in Middleton. Crowley sat at the head of the table next to Godlewski and Senate Minority Leader Dianne Hesselbein (D-Middleton).
The elected officials and losing primary candidates departed the breakfast while Crowley and Godlewski addressed reporters. 
Crowley, who in July restarted his campaign 10 days after he dropped out, said Gov. Tony Evers, who endorsed him, was his campaign’s “secret weapon.”
“He has a lot of trust and he’s done a lot of work. He’s one of the very few governors that we know has continued to deliver year after year,” Crowley said, adding that Evers’ message and experience helped as well. “We’re not going to win this race focusing on ideology alone. It’s about focusing on Wisconsin values. We cannot allow Washington politics to creep up into our own backyard.”
Godlewski, who won her primary and introduced Crowley, said national politics are a “clear distinction from that guy, Tom Tiffany, who is an election denier, career politician who only cares about the wealthy and corporations.”
“That’s not who Wisconsin is, and that’s not who we are going to elect this November,” Godlewski said
Hong did not speak to reporters, but released a statement congratulating Crowley around the time of the breakfast.
“This campaign was not about getting one person into office. It is about building a movement for permanent affordability and a government that puts working people first. Our movement is strong, and the work isn’t done,” Hong said. “I fully support [Crowley] and look forward to working with him to defeat Congressman Tiffany in November.” 
Crowley also criticized Tiffany and promised to ensure that northern communities, many of which are represented by Tiffany, are not forgotten.
“We’re going to make sure they’re a part of this process and we can lend their voices to the solutions. We know no one has been listening to them across this state,” Crowley said, adding that Tiffany has not been hearing the concerns of his constituents and is only loyal to President Donald Trump. 
Tom Tiffany in Deforest
Tiffany, who has Trump’s endorsement, met with supporters in the afternoon at a bar in Deforest alongside lieutenant governor nominee David Varnam and attorney general nominee Eric Toney.
“Well, it appears that Thanksgiving may be safe this year,” Tiffany said, referring to the late-in-the-race controversy over a post made by Hong about canceling the holiday. The joke got  laughs in the bar. 
Ahead of the election, Republicans spent millions on ads to help boost Hong’s campaign, hoping she would become the Democratic nominee. 
In his remarks Wednesday, Tiffany tried to tie Crowley to Hong.
Tom Tiffany (left), who has Trump’s endorsement, met with supporters in the afternoon at a bar in Deforest alongside lieutenant governor nominee David Varnam (right). (Photo by Baylor Spears/Wisconsin Examiner)
“There is not a dime’s worth of difference between the candidates that ran for the Democrat,” he said. “David Crowley will do the same stuff that Francesca Hong would have. He just didn’t say it.”
Tiffany also criticized Crowley for his leadership of the state’s largest county, including a lapse in health insurance coverage for Milwaukee County employees and the projected future budget deficits that the county faces, despite  Crowley’s talking point that he has only signed balanced budgets as county executive. 
Tiffany was also asked whether Crowley’s nomination changes his approach to the race. 
“It’ll be the same stuff, the same socialism, whether it’s David Crowley or anyone else,” Tiffany said. “You know, he was in the race, then he was out of the race, and then he was asked to get back in the race. He didn’t know whether he wanted to be governor or not. I want to be the governor of the state of Wisconsin, and we’ve had a plan from the very beginning that we’ve been sharing.” 
The Republican ticket will include Jay Schroeder, who won the GOP primary for secretary of state. Schroeder wants to eliminate the Wisconsin Elections Commission and put it back under the control of the secretary of state. 
Tiffany did not disavow the idea of eliminating the Wisconsin Elections Commission, which was created under former Gov. Scott Walker. 
“We’ll assess that after I am elected,” he said. “It should be easy to vote but hard to cheat, right, and we’re counting on that happening here with this election here in November.” 
Republican Party of Wisconsin Chair Brian Schimming told reporters that it is a new race and that he wouldn’t put much stock in polling or primary results. 
“Democrats spent the last several months fighting with each other. It took them three candidates to finally get to one that they could push through the primary, and the fact is that the last four or five months has been all about stopping Francesca,” Schimming said. “So it’s a new race.” 
Schimming added that “a primary winner will get a bump, you know, so I’m not going to be surprised by anything I see in the polls in the next week or two.”

Data centers and young voters 
In the Democratic primary for governor, Hong built much of her campaign on motivating young voters and leveraging her stance on AI data centers. She supported a one-year moratorium. Both Crowley and Tiffany addressed how they would approach the issue Wednesday. 
Asked about winning over Hong voters, Crowley said young people should have a seat at the table. 
“They need to be a part of creating the strategy and making sure that you know they have opportunities as well,” Crowley said. “Young people don’t feel that they can look into their future right now. When the average home-buying age is 40 years old, when right now they’re looking at data centers and artificial intelligence taking the jobs in the future, and so we have to focus on making sure that we’re lifting up their voices and protecting what they believe needs to be protected.”
Tiffany said that his message to young voters is “we’re going to make life more affordable for you.” He said he would do that by cutting property taxes by eliminating Evers’ 400-year veto that gives school districts authority to bring in more revenue by raising taxes, and by cutting regulations on homebuilding to make it more affordable to build a home. 
“I understand the frustration. I mean, I have three daughters in their twenties, and it’s not easy to make ends meet at this point,” Tiffany said. 
David Crowley, who in July restarted his campaign 10 days after he dropped out, said Gov. Tony Evers, who endorsed him, was his campaign’s “secret weapon.” (Photo by Baylor Spears/Wisconsin Examiner)
Crowley, who has said he supports banning nondisclosure agreements for data center projects, did not offer his support for a moratorium on AI data centers when asked by a reporter.
“We have to focus on making sure that we have accountability with these data centers,” Crowley said. “They have to pay their own way, they need to pay for their own infrastructure and they need to bring their own new clean energy. I am committed to working with the state Legislature to make sure we have as many guardrails as possible.”
Tiffany said he would end subsidies for data centers that were signed into Wisconsin law under Evers, work to ensure that utility rates don’t go up and would ban nondisclosure agreements. 
“Well it sounds like David Crowley will give a blank check to data centers,” Tiffany said. “They do not need to be subsidized by us, the taxpayers, and we’re gonna make sure that people’s electricity rates do not go up. We’re going to make sure that we have full transparency.”

name: Nebraska Examiner
title: Judge hears arguments in cases challenging two new Nebraska parties
description: Attorneys in court got into the weeds of a law meant to stop a candidate or party from deliberately confusing voters.
text:
Nebraska Deputy Solicitor General Zach Pohlman, representing  Nebraska Secretary of State of Bob Evnen, presents his case during a hearing at the Lancaster County Courthouse on Wednesday, Aug. 12, 2026, in Lincoln. (Photo by Kenneth Ferriera-Pool/Lincoln Journal Star)LINCOLN — Attorneys for Nebraska’s two major parties and two potential new political parties in court Wednesday got into the weeds of a law meant to stop a candidate or party from deliberately confusing voters.
A Lancaster District Court judge could decide whether the two new parties appear on the fall ballot. 
In their suit against the America First Party, the Nebraska GOP lawyers asked Judge Darla Ideus to give Nebraska Secretary of State Bob Evnen more authority to reject a party or candidate. In a second case, attorneys for the Nebraska Democratic Party and the national Working Families Party sought to compel Evnen to remove the Nebraska Working People Party because its name is too similar to the Working Families Party.
America First Party lawyers argued Wednesday that the law is clear that objections can be made against parties with similar names, but that no other party in Nebraska has “America First” in its name. In the other case, Nebraska Working People Party lawyers contended that only official parties in the state can object to another party. 
Meanwhile, Evnen, a Republican, is arguing through his attorney, Zachary Pohlman, that he should be able to reject the America First Party but not the Nebraska Working People Party because state Democrats objected too late.

The deadline to object was seven days after July 15. His arguments echo the Nebraska Supreme Court’s ruling on the candidacy of former Democratic Senate candidate Cindy Burbank, which overruled Evnen’s decision to remove her because Republicans had filed their objection too late. 
“The idea that somehow the Nebraska Republican Party owns the phrase ‘America First’ or owns conservative issues or conservatism itself is wrong,” Jason Grams, the attorney for the America First Party, said in court Wednesday. 
In its lawsuit, the GOP has called John Cartier’s effort to establish the America First Party as “political sabotage.” They point to his connection to Legal Marijuana Now Senate candidate Mike Marvin and to legal fees he received from Dan Osborn’s 2024 Senate campaign.
Both major-party officials have noted the sponsors of the new parties as grounds for their suspicion. 
State Democratic Party Chair Jane Kleeb has accused U.S. Sen. Pete Ricketts of being behind the effort to establish the Nebraska Working People Party.  
Registered Democrat Robin Richards is the sponsor of the Nebraska Working People Party. She lost as a write-in candidate in Legislative District 12 earlier this year; after her loss, she endorsed incumbent Republican state Sen. Merv Riepe for the general election.
Christopher Dodge, the attorney for both the Working Families Party and the Democratic Party, said their argument is straightforward because of what the law says. He said the Nebraska Working People Party is trying to mislead voters by using the Working Families Party’s decades of “credibility” with voters nationwide. 
But lawyer Dallas Jones, representing the Nebraska Working People Party, argued that only parties registered in Nebraska can object. 
Dodge also challenged Evnen’s reading of the timeline in which someone can object to a party name – saying that he “very conveniently chooses the earliest one, despite its lack of precedential or textual grounding.” Pohlman, Evnen’s lawyer, wrote in a brief that the seven-day deadline to object would start after the last day to turn in signatures for a new party — which was July 15.
The Democratic Party filed its objection Aug. 9. Evnen rejected it on Aug. 11. 
Ideus declined a request to have the cases heard together. Both cases have hearings next week at different times. An emergency injunction delayed certification of both parties until Aug. 20.

name: Alaska Beacon
title: Dunleavy introduces new LNG tax-concession bill as special session nears end
description: Gov. Mike Dunleavy on Wednesday introduced a new natural gas pipeline bill that he characterized as a compromise between conflicting philosophies on oil and gas taxes that he wants lawmakers to pass during the ongoing special session. The new bill would nearly eliminate property taxes that would be charged on the operator of a yet-to-be-built […]
text:
Glenfarne CEO Brendan Duval speaks on May 21, 2026, at the Alaska Sustainable Energy Conference in Anchorage, while Gov. Mike Dunleavy listens. Glenfarne is the company now proposing to build a liquefied natural gas project to commercialize North Slope's stranded reserves. Dunleavy on Wednesday introduced a new bill proposing tax concessions to encourage construction of the LNG project. (Photo by Yereth Rosen/Alaska Beacon)Gov. Mike Dunleavy on Wednesday introduced a new natural gas pipeline bill that he characterized as a compromise between conflicting philosophies on oil and gas taxes that he wants lawmakers to pass during the ongoing special session.
The new bill would nearly eliminate property taxes that would be charged on the operator of a yet-to-be-built gas pipeline. Dunleavy and Glenfarne, the Texas-based investment company that is now the main sponsor of the gas pipeline project, have argued in recent months that such concessions are a major requirement for the project to be built.
The special session is due to end in less than two weeks. Lawmakers are still evaluating the proposal, but on Monday members of the Senate’s bipartisan majority expressed reticence to make quick decisions on a gasline bill.
Dunleavy’s new bill contains a concession to a tax previously sought by the Senate majority. It would also impose a small corporate income tax on certain private oil- and gas-producing corporations. Those companies, also known as S corporations or pass-through corporations, are currently exempted from such taxes in Alaska law. For now, the main corporation that would be affected is Hilcorp, a privately held Texas-based company that operated the Prudhoe Bay field and other North Slope assets that used to be owned by BP. Several legislators view Hilcorp’s exemption from corporate income taxes as a loophole that should be closed.
The governor said legislators should pass his bill in what is now the third special session he has called on the subject.
“I have never been in favor of new taxes on Alaska’s producers, and I still am not,” Dunleavy said in a statement. “This bill is a compromise that removes a significant barrier to moving the gas line forward. Given the robust discussion and work that has already gone into this bill, I am hopeful the legislature can swiftly pass a bill that will help the AK LNG project get the financing it needs to start construction as soon as possible.”
The 2% tax rate Dunleavy proposed on petroleum-producing S corporations is significantly lower than the lower than tax rates  legislative leaders have previously proposed, which went up as high as 9.4%.
 

Doug Fletcher, a Glenfarne employee, prepares to close down the company’s “Build The Line” booth at the Fairbanks Golden Days street fair on June 25, 2026. The campaign aims to convince state lawmakers to pass tax concessions that Glenfarne argues are needed to make the LNG project a reality. (Photo by Yereth Rosen/Alaska Beacon)
 

	Officials and energy companies in Alaska and elsewhere have been pushing since the 1970s — even before oil began flowing through the Trans Alaska Pipeline System — for a second pipeline to deliver the North Slope’s vast but stranded natural gas resources to markets. None of the plans has been economically feasible, even though politicians at various points over the past decades declared that construction was imminent.
Alaska natural gas pipeline dreams stretch over half a century

The current iteration of the gas commercialization plan calls for a pipeline to run about 800 miles from Prudhoe Bay to tidewater at Cook Inlet, where the product would be liquefied for shipment by tanker to markets. The estimated price tag is $65 billion to $70 billion, according to legislators.
A bill considered during an earlier special session, House Bill 381, proposed to grant the property tax concession, but it also included several conditions for any LNG sponsor to meet, such as timeline assurances, labor protections, alternative sources of state revenue and required financial support of local school districts.
The bill also included a bracketed income tax with rates up to 9.4% on petroleum-producing S corporations such as Hilcorp — significantly higher than the 2% that Dunleavy is now proposing.
That bill passed the state Senate narrowly last month but was rejected by the House.
One lawmaker on Wednesday said Dunleavy’s new bill, just like any oil tax legislation, should not be rushed.
“It would be wildly irresponsible to pass complex oil and gas legislation without due diligence to understand the consequences,” said Rep. Zack Fields, D-Anchorage.
Leaders of the state Senate majority caucus, in a statement on Monday, expressed skepticism about the need for any further concessions to help Glenfarne’s plan.
“For more than fifty years, Alaskans have worked to bring our gas to market, and every member who has served in this building shares that goal. The Senate has done its part in good faith, passing two bills that would let this project move forward while protecting the people we answer to,” Senate President Gary Stevens, R-Kodiak, said in the statement. “A decision of this scale will outlast all of us, and it deserves to be made with care rather than in haste. We are ready to evaluate the project further once the producer, Glenfarne, and the Administration bring us the numbers this year. These are Alaska’s resources, and they must work first and foremost for Alaskans.”
The special session is scheduled to end on Aug. 25.
